co.berkshire.sections.0.bodyMarkdown:
**Vehicle:** the public equity portfolio = Berkshire Hathaway's Form 13F-HR (CIK 1067983), filed 15.05.2026 for the period ending 31.03.2026. The total 13F value is **$263.10bn** (90 lines in the filing, aggregating into **29 positions / ~26 issuers** — Alphabet, Lennar and Liberty Live are each disclosed in two classes). This is only part of the group: besides public equities, Berkshire owns operating businesses (BNSF, BHE, GEICO + the insurance float) and a cash position.

The full value of public equities on the balance sheet (10-Q, the equity securities note) at **31.03.2026 = fair value $288.0bn against a cost basis of $84.6bn** (net unrealised gains of $203.4bn). At 31.12.2025 fair value was $297.8bn. In addition there are equity-method investments (Kraft Heinz, Occidental common) of $20.0bn and Occidental preferreds ($8.5bn liquidation value) plus warrants.

#### Concentration and breakdown
- **Top 2 (Apple + AmEx):** 39.4% of the 13F ($103.7bn).
- **Top 5 of the public 13F:** 67.1%. In the 10-Q's wording the five largest positions = **61% of all equities on the balance sheet** at 31.03.2026 (65% at 31.12.2025) — concentration fell on sales and on Alphabet's growth.
- **Listed vs unlisted:** the whole 13F portfolio is listed equities. What has no market quote in the group are the operating businesses (BNSF, BHE, GEICO, Marmon, Precision Castparts, See's, OxyChem and others), which sit outside the 13F.
- **Geography:** the 13F portfolio is almost entirely US. The only non-US exposure in the 13F is Chubb (domiciled in Switzerland). Outside the 13F are the five Japanese trading houses (see below).
- **Themes:** (1) payments/financials — AmEx, BAC, Capital One, Ally, Moody's (Visa/Mastercard sold); (2) energy — Chevron + Occidental at ~13% despite the Chevron cut; (3) consumer staples — Coca-Cola, Kraft Heinz; (4) technology — Apple steady, Alphabet growing.

co.berkshire.sections.1.bodyMarkdown:
Source: the 13F-HR of 15.05.2026 (period ending 31.03.2026) against the 13F-HR of 17.02.2026 (period ending 31.12.2025). Greg Abel's first reporting quarter as CEO. The number of 13F positions fell from **39 to ~26 issuers**; the 13F value fell from **$274.2bn to $263.1bn**.

#### Purchases and additions
| Issuer | Action | From → to (shares) | Size | Vehicle |
|---------|----------|----------------------|--------|---------|
| Alphabet (A+C) | INCREASED ~3x | 17.85M → 57.83M | ~$16.6bn of fair value at 31.03 | 13F |
| Delta Air Lines | NEW | 0 → 39.81M | ~$2.65bn | 13F |
| New York Times | INCREASED ~3x | 5.07M → 15.15M | to ~$1.27bn | 13F |
| Lennar (A+B) | INCREASED | 7.23M → 10.34M | +43% | 13F |
| Macy's | NEW | 0 → 3.04M | ~$0.05bn | 13F |

#### Sales and reductions
| Issuer | Action | Size | Note |
|---------|----------|--------|---------|
| Chevron | TRIM −35% | 130.2M → 84.4M | ~$8bn taken off |
| Constellation Brands | TRIM −95% | 13.0M → 0.63M | almost liquidated |
| Nucor | TRIM −39% | 6.41M → 3.91M | |
| DaVita | TRIM −5% | 31.76M → 30.10M | under the buyback agreement |
| Bank of America | TRIM −1% | 517.3M → 513.6M | minimal |
| **COMPLETE EXITS (16 positions)** | EXIT | ~$14bn in total | Visa, Mastercard, UnitedHealth, Amazon, Domino's, Aon, Pool, Heico, Charter, Lamar, Allegion, Diageo, Liberty Latin America, Liberty Media, Atlanta Braves Holdings and others |

A reconciliation note: some lines show 'exit+new' in the diff because the filer renamed a CUSIP/class — the actual stakes did not change. Chevron's 'exit+new' is a genuine 35% trim alongside a change in the issuer's name in the form.

#### The AI lens (where it is real)
Tripling Alphabet is the only direct AI expression in the public portfolio: a bet on Google Cloud / TPUs / Gemini and data centres. Apple (on-device AI) is not being added to. The AI lens does not stretch over the insurance/infrastructure core (BNSF, BHE, GEICO); the one genuine AI/power point in the operating block is BHE's capex cycle driven by data-centre demand (see 'The view on the market').

#### Dry powder
- **Cash + T-bills (net of payables for unsettled T-bill purchases, from the 10-Q MD&A):** **$373.5bn** at 31.03.2026. This is the 10-Q's own canonical measure.
- **The gross figure of $397.4bn** = $51.5bn of cash + $339.3bn of T-bills (insurance & other) + $6.6bn of cash (railroad/utilities/energy). The difference from $373.5bn is the deduction of $17.2bn of unsettled T-bill purchases and segment aggregation. Both figures are correct and reconciled line by line with the 10-Q balance sheet; the canonical figure for this dossier is $373.5bn net.
- The buyback floor: Berkshire does not repurchase shares if doing so would take cash + T-bills below **$30bn**.

#### Deal status
As at 28.06.2026 no pending M&A has been announced. The largest deal of the period — OxyChem — closed on 02.01.2026 (see 'Future deals').
There is no pending M&A as at 28.06.2026; the largest deal of the period was OxyChem (closed 02.01.2026)

Sources: the FY2025 results press release (28.02.2026), the Q1 2026 10-Q, Abel's letter.

#### Operating earnings by segment (Berkshire-defined, after tax, $M) — Q1 2026 reconciled with the 10-Q
| Segment | Q1 2026 | Q1 2025 |
|---------|--------:|--------:|
| Insurance — underwriting | 1,717 | 1,336 |
| Insurance — investment income | 2,679 | 2,893 |
| BNSF (railroad) | 1,377 | 1,214 |
| Berkshire Hathaway Energy | 1,114 | 1,097 |
| Manufacturing, service & retailing | 3,199 | 3,060 |

Operating earnings (Berkshire-defined, annual series): **FY2024 $47,437M (a record) → FY2025 $44,486M** (−6.2% YoY, on insurance underwriting). Q1 2026 underwriting +28.5% YoY.

#### GAAP net earnings (including investment gains/losses — volatile) — reconciled with the press release
- **FY2024: $88,995M; FY2025: $66,968M** (−24.8% YoY, under pressure from an $8,255M OTTI on Kraft Heinz/Occidental and smaller investment gains).
- **Q1 2026: $10,106M** (including an after-tax investment loss of $1,240M).
- Realised gains on sales: **FY2025 $17.8bn** after tax (FY2024 $79.6bn).

#### Book value per share and equity — reconciled with the 10-Q
- **Berkshire shareholders' equity: $727,181M** at 31.03.2026 (from $717,419M at 31.12.2025). Total shareholders' equity (including NCI): $729,450M.
- The Class A share equivalent is ~1,437,928 at 31.03.2026 → **book value per Class A ≈ $505,951**; per Class B ≈ **$337** (1/1500).
- **Berkshire pays no dividend** (the last was in 1967); the entire return comes through book value growth and buybacks.

#### Float and combined ratio
- **Float: $176.9bn** at 31.03.2026 (up ~$500M from 31.12.2025; it was $176bn at end-2025 per Abel's letter, against $171bn in 2024). The cost of float is negative (underwriting is profitable).
- **The P&C group's FY2025 combined ratio: 87.1%** (confirmed by Abel's letter as a primary source). GEICO made the main contribution to the lower combined ratio.

#### Liquidity and debt — reconciled with the 10-Q
- **Cash + T-bills (net): $373.5bn** (31.03.2026).
- Debt at Berkshire + BHFC (excluding BHE/BNSF): **$42,835M**; BNSF: **$23,560M** (not guaranteed by Berkshire); BHE: separate (not guaranteed by Berkshire). Structurally low leverage at the holdco level.

#### Benchmark
Per-share market value compounding 1965–2025 = **19.7%** against the S&P 500 TR at ~10.5% (NOT a DCF — a historical company disclosure).
Q1 2026 net earnings $10,106M (including a $1,240M after-tax investment loss)

co.berkshire.sections.3.bodyMarkdown:
| Risk | Level | The specifics at 31.03.2026 | What triggers it |
|------|---------|--------------------------|----------------------|
| **Concentration (top 1)** | Medium | Apple = 21.99% of the public portfolio ($57.8bn); the top 5 = 61% of all equities | A 30% fall in Apple → ~$17bn of unrealised loss, ~2.4% of equity |
| **Energy concentration** | Medium | Chevron + Occidental ~13% of the portfolio; OXY equity method + $8.5bn of preferreds | Oil sustainably below $50/bbl → further OTTI on OXY (as already happened in FY2025) |
| **Cash drag / reinvestment risk** | High | $373.5bn in T-bills; rates are falling | Short rates below 3% → ~$10bn+ a year of forgone investment income; underperformance vs the S&P |
| **Key person (post-Buffett)** | Medium→High | Q1 2026 is Abel's first full quarter as CEO; Buffett is Chairman | A badly received Abel deal → a re-rating of the 'Buffett premium' and a wider holdco discount |
| **Insurance catastrophe / cycle** | Medium | Float $176.9bn; the company has said it will write less P&C 'for a period of time' | A large catastrophe year → a combined ratio above 100% and a hit to underwriting earnings |
| **Single asset (Kraft Heinz)** | Low→Medium | KHC after the 2025 OTTI; Abel called the bet 'disappointing' | A further fall in KHC → a new OTTI write-down |
| **Regulatory (BHE/utility)** | Medium | BHE is a regulated utility; PacifiCorp wildfire liabilities of ~$2.9bn cumulatively (per the 10-Q/transcript) | A large wildfire verdict above the reserves → a hit to BHE earnings |
| **Leverage** | Low | Berkshire/BHFC debt of $42.8bn against equity of $727.2bn; BHE/BNSF are not guaranteed by Berkshire | Structurally low leverage — not a systemic risk |
| **Recession sensitivity** | Medium | BNSF, the MSR segment and GEICO are cyclical | A US recession → lower BNSF volumes and MSR profits; partly offset by T-bill income |
| **AI disruption (indirect)** | Low | Direct AI exposure is small (Alphabet ~6.3%); the core is insurance/infrastructure | Not material to the thesis; the AI lens is real only through Alphabet and BHE's power cycle |
co.berkshire.sections.3.deep.0.body: Berkshire has two kinds of risk: **structural** (cash drag, Apple concentration, succession) and **operational** (catastrophe losses, wildfire, a BNSF downturn). The structural ones are slow but they set the share price. The operational ones are volatile, but Berkshire is better equipped than anyone to absorb them. A P/B of 1.45x says the market is pricing a smooth transition, but not a mega-deployment.

co.berkshire.sections.4.bodyMarkdown:
#### Open-market purchases by senior management (Form 4, SEC primary) — the strongest signal in this section

Two genuine open-market purchases (transaction code 'P') in 2026, both the first since the change of CEO. These are purchases with personal money — not grants, not charity.

- **Greg Abel (President & CEO, from 01.01.2026) — bought 21 Class A shares on 04.03.2026** at $725,210–$733,300 a share, **~$15.31M in total** (average ~$728,970). After the transaction he holds **249 Class A shares directly** plus 2,289 and 74 Class B shares through the Gregory E. Abel Revocable Trust. This is Abel's first open-market purchase as CEO, a day after the annual letter was published (28.02.2026) and with BRK.A in the upper third of its 52-week range. A signal of the new CEO's conviction in his own shares at full market price. (Form 4, accession 0001193125-26-092556, filed 05.03.2026; 18 code 'P' lines dated 04.03.2026, reconciled line by line against ownership.xml.)
- **Michael J. O'Sullivan (Senior Vice President, General Counsel & Secretary) — bought 536 Class B shares on 06.05.2026** (483 @ $467.13 + 53 @ $470.22), **~$250.5k in total** (average $467.44). After the transaction he holds 663 Class B shares in a living trust (+422% on the position). The purchase came two days after the Q1 10-Q was filed. Cross-validated by openinsider.com (+536 @ $467.44, +$250,545). (Form 4, accession 0001193125-26-209661, filed 06.05.2026.)

No direct open-market sales (code 'S') of Berkshire shares by insiders were recorded in Form 4s in 2026. Buffett's and Jain's activity is limited to conversions and charity (below).

#### Conversions and charitable transfers (not a market signal)
- **Warren Buffett (Chairman; director):** on 18.05.2026 he converted **25 Class A shares → 37,500 Class B** (code 'C') and the same day gifted (code 'G', price $0) **two tranches of 18,646 Class B each**; on 22.05.2026 he gifted 160 Class B. On 17.03.2026 he gifted 2 Class A shares. These are the annual charitable transfers to family foundations and the Gates Foundation, converted from A to B before transfer — structurally not market sales, and they affect neither the free float nor the signal. (Form 4 accessions 0001193125-26-232543, -239886, -116315.)
- **Ajit Jain (Vice Chairman, Insurance):** on 27.03.2026 he gifted (code 'G') 22 Class B shares; the remainder is 330 Class B directly plus family trusts and the Jain Foundation (17 + 38 + 50 Class A shares). A small volume, and charitable. (Form 4 accession 0001728451-26-000001.) For comparison, in 2025 Jain did sell on the open market: on 08.08.2025, −2,000 Class A @ $464.73 (~$929k) and on 26.09.2025, −15,000 Class A (gift/OE). In 2026 Jain has made no market sales.
- **Charlotte Guyman (director):** on 14.05.2026 she gifted 574 Class B (code 'G'). Not a signal.

#### Buybacks (the key capital-allocation signal)
- **Q1 2026: a token resumption after a year's pause.** **$235M** was bought back — **33 Class A shares and 431,462 Class B shares** at a P/B of ~144%. The 10-Q describes it as 'relatively minor amounts of treasury stock'. (Reconciled against the 10-Q statement of equity and cash flow.) The contrast with Abel's $15.31M of purchases from his own funds is instructive: the company barely buys the shares at this price, yet the CEO takes them personally — a signal that Abel sees the shares around intrinsic value, but not far below it.
- The pace over time: 2021 ~$27bn → 2022 ~$8bn → 2023 >$9bn → 2024 ~$3bn → **2025 $0 → Q1 2026 $0.235bn**.
- The buyback programme has no limit or expiry; it is barred if cash + T-bills fall below $30bn. Buybacks are done at prices below a conservative estimate of intrinsic value (Abel's letter) — the token volume in Q1 2026 confirms that the shares are not considered materially undervalued.

#### The company's actions as an insider of other holders (Form 4 for DaVita / Liberty Live)
Berkshire is a >10% shareholder in DaVita and Liberty Live, so it files Form 4s for their shares; these disclose real sales:
- **DaVita (DVA):** on 29.01.2026 it sold **1,658,480 shares @ $120.56** (~$199.9M); on 01.05.2026 it sold **1,220,376 shares @ $149.84** (~$182.9M). That is **~2.88M shares** over the period; the balance after 01.05 is 28,880,209 shares (13.9M of them through GEICO, 15.0M through the BNSF/Berkshire pension plans). This is the execution of a buyback/standstill agreement with DaVita (Berkshire sells back into DVA's buyback, keeping its stake below the threshold). It is consistent with the −5% DVA trim in the 13F. (Form 4 accessions 0001193125-26-033900, -207021.)
- **Liberty Live (Series C):** between 06 and 16.01.2026 it sold **330,518 shares** at $81.22–$84.04 (~$27.4M) in a series of code 'S' transactions. (Form 4 accession 0001193125-26-054947.)

#### Dividend / issuance / spin-offs
- **Dividends:** none paid (since 1967); the board reviews the policy annually. The entire return is book value growth plus buybacks.
- **Share issuance:** no new shares have been issued to pay for deals (OxyChem's ~$9.5bn was paid in cash). The Class A share equivalent is falling through the buyback.
- **Debt issuance:** yen senior notes of ¥272.3bn (~$1.7bn, 424B5 of 14.04.2026, maturing 2029–2056) — funding for the yen positions in the trading houses, non-dilutive to shareholders.
- **Berkshire preferreds:** 1M authorised, 0 issued. **Spin-offs:** none.

**How to read this for hold/add/cut:** the combination of 'the CEO buying $15.31M with his own money at full price + a buyback near zero + zero open-market sales of shares by insiders in 2026' is a moderately bullish insider signal at management level, but not a signal of deep undervaluation. The Buffett/Jain transfers are charity — discount them. The DVA/Liberty Live sales are the technical execution of agreements, not a change of thesis.

co.berkshire.sections.5.bodyMarkdown:
The closest comparables are insurance-centric holdcos with an investment portfolio: Markel (MKL), Fairfax Financial (FFH), Loews (L). All FY2025.

| Metric | Berkshire | Markel | Fairfax | Loews |
|---------|-----------|--------|---------|-------|
| Combined ratio FY2025 | **87.1%** (P&C group) | ~93% | ~93.0% | 95.1% reported / 91.7% underlying (Q3 '25) |
| Float / insurance leverage | $176.9bn | considerably smaller | growing | CNA-centric |
| P/Book | ~1.45x | ~at or below book | ~at or below book | a holdco discount |
| BVPS growth | 19.7% CAGR 1965–2025 | methodical compounding | +21% YoY FY2025 | steady |
| Dividends | 0% | 0% | pays | pays |
| Cash/dry powder | $373.5bn (a record) | moderate | deployed more actively | moderate |

The Markel/Fairfax/Loews peer metrics are taken from the agents' drafts and secondary sources/Q3 data rather than from each peer's FY2025 10-K line by line — see the gaps.

**The implication for hold/add/cut:**
- **Underwriting:** Berkshire leads on combined ratio (87.1%) — the best-quality insurance core in the group (supports hold/add).
- **Valuation:** Berkshire is more expensive than its peers on P/Book (~1.45x against ~1x and below) — a premium for scale and the balance sheet, but a smaller margin of safety on price (which limits the case for adding aggressively).
- **Book growth:** Fairfax has the strongest annual BVPS growth (+21% in FY2025); Berkshire has the best long-run CAGR but a lower current pace because of the cash drag.

co.berkshire.sections.5.deep.1.body:
**The advantage:** $176.9bn of float at a negative cost — free leverage for investing. A combined ratio of 87.1% in FY2025 against a 10-year median of 93.0%. Only Fairfax is comparable on discipline, and at a fifth of the scale.

**The evidence:** 60+ years of profitable underwriting. Float has grown from $88bn (2015) to $177bn (2026). The cost basis of the top 5 positions is $24.5bn against $2.5bn a year of dividends (a yield on cost of ~10%). Berkshire's CAGR is 19.7% against the S&P's 10.5%.

**Why it is hard to replicate:** the scale of the float plus the 'we never sell a good business' brand lets it buy whole companies on terms unavailable to PE. With $34bn of float, Fairfax cannot do $10bn+ deals.

**The honest trade-off:** $397bn of cash at ~3.7% = ~$25–30bn a year of forgone income. Succession: three key people on the way out. Apple at 22% = concentration. BHE wildfire — potentially $8bn+. A P/B of 1.45x is around the norm, not cheap.

**The conclusion:** below a P/B of 1.2x, add aggressively. Above 1.7x without a mega-deal, take profits.

co.berkshire.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
**Who writes the canon.** The figures come from CEO **Greg Abel's first annual letter of 28.02.2026** (CEO from 01.01.2026; Buffett is Chairman) and **Warren Buffett's farewell letter of 10.11.2025**. For the first time in 60 years the canonical document is not signed by Buffett.

**Management's edge thesis (verbatim, Abel's letter).** *"Berkshire is a unique conglomerate, intentionally designed to allocate capital rationally and efficiently. Insurance is our core, and we also hold substantial investments in businesses across many other sectors."* The goal is *"maximizing the growth in Berkshire's intrinsic value per share over the long term."* The advantage is structural: insurance float plus a fortress balance sheet.

**Capital allocation rules (the verbatim list from Abel's letter):**
- Invest in businesses with durable advantages that management fully understands;
- Partner with managers of high integrity who think like owners;
- Avoid businesses capable of damaging Berkshire's reputation;
- *"Act quickly and concentrate our capital in a few high conviction ideas"*;
- *"Maintain discipline and let compounding unfold."*

Asset priority: *"We will always aim for ownership of productive businesses over U.S. Treasuries."*

**Buybacks:** *"We will buy back Berkshire shares when they trade below our estimate of intrinsic value, conservatively determined."* The fact: only **$235M** was bought back in Q1 2026 (10-Q) — a signal that management does NOT consider the shares materially undervalued.

**Dividends:** none are paid while every dollar retained can create more than a dollar of market value; the board reviews the policy annually.

**The layers of the strategy:**
1. **Insurance (the core).** GEICO + National Indemnity + reinsurance. Float of **$176bn** at end-2025 (from $171bn in 2024). The 2025 combined ratio = **87.1%**. Ajit Jain runs insurance; the CEO is designated Chief Risk Officer.
2. **Operating businesses.** BNSF, BHE, industrials (Precision Castparts, Marmon, Lubrizol), building products (Clayton), services/retail (NetJets, Pilot, McLane). The model is decentralisation: *"There are no layers of management and no allocated goals or targets set by Berkshire."*
3. **The equity portfolio** — *"an integral extension of our insurance operations and capital base"*; the concentration will remain: *"This concentrated approach will continue, with limited activity in these holdings."*
4. **Cash + treasuries** = $373.5bn net (10-Q) — *"our dry powder."*

**Recent deals as an illustration:** OxyChem (~$9.5bn) and Bell Laboratories (rodent control; *"We only wish it had been ten times bigger"*).

Dividends only if $1 retained fails to create more than $1 of value (none since 1967). Abel has formalised the foundational values for the first time: a partnership culture, decentralisation, integrity, financial strength, capital discipline.

co.berkshire.sections.7.bodyMarkdown:
**The basic macro stance.** Management makes no market forecasts and holds liquidity as an option on dislocations. The signal on valuations is negative: Buffett (10.11.2025): *"Because of Berkshire's size and because of market levels, ideas are few – but not zero."* That explains the record cash and its status as a net seller of equities.

**What they believe:**
- A long-term bet on the US (Buffett: *"America will come back and so will Berkshire shares"*).
- Insurance as a structurally winning business given discipline.
- **The AI lens is real ONLY in energy:** BHE is entering an investment cycle *"driven by rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence computing"* (Abel). At the annual meeting on 02.05.2026 Abel said data-centre demand is ~8% of BHE's peak consumption in Iowa; *"not going to do AI for the sake of AI."*

**What they avoid:**
- Overpaying in an expensive market (minimal buybacks).
- Buying another Class I railroad: on the Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern merger Berkshire stated that *"it is not interested in acquiring one of the other Class I railroads."*
- A soft insurance market: *"we will write less property and casualty business for a period of time."*
- Kraft Heinz is named plainly: *"Our investment in Kraft Heinz has been disappointing... our return has been well short of adequate."*

**What they are watching:**
- The insurance cycle: softening prices in P&C/reinsurance.
- Retention at GEICO after the 2022–2024 rate increases.
- Wildfire risk (BHE/PacifiCorp): cumulative estimated losses of ~$2.9bn (per the transcript/10-Q).

co.berkshire.sections.9.bodyMarkdown:
*What follows is analyst commentary, NOT management quotes. Not a valuation, and no DCF.*

**The main event: a change of pen and Abel's first portfolio shake-up.** The Q1 2026 13F is the first canon under Abel's full control: the portfolio has been compressed from 39 to ~26 positions, with 16 complete exits. The signal: Abel will rotate more actively than Berkshire's reputation as an 'eternal holder' implied. The trimming is mainly out of financial/payments and 'incidental' positions.

**Specific moves and how to read them:**
- **Apple ($57.8bn, 227.9M shares) — HOLD.** The share count has been untouched for three quarters; the fall in value is market-driven. Abel's letter confirmed Apple as core. Do not expect sales.
- **Alphabet (~6.3% combined, ~$16.6bn) — ADD/conviction buy.** The ~3x increase is the quarter's largest purchase and the only meaningful AI exposure in the equity portfolio. Confirmation of the thesis would be a further addition in the Q2 13F; if it is frozen, it was a one-off bet.
- **Chevron (−35%) vs Occidental (untouched) — a reallocation within energy:** they are cutting the public Chevron and holding the strategic OXY (the preferreds plus the just-purchased OxyChem). The energy bet is concentrating in the OXY complex.
- **Complete exits** (Visa, Mastercard, UnitedHealth, Domino's, Aon, Pool, Amazon, Charter, Lamar, Allegion, Heico, Diageo and others): a clear-out of the 'tail' of small Combs/Weschler positions and locking in gains in an expensive market — consistent with the *"ideas are few"* thesis. The quick exit from UNH signals low conviction.
- **New/added** (Delta, Macy's, Lennar +43%, NYT ~3x): probably the deputies' work rather than Abel's signature; the scale is small relative to $263bn.

**The effect on the holding:**
- **$373.5bn of net cash against a $235M buyback** is the loudest signal: management is not buying back the shares (it does not consider them cheap) and is not finding large deals (the market is expensive). The near-term catalyst for growth is operating earnings and underwriting, not the buyback or a mega-deal.
- **The insurance cycle has turned to softening** — lower premiums in 2026 remove part of the underwriting upside (a combined ratio of 87.1% in 2025). The effect on the equity is moderately negative, but the discipline ('saying no') protects the downside.
- **The AI/power lens is the one genuine growth point** in the operating block: BHE's capex cycle driven by data-centre demand. A long story (regulated returns), not a quick win.

**Signals for the BRK decision:**
- **HOLD / accumulate on dips.** Buffett gave the marker: the shares have fallen ~50% three times in 60 years — historically entry points. The trigger to ADD: a significant correction plus management resuming buybacks.
- **Downside triggers (trim/watch):** (1) a change in the Apple position for the first time since 2024; (2) a sharp rise in buybacks WITHOUT a fall in the price; (3) large BHE wildfire settlements above $2.9bn; (4) a combined ratio above ~95% against a softening backdrop.
- **Key-person risk is reduced but not zero:** Buffett remains Chairman and holds his 'A' shares until shareholders have 'got used to' Abel; CFO Marc Hamburg's departure is planned.

**Operating businesses with no market quote (valuation not disclosed):** BNSF, BHE, GEICO, Precision Castparts, Marmon, NetJets, Pilot, Clayton, See's, OxyChem — valued only on cash flow / margin / segment earnings.
co.berkshire.sections.9.deep.0.body: At a P/B of ~1.45x Berkshire is fair value, not cheap. The bet is not on a discount but on three things: (1) $397bn of cash — the largest dry powder in the world; when Abel deploys it, pricing power returns; (2) $177bn of float at a negative cost — a competitive advantage that grows every year; (3) operating earnings of $44.5bn, steadier than any peer's. Fourteen quarters of net selling — Berkshire is waiting for the market to offer a price.
co.berkshire.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essentials
co.berkshire.sections.9.deep.1.body:
**Cash drag:** $397bn at ~3.7% while the businesses earn 10%+ ROIC. Forgone income of ~$25–30bn a year. Cash is 31.7% of the company's value.

**Succession:** Buffett is 95, Combs has left, Jain is 74. Abel is an operator, not a stock picker. Who runs the portfolio? Formally Abel + Weschler. So far the market believes in a soft landing — the P/B has not fallen.

**Apple at 22%:** concentration. The embedded capital gains tax is a deferred tax liability of $48.4bn. It cannot be sold without a 21% tax hit.

**BHE wildfire:** $54–55bn of claims. An accrual of $2.9bn. Potentially ~$8bn. Not fatal for Berkshire, but it weighs on BHE's unit economics.

**Scale:** at a $1tn market cap it takes a $50–100bn+ deal to move the needle. Mathematically there are only a handful of such targets.

co.berkshire.summary: Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A / BRK.B) is the world's largest insurance conglomerate. Insurance float of $176.9bn funds its investments at a negative cost: a combined ratio of 87.1%. It owns BNSF, BHE, GEICO, Precision Castparts and dozens of other businesses; operating profit is $44.5bn. The public portfolio of $263.1bn is concentrated in Apple (22%). Since 1 January 2026 the CEO has been Greg Abel (63), with Warren Buffett (95) staying on as Chairman. A record $397bn of cash (31.7% of the value) is both a strength (dry powder) and a risk (a drag of ~$25bn of forgone income a year).
co.berkshire.tagline: Berkshire is valued close to its own historical norm (P/B ~1.45x against a 10-year median of ~1.42x) on a record $373.5bn of cash and a token $235M buyback — a price-neutral HOLD signal with buying on dips; the key nodes for the decision are Greg Abel's first full quarter as CEO, the cash drag as rates fall, and the best insurance core in the peer group (a combined ratio of 87.1%).

co.berkshire.verification: Re-confirmed line by line against primary sources: (1) the whole 13F portfolio — parsed from the SEC XML, with all 29 positions, share counts, values and weights reconciled to the dollar, totalling $263.10bn; (2) the 10-Q balance sheet — shareholders' equity $727,181M, net cash + T-bills $373.5bn (and the gross reconstruction of $397.4bn), float $176.9bn, equity securities fair value $288.0bn / cost $84.6bn, Q1 2026 segment operating earnings, the $235M buyback (33 Cl A + 431,462 Cl B), OxyChem ~$9.5bn, the OXY/KHC stakes; (3) FY2025 net $66,968M, operating $44,486M, OTTI $8,255M — from the press release; (4) the 87.1% combined ratio, float and the Japanese houses at $35.4bn (stakes of 9.7–10.8%) — from Abel's letter; (5) the BRK.B price/P-B — from aggregators. Three FACTS errors were corrected: the $297.8bn equity portfolio refers to 31.12.2025 (at 31.03.2026 it is $288.0bn, cost $84.6bn); the 18.1% CAGR was out of date (19.7% vs 10.5% is correct); the buyback was refined to $235M; and the missing second Liberty Live line ($0.46bn) was added. The 'Insider activity' section was reinforced with primary Form 4 data (Abel's and O'Sullivan's purchases, Buffett's and Jain's conversions/gifts, and the DVA and Liberty Live sales were all reconciled). Overall confidence is high: every load-bearing number is confirmed by primary SEC filings and IR documents. The residual gaps (FY2025 segments, some peer metrics) do not affect the decision-grade conclusions.

BlackRock reported Q2 2026: assets under management (AUM) of $15.34T (+22% YoY), net inflows of $191.7bn in the quarter and a record $321bn for the half year. Organic base fee growth was +10% over the year. iShares passed $6T of AUM for the first time — doubling in 3 years.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.0.why: A record quarter: $191.7bn of inflows, $7.08bn of revenue (+31%) and an adjusted margin of 45.9%. It confirms the fee machine is growing at a double-digit rate.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.1.deta: large DC plans need a shift in legal and regulatory practice
An option, not a fact: inflows will only follow once regulation lets large plans hold private assets. If it opens, it is the deepest channel for new fees; keep it in view as an ADD trigger.

CFO Martin Small confirmed on the Q2 2026 call that 2026 will see the launch of the first LifePath target-date fund holding private markets assets (private credit plus private equity), in partnership with Great Gray Trust. Today the average target-date fund holds no private markets at all.

co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.3.deta: The return is measured rather than aggressive: capital priority goes to reinvestment in private markets, not to maximising the buyback. Sensible for growth; accelerating the buyback into a drawdown would be a strong ADD signal.
From Q1 2026 the quarterly dividend was raised 10% to $5.73 a share (~$22.92/yr). The 2026 buyback plan was lifted to $2bn, at a quarterly pace of up to $550m ($450m was repurchased in Q2).
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.3.titl: Dividend +10% to $5.73/quarter; the buyback plan raised
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.3.why: A 17th consecutive year of dividend growth plus a raised buyback plan signal management's confidence at record earnings.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.4.deta: Small in BLK's contribution but strategic: access to sticky insurance assets that can be routed into BlackRock strategies. It builds permanent capital — a plus for fee durability.

A consortium (Allianz, BlackRock, T&D Holdings, with Generali and Hannover Re participating) completed the purchase from Cinven of the life insurance consolidator Viridium (3.4m policies, ~€67bn of assets). Total value ~€3.5bn; BlackRock is a minority investor.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.4.why: An entry into European life insurance permanent capital — long-dated assets to run through BlackRock's strategies.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.5.deta: The core of the ADD case: a shift from index base fees to higher performance fees. But the deal was paid in stock (dilution) and needs integrating — the test is whether the promised +40% in fee-paying AUM materialises.

The all-stock (~$12bn) acquisition of HPS Investment Partners (~$157bn of private credit assets at 31.03.2025) closed 01.07.2025. BlackRock's combined private credit platform is ~$220bn. Management's estimated effect: fee-paying private markets AUM +~40%, private markets fees +~35%.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.5.titl: HPS closes — private credit becomes a $220bn business
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.5.why: The biggest step into private credit: a combined platform of ~$220bn, lifting fee-paying private markets AUM by ~40% on management's estimate.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.6.deta: The smallest by price but possibly the longest-lived deal: data creates recurring subscription revenue and raises the value of the whole private markets complex. A plus for earnings quality and for the durability of the valuation.

Preqin (the leading independent provider of private markets data) closed 03.03.2025 for £2.5bn (~$3.2bn) in cash. The data is being integrated with Aladdin and eFront; expanded Preqin Benchmarks and Indices launched by July 2026.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.6.titl: Preqin closes — private markets data inside Aladdin
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.6.why: It turns Aladdin into a private markets data engine on a subscription model — a technology moat rather than simply more AUM.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.7.deta: The starting point of BlackRock's pivot into private markets, and the first large debt raised for a deal. It gives ownership of AI infrastructure at high fees; watch whether infrastructure fundraising grows and whether the debt is serviced out of rising free cash flow.

GIP closed 01.10.2024: $3bn in cash (funded by a $3bn senior note issue of 05.03.2024) plus ~12m BLK shares. A platform of ~$170bn of infrastructure assets, 600+ professionals and 300+ active investments.
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.7.titl: GIP closes — ~$170bn of infrastructure for AI
co.blackrock.changesDeep.timeline.7.why: An entry into infrastructure (power, data centres, transport) — the physical layer of AI demand, with long-dated performance fees.

**Methodological frame.** BlackRock manages client assets rather than holding positions on its own balance sheet. Its 13F-HR (at 31.03.2026: $5.72T, ~50,651 positions; filed 13.05.2026) is CLIENTS' US-listed equities, not the holding company's assets, so the 13F top positions are deliberately absent here. The franchise's "portfolio" is the mix of assets under management (AUM). Balance sheet seed and co-investments in its own funds are disclosed in principle, without a line-by-line breakdown in this cycle (see gaps).

**AUM by product at 31.03.2026 (Q1 2026 earnings release, confirmed line by line):**

| Product | AUM, $m | % of AUM | Q1 base fees, $m | % of base fees | Q1 net flows, $m |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 7,661,385 | 55% | 2,626 | 48% | +71,842 |
| Fixed income | 3,270,863 | 24% | 1,058 | 19% | +34,314 |
| Multi-asset | 1,222,612 | 9% | 381 | 7% | +17,827 |
| Private markets | 320,431 | 2% | 658 | 12% | +9,076 |
| Liquid alternatives | 108,639 | 1% | 197 | 4% | +5,551 |
| Digital assets | 60,671 | 0% | 42 | 1% | +935 |
| Currency & commodities | 176,676 | 1% | 136 | 3% | −3,644 |
| **Long-term total** | **12,821,277** | 92% | 5,098 | 94% | +135,901 |
| Cash management | 1,073,323 | 8% | 340 | 6% | −6,177 |
| **Total** | **13,894,600** | 100% | 5,438 | 100% | +129,724 |

**By investment style (31.03.2026):**

| Style | AUM, $m | % of AUM | Q1 base fees, $m | % of base fees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| iShares ETFs | 5,485,544 | 39% | 2,406 | 44% |
| Active | 3,410,923 | 25% | 2,350 | 43% |
| Non-ETF index | 3,924,810 | 28% | 342 | 7% |

**The economics of the concentration:** ETFs plus non-ETF index (passive) are 67% of long-term AUM but only ~51% of base fees. Active plus private markets is ≈27% of AUM but ~55% of base fees — that is where most of the fee income is generated. iShares is the single most profitable franchise: $5.49T of AUM, $2.41bn of base fees in the quarter. The effective base fee rate on long-term AUM is ≈0.16% a year.

**Private markets sub-classes (NOT confirmed against primary sources).** The FACTS agent gave a split of private credit $147.0bn / infrastructure $111.9bn / private equity $30.2bn / real estate $21.7bn / multi-alts $9.6bn. Those figures are **absent** from the Q1 2026 release and from the earnings call transcript; the release carries only the private markets aggregate of $320,431m and a note that the $9bn of inflows was "led by private credit and infrastructure". Another internal estimate gives conflicting numbers (infra $210bn, private credit $40bn→$111bn). Both splits are flagged as unconfirmed — see gaps.

**Q1 2026 geographic flows (long-term net flows of $136bn):** Americas +$123bn, EMEA +$13bn, APAC ~$0. LTM: Americas +$490bn, EMEA +$192bn, APAC −$62bn (release). **Listed vs unlisted:** the overwhelming majority of AUM is listed/liquid (ETFs, index, public fixed income); unlisted is ≈ private markets at $320bn (~2.3% of AUM). **Aladdin:** ~$25T of assets on the platform (not extracted line by line from a primary source this cycle — see gaps).

| Risk | Level | What triggers it | Context (a number) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity beta concentration | High | A 20%+ drawdown in the S&P 500 → equity AUM of $7.66T (55%) falls almost 1:1, and base fees follow | Market revaluation has already taken part of the AUM; Q1'26 AUM −$147bn QoQ |
| The passive price war | High | Competitors (Vanguard, State Street, Fidelity) cut ETF fees → the base fee rate falls below ~0.16% | iShares = 44% of base fees; the competition is structural |
| M&A integration risk | Medium-high | Earnout revaluations (a swing from a $455m charge to a +$549m gain) recur; outflows in the GIP/HPS funds | ~$27bn on GIP+HPS+Preqin in 18 months; the GAAP margin fell to 29.1% in 2025 |
| Shareholder dilution | Medium | Deals paid in stock → diluted shares already +5% YoY to 165.0m | GIP/HPS were paid mostly in stock; 7.6m SubCo Units convert |
| Regulatory / antitrust | Medium | The states' common-ownership suit against BLK/Vanguard/State Street advances; the FTC and DOJ have filed a statement of interest | The first Section 7 case over minority stakes — material for the whole passive complex |
| Institutional index outflows | Medium | The outflow continues (−$34.7bn in Q1 2026, −$108bn LTM) | Low-margin, but a signal on mandates |
| Key person (Fink) | Low-medium | Laurence Fink departs → the strategy and culture are re-rated | Fink is CEO and the face of the franchise; succession runs through Kapito/Small/Goldstein |
| Recession sensitivity | Medium | A recession → markets fall (AUM falls) plus a rotation into cash plus lower performance fees | Performance fees are volatile: $754m in Q4'25 → $272m in Q1'26 |
| A single-asset blow-up in private credit | Low-medium | A default in a large HPS/HLEND position → a reputational and flow hit | Private credit is still in inflow; the credit cycle has not been stress-tested |
co.blackrock.sections.3.deep.0.body:
First, what takes the panic out. BLK is not facing insolvency: it is a capital-light, fee-only manager — the ~$15.34T of assets under management (AUM) at 30.06.2026 (+22% YoY, $12.53T → $15.34T) is CLIENTS' money, not BlackRock's balance sheet. FY2025 delivered $5,553m of GAAP net income on $24,216m of revenue; debt is token against the cash flow. The Q2 2026 report (released 15.07.2026) settled the main question on the operating trend: the adjusted operating margin reached 45.9% — an almost five-year high — against a through-cycle target of ≥45% (for comparison: 44.1% for full-year FY2025, 44.5% in Q1 2026). Inflows are at records: $868bn of net inflows over 12 months, a record $321bn in H1 2026 ($192bn in Q2), and organic base fee growth of 8% in Q2 (~10% LTM); iShares passed $6T. As an issuer, BLK is resilient.

But a resilient balance sheet is not the absence of risk, and the risk here sorts by origin into two groups worth holding apart:

**The fee base — what the AUM is tied to (positioning).** BLK's income is base management fees on AUM. ~55% of AUM ($7,661m, per the Q1 2026 disclosure) is equity, which falls almost 1:1 in a market drawdown and drags base fees with it. Inside that sits iShares, now past $6T: 44% of base fees on ~39% of AUM at a ~0.16% rate — the most profitable franchise and, simultaneously, the epicentre of a structural passive price war (Vanguard, State Street, Fidelity). Add the low-margin institutional index outflow (−$108bn over 12 months) as a signal on mandates.

**The business model — how the value is built.** Over 18 months BLK has spent ~$27bn on GIP, HPS and Preqin, pivoting into private markets and data. The risk here is integration and marks: earnout revaluations have already swung wildly — from a $455m charge (Q1'25) to a $549m gain (Q1'26) year on year (sequentially: a $96m charge in Q4'25 → a $549m gain in Q1'26, a swing of ~$645m); the GAAP operating margin fell to 29.1% in 2025 against 44.1% as-adjusted; and the deals were paid mostly in stock (dilution of +5% YoY to ~165m shares). To that add the antitrust common-ownership suit against the Big Three and the question of succession after Fink. This is a story about the multiple and about execution, not about a break: base fees and inflows are growing.

Each group is taken apart below: what it is, what supports it and what breaks it.

The second is a structural price war: iShares passed $6T in Q2 2026 and delivers 44% of base fees on ~39% of AUM at an effective rate of ~0.16%; Vanguard, State Street and Fidelity push rates down. What softens it: the mix shift and the momentum — active plus private markets still deliver the lion's share of base fees, organic base fee growth was 8% in Q2 (≥5% for many consecutive quarters), and technology revenue (Aladdin) is $566m a quarter.

co.blackrock.sections.3.deep.4.body: Hold. Solvency is not in question — a capital-light, fee-only model with FY2025 net income of $5,553m — and the Q2 2026 report settled the main operating question: the as-adjusted margin reached 45.9% (an almost five-year high, against a ≥45% target), organic base fee growth was 8%, H1 inflows hit a record $321bn, iShares passed $6T, and as-adjusted EPS was $13.91 (+15% YoY) — the "margin ≥45% plus private markets inflows" trigger partly fired. The argument now is about the multiple (a forward P/E of ~19–20x, having recovered part of the de-rating, against ~22–23x historically), where the market pays grudgingly for three things: integration and marks in private markets after ~$27bn of deals, the passive price war through iShares (44% of base fees at a ~0.16% rate), and the regulatory overhang (the common-ownership suit, succession after Fink). Add if the Q3 2026 report confirms an as-adjusted margin ≥45% and net private markets inflows for another two consecutive quarters, with the multiple recovering. Reduce if the S&P 500 falls −20%+ (equity AUM of $7,661bn and base fees fall ~1:1), or if the Section 7 common-ownership suit advances, or if credit stress appears in HPS/HLEND: those are a permanent de-rating of the fee base and the private markets block, not a one-off episode.

FY2025 actually paid $20.84 per share (against $20.40 in 2024); the forward run-rate is $22.92 ($5.73 × 4), a ~2.1% yield at a price of ~$1,093. The dividend has been raised for about 22 consecutive years (not re-confirmed line by line). The capital return priority is the dividend first, then buybacks on a residual basis after M&A for platform objectives. Buybacks: $450m in Q2 2026; management raised the full-year FY2026 buyback plan to $2bn (a forward run-rate of $550m a quarter after a record Q2); FY2025 saw $1.6bn repurchased (part of $5bn of total shareholder returns for 2025); the Board extended the authorisation by a further 7m shares. Importantly: the buyback does NOT offset the dilution from paying for deals in stock — weighted-average diluted shares (with Subco Units) rose from 156.3m to 164.6m (+5.3% YoY) on shares issued for GIP (~12m, closed 01.10.2024) and HPS (BLK shares plus Class B-2 Subco Units, closed 01.07.2025). No spin-offs; no preferred shares; no new cash offerings of common stock. The only source of share count growth is offsetting issuance for M&A.

VERIFIER'S NOTE: the BLK figures are verified; the peer figures (BX/APO/BAM) come from the FACTS agent and were NOT re-opened line by line against primary sources this cycle (SEC 403) — treat as validation, see gaps.

**Reading it for the decision:** BLK is an order of magnitude larger by AUM and more resilient to any single asset class, but grows more slowly in percentage FRE terms than the pure alts (Apollo/Blackstone). BLK's as-adjusted operating margin of 44.5% is comparable to the alts managers'; its unique advantage is Aladdin (high-margin tech revenue, 98% retention — not re-confirmed line by line). BLK trades at a forward P/E discount to the alts peers. The hold/add/cut decision depends on believing that GIP/HPS/Preqin convert into accelerating private markets fees at a discounted valuation.
The largest in the world: $15.34T of AUM, nearly three times the next (State Street). But the lowest effective fee at ~14–15 bp (an index/ETF mix) and the weakest 12-month return of the four (+11.7%) — you buy it for scale and durability, not pace

The best return in the group (+77.6% over the year): record AUM of $2.47T (June 2026), the QQQ ETF and a recovery in flows after years of active fund outflows

An active manager with the highest fee (~40 bp) and a ~46% margin, but structural outflows (−$13.7bn in Q1'26) and the only negative return of the four (−8.5% YTD) — the shift of money into passive hits it hardest

co.blackrock.sections.5.deep.3.body:
**BlackRock** is the only manager combining four pieces that no peer has together: number one in the world in index/ETF (iShares >$6T, including the spot Bitcoin fund IBIT), a large active business, a fast-growing private markets arm (GIP/HPS/Preqin, $329bn of AUM, +$15.4bn of inflows in the quarter) and the Aladdin technology platform the whole industry runs on (technology revenue of $566m a quarter, +13% YoY, sold to competitors among others). Proof the model works: a 45.9% adjusted operating margin at $15.34T of scale — and that on the lowest effective fee in the group, ~14–15 bp (index drags it down): scale plus tech offsets the thin fee. The honest negative: percentage organic growth is slower than the pure alts', the 12-month return is the weakest of the four (+11.7% against Invesco's +77.6%), plus the political ESG backlash, the antitrust question over Big Three voting concentration and the open question of succession after Fink. The decision: **hold/add** — you pay for durability and the private markets option at a forward P/E of ~19–20x (after the Q2 bounce), not for the fastest growth; the trim signal is organic base fee growth falling below 5% with private markets inflows stalling.

**State Street** is second by AUM ($5.7T) and first in custody ($54.5T), but the economics are different: income is tied to rates, FX and custody volumes rather than alpha; the +39.6% over the year reflects a re-rating of the banking story, not the management one.

**Invesco** is the best performer (+77.6% over the year): record AUM of $2.47T and recovering flows around the QQQ ETF; but the story stands on one leg — concentration in a single flagship product.

**T. Rowe Price** has the highest fee (~40 bp) and margin (~46%), but sits structurally on the wrong side of the shift: the active strategies are losing money (−$13.7bn in the quarter), and −8.5% year to date makes it the only one in the red; the premium for active management is compressing.

co.blackrock.sections.5.deep.4.takeaway: BLK's real moat is not size in itself but that it is the only one present in EVERY segment at once, and uniquely owns two the traditional peers have not at all: the Aladdin technology platform (revenue $566m a quarter, +13% YoY, ~98% retention, sold to competitors — quasi-SaaS inside an asset manager) and a large private markets arm after GIP/HPS/Preqin ($329bn of AUM, +$15.4bn of inflows in Q2'26). State Street is strong only in index and custody; T. Rowe Price only in active; Invesco in ETFs. BLK assembles all of them plus two of its own. Proof of the efficiency: a 45.9% adjusted operating margin at $15.34T, despite the thinnest fee at ~14–15 bp. The other side: in percentage terms BLK grows more slowly than both the pure alts (Blackstone/Apollo/KKR) and the peers that have run hard (Invesco +77.6% over the year). The hold case: platform breadth plus Aladdin plus the private markets option outweigh the slower pace and the political risk.

co.blackrock.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
**Who they are (in management's words).** Larry Fink (Q4 2025 release, 15.01.2026): "BlackRock is differentiated as a scale operator in public and private markets investing and technology… We bring it all together to deliver BlackRock to our clients in a consistent, unified way." The thesis: one platform (public plus private markets plus technology and data) sells more to a single client.

**Layers of the strategy (Investor Day 12.06.2025; details from secondary press, as the original blackrock.com deck returns 403):**
1. iShares ETFs — the structural engine: in 2025 ETFs delivered $527bn of the $698bn total inflows; Q4 2025 alone was $181bn.
2. Private markets — a target of $400bn of total fundraising across 2025–2030; assembled through GIP (infrastructure), HPS (private credit), Preqin (data) and ElmTree Funds (net-lease real estate).
3. Technology / Aladdin + Preqin — tech revenue of $1,981m in 2025 (+24% YoY).
4. Four new businesses at ~$500m of revenue each: private markets to insurance, private markets to wealth, digital assets, and active ETFs.

**2030 targets (Investor Day):** revenue above $35bn (from ~$20bn), private markets plus technology rising from 15% to 30% of revenue, and a doubling of operating income and market cap; through the cycle, ≥5% organic base fee growth and a ≥45% operating margin.

**Capital allocation (Fink, Q4 2025 release; Small, Q1 2026 call — verified):** $5bn returned in 2025, including $1.6bn of buybacks; the dividend raised 10% to $5.73; +7m shares added to the authorisation. Small (Q1 2026 call): "We can confidently and consistently deliver 6% to 7% growth from our structural growth segments"; the buyback target is ≥$450m a quarter for the rest of 2026. The priority: M&A for platform objectives → a growing dividend → buybacks as the residual.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.0.body: BlackRock is the world's largest asset manager: $15.34T of assets under management (AUM) at the end of Q2 2026 (+22% YoY). The thing that matters for valuation: that is CLIENTS' money, not BlackRock's balance sheet. The firm's own economics are not the appreciation of those assets but the fees on them: base management fees, performance fees, technology revenue (Aladdin) and private markets management. The model is capital-light: BlackRock does not risk its own capital but earns a percentage of other people's. That makes the size of AUM less important than its mix: 2% of assets in private markets deliver 11% of base fees (an effective rate of ~0.78%), while 28% of assets in institutional index deliver only 7% of fees (~0.03%). The entire strategy is shifting that mix towards high-margin products: iShares has passed $6T, the acquisitions of HPS (private credit, $150.9bn) and GIP (infrastructure, $113.5bn) build the private markets block, and Aladdin delivers recurring revenue that does not depend on the market. The metric management judges itself by is not headline AUM but organic base fee growth: 8% in Q2 and 10% over the last 12 months, against a 5% target.

The edge: the only real access BlackRock has to AI infrastructure capex.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.3.items.3.v: Position: technology revenue of $566m in Q2 (+13% YoY), $1.096bn in H1; recurring and independent of AUM. How it earns: subscriptions to Aladdin, eFront and Preqin. The edge: ACV at +15% YoY runs ahead of recognised revenue — a high-margin stream resilient to market drawdowns, unlike AUM fees.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.3.items.4.v: Position: active strategies are 24% of AUM but 42% of base fees ($2,403m); fixed income delivered the largest inflow, +$92.1bn in Q2. How it earns: a higher fee rate than index. The edge: active bond and multi-asset funds are a fee-efficient inflow precisely in a high-rate cycle.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.3.items.5.v: Position: institutional index is 28% of AUM but only 7% of fees; outflows of −$41.5bn in Q2. How it earns: a minimal ~0.03% rate. What that means for the decision: outflows here barely dent fees — this is cheap ballast. The other side: 58% of all AUM is equity, so a market drawdown reduces AUM (and the fees with it) almost 1:1.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.3.note: for each segment: BlackRock's position → how it earns → what the edge is. All AUM figures are client money, a fee base, not BlackRock's assets. Product names are clickable
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.3.title: Segment bets — where the fees actually come from
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.0.k: Judge yourself on organic fee growth, not headline AUM
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.0.v: Management's main metric is organic base fee growth: a 5% target against 8% in Q2 and 10% over the last 12 months. The $15.34T of AUM is client money; what matters is not how much of it there is but how much fee it generates.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.1.k: Move the mix towards higher fees
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.1.v: The entire strategy is a shift from cheap index (~0.03%) to private markets (~0.78%) and active. That is exactly why 2% of assets in private markets deliver 11% of fees: the economics are driven by the composition of the assets, not their size.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.2.k: Build private markets by acquisition, not from scratch
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.2.v: HPS (private credit, $150.9bn), GIP (infrastructure, $113.5bn) and Preqin (data) were bought to assemble the private markets block quickly. The target is $400bn of gross fundraising across 2025–2030 (said on the call, not in the written release).
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.3.k: Technology is a moat, not an add-on
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.3.v: Aladdin delivers $566m of recurring revenue a quarter (+13% YoY), with ACV at +15%. That stream does not depend on AUM and cushions market drawdowns — something a pure asset-fee model cannot do.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.4.v: BlackRock manages other people's money and does not stake its own balance sheet. The economics are fees, not returns on its own capital. So the $15.34T of AUM is a fee base rather than BlackRock's assets, and the firm should be valued on margin and inflows rather than on the value of client portfolios.
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.5.k: Return capital, but watch the dilution
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.5.v: The buyback was raised to $550m a quarter, with an FY2026 plan of $2bn; the dividend is $5.73 a quarter. The caveat for the decision: the HPS deal added 7.6m Subco Units, dilution of +5% YoY — which is why adjusted EPS (+15%) lags operating income (+39%).
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.6.k: Sell the client the whole portfolio
co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.4.items.6.v: Index plus active plus private markets plus technology — to one client at once, tied together by Aladdin. A whole-portfolio relationship is what keeps the money: it is harder for a client to leave when their entire operating infrastructure runs on BlackRock.

co.blackrock.sections.7.bodyMarkdown:
**What they believe (quotes from Fink's letter of 23.03.2026 as relayed by the secondary source Semafor; the original blackrock.com PDF returns 403, so not checked verbatim):**
- "Self-reliance is costly" — economies are making a hawkish turn and investors will have to put more money to work at home; private capital has to close the gaps in AI, energy and defence.
- "There's a real risk artificial intelligence could widen wealth inequality if ownership does not broaden" — hence broadening retail access to private and early-stage AI assets.
- AI/cloud/electrification = demand for infrastructure (the "$1.5T into data centres by 2030" thesis, Investor Day); BlackRock is top-3 in infrastructure through GIP.
- A shift from 60/40 to 50/30/20 with 20% in private assets (the 2026 Private Markets Outlook).
- The 401(k) as a channel into private assets — Fink supports admitting unlisted assets into retirement accounts.

**What they avoid:** they left Climate Action 100+ and the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative (against the backdrop of the states' antitrust suit under a common ownership theory). Cash management is not a growth priority (low margin, despite $1,073bn of AUM).

**What they are watching:** asset-based finance and private high-grade credit (a "profound increase" in opportunities in 2026, per the 2026 Private Markets Outlook); international and EM equities (the driver of Q1 2026 iShares inflows); tokenisation and digital assets.

co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.0.items.3.n: NOT a growth priority (low margin): 7% of AUM but only 6% of base fees; net outflows of −$7.4bn in Q2
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.0.items.4.n: for Q2; the ~$48.8bn AUM product line delivers only $40m of fees — the most volatile part, which management keeps small
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.0.d: They gather it through the fastest channel — iShares ETFs (+$177.9bn in the quarter) — and shift the economics into high-margin private markets (+$15.4bn) and active strategies (+$53.3bn). At the same time they deliberately do not chase low-margin volume: non-ETF index −$32.1bn, cash −$7.4bn. The model: build scale on ETFs → sell the same client private markets and Aladdin → lift the margin of the mix.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.0.f: 8% organic base fee growth in Q2 — "well in excess of our target"
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.1.d: Economies are making a hawkish turn: energy, defence and technology are now questions of national self-sufficiency. Fink: "Self-reliance is costly" — building AI, energy and defence costs more than budgets can carry, and private capital will close the gap. For example: "a natural logic to making sure more of [the money] comes from domestic investors" — a direct bet on private markets as the source of that capital.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.1.f: "Self-reliance is costly" — Fink, Annual Letter 23.03.2026 (via Semafor, not checked verbatim)
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.1.t: They believe: self-reliance sends capital home
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.2.d: AI, cloud and electrification run up against physical infrastructure and electricity, not software. The Investor Day thesis is $1.5T of data centre capex by 2030. GIP was bought precisely for that: BlackRock is top-3 in the world in infrastructure. For example: +$5.2bn came into infrastructure in Q2 — the highest-margin inflow there is.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.2.f: $1.5T into data centres by 2030; top-3 in infrastructure through GIP
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.2.t: They believe: AI is demand for infrastructure and power
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.3.d: Private markets should be accessible to retail and to retirement accounts, or AI will deepen inequality. Fink proposes admitting unlisted assets into 401(k)s and a model along the lines of the Thrift Savings Plan — $1.5T upfront, a 75-year horizon. For example: the allocation shift from 60/40 to 50/30/20 with 20% in privates is what the four new ~$500m businesses were assembled for.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.4.d: They left Climate Action 100+ and the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative against the backdrop of the states' antitrust suit (the common ownership theory — that the "Big Three" jointly pressure oil and gas). At the same time they do not inflate the low-margin business: cash ($1.07T) and non-ETF index ($4.36T) are not growth priorities. For example: −$32.1bn left non-ETF index in Q2 — and management is not trying to hold it.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.4.f: Left Climate Action 100+ / NZAM; cash and index are not priorities
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.4.t: They do NOT believe in ESG activism or low margins
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.1.items.5.d: Three businesses — public markets, private markets, technology — compound together under "One BlackRock"; the 2030 target is revenue above $35bn (from ~$20bn), operating income doubling to $15bn and market cap to $280bn. A bet on structural growth, not on the cycle. For example: even at record AUM, management measures itself by organic base fee growth (8% in Q2), not by size.

co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.4.items.0.v: AUM +22% YoY; H1'26 net inflows of $321bn — a record, "more than doubled year on year". iShares passed $6.25T (nearly doubling in 3 years), +$177.9bn in the quarter — 45% of all base fees on 41% of AUM. Important: the GIP/HPS deals did not merely expand AUM but began feeding the P&L at the highest margin ($639m of base fees on $329bn of AUM).
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.4.items.2.v: Aladdin: technology revenue $566m (+13%), contract base (ACV) +15%. Why it matters for the decision: subscriptions do not depend on the market — a stabiliser that holds revenue up when AUM-based fees fall in a drawdown.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.4.items.3.k: A 45.9% margin — an almost five-year high
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.4.items.3.v: The adjusted operating margin reached 45.9% (from 43.3%), above the through-cycle target of ≥45%; adjusted operating income $2.92bn (+39%). Performance fees of $305m (+224%) added leverage. An argument for hold/add: the conversion of inflows into margin is working.
co.blackrock.sections.7.deep.4.items.4.v: Q2 buybacks were $450m; the plan was raised to $550m a quarter and to $2bn for the whole of 2026 — "our conviction in the growth ahead" (Fink). Plus a dividend up 10% to $5.73 (2025). Capital goes into growing the platform and into rising shareholder returns, rather than piling up idle.

It sets the frame for where the platform goes over the coming years (via Semafor, not checked verbatim).

**Earnings / reporting:**
- ~21.07.2026 (before open) — Q2 2026 earnings (release plus call). The date comes from aggregators; the 21.07 vs 14.07 discrepancy needs confirming at investor.blackrock.com (a gap).
- The Q2 2026 10-Q — within days of the release (the pattern: the Q1 2026 10-Q was filed 06.05.2026).
- Q3 2026 — around mid-October 2026.

**Comparison base (already out):** the Q4/FY2025 release of 15.01.2026 (AUM $14.04T, EPS $35.31 / $48.09 adj.); the FY2025 10-K of 25.02.2026; the Q1 2026 release of 14.04.2026 (AUM $13.89T, EPS $14.06 / $12.53 adj., inflows $130bn); the Q1 2026 10-Q of 06.05.2026.

**13F (client assets, not the balance sheet):** the Q1 2026 13F-HR was filed 13.05.2026 ($5.72T, ~50,651 positions). The next window (Q2 2026) is by ~14.08.2026.

**Corporate events / Form 4:** 03.06.2026 Fink gifted 4,780 shares; 29.04.2026 Fink sold 33,900; 22.05.2026 8-K on the annual meeting (all directors re-elected). Track new executive sales as a signal.

**Dividend/buyback:** DPS of $5.73 (paid 24.03.2026); the next ex-div dates are roughly early June and September (a quarterly rhythm); the buyback of ≥$450m a quarter — check the actual volume in each release.

**Regulation:** the states' antitrust suit (Texas and others) against BLK/Vanguard/State Street over common ownership plus ESG; the FTC and DOJ have filed a statement of interest. Watch hearing dates and the motion to dismiss (the primary source is the court docket). The next Investor Day — watch for an announcement at blackrock.com/newsroom (the previous one was 12.06.2025).

In Q2 2026 it was 8%, and 10% over 12 months on net inflows of $868bn. Management considers ≥5% healthy. Sustained above 5% and the thesis is working, so adding makes sense; a fall below 5% alongside outflows is a signal to reduce.

co.blackrock.sections.8.deep.2.items.1.v: The economics are driven not by AUM growth but by its composition, because the fee differs sharply by product. Private markets are 2% of assets ($329bn) but 11% of base fees ($639m); non-ETF index is 28% of assets but only 7% of fees; iShares/ETFs are 41% of AUM and 45% of fees. As the share of private markets and active strategies grows, fees and margin grow even with AUM unchanged. Watch the mix, not the trillions.
co.blackrock.sections.8.deep.2.items.2.v: The most volatile income — it depends on realising profits in private markets and hedge funds. Q2 2026 was $305m against $94m a year earlier (+224%). The growth confirms the GIP and HPS acquisitions are starting to deliver carry. Acceleration signals the private markets bet is paying off; a stall signals the integration is faltering.
co.blackrock.sections.8.deep.2.items.3.v: The group's most predictable income — subscriptions to Aladdin and eFront. $566m in the quarter (+13% YoY), with annual contract value (ACV) up 15% — a leading indicator of future revenue. While ACV grows at a double-digit rate the segment is healthy; ACV slowing below 10% is an early sign of fatigue and a reason to revisit the technology premium.
co.blackrock.sections.8.deep.2.items.4.v: Q2 2026 inflows were $191.7bn (long-term $199.1bn, cash −$7.4bn), a record $321bn in the first half, and $868bn over 12 months. iShares passed $6T, having doubled in three years. Sustained long-term inflows are the base of future fees; outflows from the ETFs specifically (as opposed to low-margin index) would reverse the thesis.
co.blackrock.sections.8.deep.2.items.5.k: The pace of buybacks and the dividend
co.blackrock.sections.8.deep.2.items.5.v: The buyback was raised to $550m a quarter ($450m spent in Q2), with a $2bn plan for 2026; the dividend was raised 10% to ~$5.73 a quarter (the amount is not disclosed in a primary source — awaiting the Q1 2026 8-K). If management is buying back and raising the dividend, it considers the stock undervalued. Accelerating the buyback into a drawdown is a strong signal; stopping it is a reason to take notice.

> Below are the analyst's conclusions, NOT quotes from filings. Not a valuation: no DCF and no fair value estimates.

**What the recent events mean.**
- The engine is running steadily: Q1 2026 delivered $130bn of inflows, 8% organic base fee growth (a seventh consecutive quarter at ≥5%, 10% LTM) and an as-adjusted margin of 44.5% (+130 bp). The organic growth is no longer a one-off. iShares ($132bn of inflows, 44% of base fees on 39% of AUM) is the main source of predictability.
- M&A is moving from "cost" to "income": GIP/HPS/Preqin hit GAAP in 2025 (EPS $35.31, −16% YoY on non-cash items), but as-adjusted EPS was $48.09 (+10%). 2026 is the first full year of the combined platform; HPS delivered $121m of performance fees in Q1 2026, and GIP V is majority committed. The signal: the GAAP/adjusted gap will narrow as the one-off charges disappear — but the contingent consideration line is volatile in both directions (Q1'26 produced a +$549m gain), so it must be normalised in every release.
- The $400bn private markets target by 2030 is the main checkable KPI. Slowing fundraising or problem loans at HPS/HLEND would hurt the thesis more than swings in AUM.

**Context for a BLK holder.** BLK is a proxy for (a) rising markets (55% of AUM in equity → beta to the indices), (b) ETF inflows (structural) and (c) the expansion of private credit (cyclical risk). Holding BLK already gives an investor diversified fee-based access to markets; a separate broad index position partly duplicates it, and a direct private credit position doubles down on the same cycle. Antitrust risk (common ownership) is systemic across the whole BLK/Vanguard/State Street trio.

**Signals (triggers, not a recommendation):**
- HOLD/ADD: organic base fee growth ≥5%; as-adjusted margin ≥45%; ETF inflows ≥~$100bn a quarter; private markets fundraising running at ~$65–80bn a year (what $400bn by 2030 requires).
- TRIM: organic base fee growth below 5% for two consecutive quarters; rising impairments or contingent consideration on HPS-GIP signalling overpayment; problem loans at HLEND (watch non-accruals in the BDC's 10-Q); Fink or Kapito selling faster than their usual rhythm.
- WATCH (not a trade): the motion to dismiss in the antitrust suit is denied → revisit the whole passive complex.

**The AI lens (where it is real):** directly, through infrastructure for data centres and electrification (GIP) and through broadening retail access to early-stage AI companies. GIP genuinely owns power and data centre infrastructure, so the lens is not a stretch. For core asset management the AI lens is secondary.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.0.body: BlackRock is a bet that the world's money flows to the broadest and cheapest manager. Assets under management (AUM) of $15.34T (30.06.2026, +22% YoY) is CLIENTS' money, a fee base, not BlackRock's balance sheet. The model is capital-light: income comes from fees, not from its own investments. The thesis rests on three parts: (1) scale and inflows — a record $868bn of net inflows over 12 months at 10% organic base fee growth (8% in Q2), with iShares past $6T; (2) the shift into a higher-margin mix — private markets are 2% of AUM ($329bn) but 11% of base fees ($639m), and the adjusted operating margin of 45.9% is an almost five-year high; (3) a de-rating on record results — a forward P/E of ~17.7x against 22–23x historically (−21% from the 52-week peak of $1,220, source stockanalysis.com), plus a private markets and technology option not in the price (GIP ~$170bn of infrastructure, HPS ~$157bn of private credit, Preqin plus Aladdin) and the 2030 target of revenue above $35bn with $400bn of private markets fundraising.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essence
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.1.body: Beta risk: 55% of AUM ($7.66T) is equity, so the fee base moves almost 1:1 with the market, and an S&P slump hits revenue directly. The passive price war: iShares/ETFs are 39–41% of AUM but base fees there are ~0.16% — constant price pressure. Index outflows: institutional index is −$108bn over 12 months (−$41bn in Q2) — money leaving a segment that already pays little (28% of AUM delivers just 7% of fees). Integration risk: GIP + HPS + Preqin (~$27bn of deals) have already diluted the shares by +5%, and contingent consideration revaluations swing (−$96m in Q4'25 → +$549m in Q1'26). Carry is a promise, not a fact: performance fees jump around ($754m in Q4'25 → $272m in Q1'26 → $305m in Q2'26), and sustained conversion from private markets is still unproven. Regulation and governance: the common-ownership (Section 7) suit and the open question of succession after Fink. The market wants proof that the 45.9% margin and $868bn of inflows will hold rather than reverse on the first market fall.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.d: Q2 2026 has already confirmed the bull case: an adjusted margin of 45.9% (clearing the ≥45% threshold), organic base fee growth of 8%, AUM of $15.34T. Private markets convert carry, and HPS/GIP grow fee-paying AUM. iShares stays above $6T and keeps growing, with inflows for a second consecutive quarter. The P/E returns to 20–22x on record results. The $2bn 2026 buyback runs below intrinsic value. The 2030 target: revenue above $35bn and $400bn of private markets fundraising.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.2.items.1.d: The S&P falls 20% — the fee base (55% in equity, $7.66T) falls almost 1:1. Rates stay higher for longer and private markets inflows freeze, leaving carry on paper. The price war compresses iShares' yield. GIP/HPS integration stalls and volatile contingent consideration revaluations hit GAAP earnings (a 34.7% GAAP margin against 45.9% adjusted). The common-ownership suit advances. The P/E stays at ~17x and no re-rating happens.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.2.title: Two scenarios
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.3.items.0.v: Hold the position. The add trigger has already partly fired: the Q2 2026 adjusted margin of 45.9% (≥45%) alongside 8% organic base fee growth. Add on confirmation of private markets inflows for a second consecutive quarter, or on a pullback below $850 (a P/E under 16x). Reduce on: the S&P falling 20%, the common-ownership suit advancing, credit stress at HPS/HLEND, or organic base fee growth below 5% YoY — which would mean the machine is losing market share.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.3.items.1.v: Mid-October 2026 — the Q3 report (the test: the margin holds ≥45%, organic growth ≥5%, and watch institutional index at −$41bn in Q2). H2 2026 — the general launch of Aladdin on AWS. The dividend of $5.73/quarter (+10%) — not confirmed against a primary source, awaiting the Q1 2026 8-K. Investor Day: the 2030 targets (>$35bn of revenue, $400bn of private markets).
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.3.title: What to do
iShares ($132bn of inflows, 44% of base fees on 39% of AUM) is the main source of predictability
The GAAP/adjusted gap is narrowing, but contingent consideration is volatile — normalise it in every release
WATCH: if the motion to dismiss in the antitrust suit is denied → revisit the whole passive complex
co.blackrock.sections.9.preview.line: The engine is running steadily (8% organic base fee growth, a 7th consecutive quarter at ≥5%); M&A is moving from "cost" to "income"; the KPI is $400bn of private markets by 2030.

co.blackrock.summary: BlackRock manages $13.89T of other people's money and lives on the fees, not on its own balance sheet. Two engines: iShares — the world's largest ETF range (41% of assets but 45% of fees, now past $6T) — and private markets: 2% of assets but 11% of fees plus almost all of the performance fees. Plus Aladdin, software with durable subscription revenue. After ~$27bn of acquisitions (GIP, HPS, Preqin) the money is flowing into private credit and AI infrastructure. Inflows this year are at a record and the margin is 45.9%. The risk: 58% of assets are equities, so in a market crash the fees fall with the market.
co.blackrock.tagline: BlackRock is the world's largest asset manager ($13.89T of AUM): its income is fees on the assets it manages, and the economics are driven by iShares ETFs (44% of base fees) and, since GIP/HPS/Preqin, by high-margin private markets. The hold/add/cut decision rests on converting record inflows ($744bn LTM) into base and performance fees at an as-adjusted margin above 45%; meanwhile the stock sits near its 52-week low and below its historical forward P/E.
co.blackrock.topBets.items.0.fact: $6.25T of assets under management (AUM) — 41% of all BlackRock's assets but 45% of base management fees, $2,595m for the quarter; +$177.9bn of net inflows in Q2 2026. The bet: iShares passed $6T this quarter, doubling in 3 years — the firm's scale engine for fees.
co.blackrock.topBets.items.1.fact: ~$230m of base fees plus $115m of performance fees in a single quarter (Q2 2026 — from the earnings call, not the written release), from a business that closed only in mid-2025. The bet: HPS turns the capital-light BlackRock into a recipient of performance fees and supplies most of the $305m performance fee line.
co.blackrock.topBets.items.2.fact: Infrastructure is $113.5bn of AUM inside private markets, with the highest fee density (~0.78%, ~5× the firm average). BlackRock's only real AI capex exposure. The bet: the Aligned Data Centers deal at a $40bn EV (>5 GW) and the AIP partnership targeting up to $100bn with Microsoft/NVIDIA/MGX.

co.blackrock.topBets.items.3.fact: $329.1bn of AUM — just 2% of assets, but 11% of base fees, $639m for the quarter, plus most of the $305m performance fee line; +$15.4bn of net inflows in Q2. The bet: management targets $400bn of gross fundraising across 2025–2030 (a target from the call, not the written release) — shifting the fee mix to a higher rate.
co.blackrock.topBets.items.3.name: Private markets
co.blackrock.topBets.items.4.fact: Technology revenue (Aladdin) was $566m in Q2 2026, +13% YoY; recurring, high-margin and independent of AUM. Annual contract value (ACV) is growing +15% YoY — faster than recognised revenue (a leading indicator). The bet: platform income does not fall in a market drawdown, unlike AUM-based fees.
co.blackrock.verification: Verified line by line through the official earnings release PDFs (q4cdn): every P&L metric for Q1 2026, Q4 2025 and FY2025 (revenue, GAAP and as-adjusted operating income/margin, net income, GAAP and as-adjusted diluted EPS, performance fees, tech revenue), the AUM breakdown by product and style with base fees, net flows by region/type/product, the $5.73 dividend (+10%), the buyback, contingent consideration of $455m (the Q4'25 charge) and +$549m (the Q1'26 gain), and the diluted share count. Confirmed on terms through primary press releases, mirrors and the earnings call: GIP ($12.55bn, $3bn cash + ~12m shares, ~$170bn of AUM), HPS ($12bn in stock, $157bn of AUM, PFS $190bn), performance fees of $272m / HPS $121m, buybacks of ≥$450m a quarter, and 6-7% structural growth. Valuation (price/mcap/P/E/yield) and Fink's transaction (33,900 shares) were confirmed through stockanalysis/investing.com/stocktitan. Two FACTS agent errors were corrected: FY2025 GAAP net income ($5,553m, not $5,942m) and FY2024 as-adjusted EPS ($43.61, not ~43.7). The insider section was strengthened: openinsider.com was read line by line (24 transactions), and five Form 4s plus Fink's gift were spot-checked directly against the primary SEC Form 4 XML (curl with a contact UA — sec.gov serves the data, unlike WebFetch's 403); the buyback ($450m in Q1'26, $1.6bn in FY2025, +7m of authorisation) and dividend ($5.73 +10%, FY2025 actual $20.84) were re-confirmed line by line from the earnings release PDFs. NOT confirmed and flagged: the private markets sub-class breakdown (agents conflict), fund IRRs, the peer Q1 2026 figures line by line, and the verbatim quotes from Fink's letter — because blackrock.com is blocked (403). Overall confidence: high on the consolidated financials and deal terms (the core of the thesis); medium on private markets granularity, peer data and voice quotes.
