co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.0.det: tax-free for US and Canadian shareholders
Structural simplification — fewer tickers in the menagerie the market has historically discounted Brookfield for. The next calendar event: the result of the 16 July vote.

Brookfield's insurance business (BWS) currently trades as a separate share. The proposal: exchange BWS shares for BN shares one for one and leave a single company. The shareholder vote is 16.07.2026, with closing before the end of 2026.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.0.why: The insurance subsidiary BWS becomes part of BN — one share instead of two, a simpler structure, and $30bn+ of assets added to BN's balance sheet.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.1.why: The first quarter after Just Group. Watch fee-related earnings and the contribution from the insurance inflow.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.2.det: The portfolio's main hidden option: a $7.9bn entry against a ≥$30bn target. If the AP1000 programme runs, the re-rating is a multiple; if the DOE loan falls through, the scenario is deferred.

Under the agreement with the US government, Brookfield and Cameco have the right to list Westinghouse if a final investment decision on the new reactors is taken by January 2029 and the company is valued at ≥$30bn. The government holds a warrant over 20% of the equity.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.2.tit: Westinghouse — an IPO at ≥$30bn under the warrant agreement
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.2.why: The warrant gives BEP and Cameco an option to monetise Westinghouse through an IPO. If AP1000 scales, that is $10bn+ of realised fund profits.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.3.det: PJM is the most power-constrained US market because of data centres. A 14 GW project queue is a multi-year pipeline against demand that is already visible.

A programmatic agreement with the developer SunEnergy1: BEP gets 510 MW of operating solar in the PJM grid (the eastern US, where the Northern Virginia data centres sit) plus access to a queue of future projects totalling 14 GW.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.3.tit: SunEnergy1: 510 MW of solar in PJM plus access to a 14 GW pipeline
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.3.why: PJM is the largest data centre market in the US. A 14 GW pipeline gives BEP years of projects against AI demand.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.pipeline.4.det: A direction rather than a deal: watch whether the announcements convert into signed projects. The IFC's participation is a mark of quality for institutional money in emerging markets.

BEP's long-term plan: grow the portfolio by $100bn by 2030, including through emerging markets — for example $12bn in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh. The World Bank (IFC) has already put $100m into the Brookfield Catalytic Transition Fund ($5bn) aimed at those markets.

co.brookfield.changesDeep.sub: Where it came from and where it went — 12 months to Q1 2026 plus announced deals
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.0.det: Brookfield is not building power plants on spec: Microsoft has pre-bought the capacity. Guaranteed BEP revenue for years ahead, and the clearest proof that Brookfield's AI thesis works in cash rather than words.

Brookfield (through BEP) commits to supplying Microsoft with 10.5 gigawatts of clean electricity across 2026–2030 — for its AI data centres. For scale: 10.5 GW is roughly ten large nuclear units. The largest corporate green power contract in history.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.0.tit: Brookfield–Microsoft: 10.5 GW of clean power for data centres
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.0.why: The world's largest green power contract for AI infrastructure. It gives BEP 10.5 GW of contracted generation across 2026-2030.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.1.det: The government is subsidising the reactor build-out — power directly for future data centres. If the programme runs to plan, Westinghouse, bought for $7.9bn, could be worth a multiple of that (an IPO target of ≥$30bn). The main risk: the conditional loan never becomes a signed one.

The US Department of Energy (DOE) has conditionally approved a loan of up to $17.5bn to build new Westinghouse AP1000 reactors — Brookfield owns 51% of Westinghouse (with partners), with the other 49% held by Cameco. The loan is still conditional: the final documents are in progress.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.1.tit: The DOE conditionally approved a loan of up to $17.5bn for Westinghouse AP1000
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.1.val: up to $17.5bn plus $500m / $1bn of equity per project (BEP+Cameco)
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.1.why: A government loan subsidises building new Westinghouse reactors — power directly for future data centres. AP1000 becomes a core BEP product.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.2.det: Insurance is a source of permanent capital: the money cannot walk away the way a fund client can, so it can be invested for the long run. Every acquisition like this grows both the balance sheet and BAM's fees at the same time.

Just Group is a British pension insurer: corporate pension schemes transfer their obligation to pay pensions to it, along with the money behind them. Brookfield is buying the company outright — and gets that long-dated money to manage for decades.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.2.tit: Just Group plc — acquiring the British insurer
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.2.why: Wealth Solutions grows from $143.5bn to ~$180bn of client assets. Insurance premiums arrive continuously — and are invested through Brookfield's strategies.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.3.det: This is not a one-off deal but a pipeline: every new data centre in the programme is an order for BEP's power and BIP's infrastructure. Together with the Microsoft contract, it is the main confirmation of Brookfield's AI thesis in real capital.

An umbrella investment programme (launched 19.11.2025): Brookfield and its partners are assembling up to $100bn of assets across the whole AI chain — power plants, data centres and fibre networks. NVIDIA participates as technology partner, and the Kuwait Investment Authority — one of the world's largest sovereign funds — as lead investor. A separate $5bn framework runs with Bloom Energy (fuel cells: fast generation right at the data centre site).
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.3.tit: AI Infrastructure Program — the programme with NVIDIA and Kuwait's sovereign fund
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.3.why: A long-term programme: building generation, data centres and fibre specifically for AI. A multi-year pipeline of projects for BEP and BIP.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.4.det: Where it sits in the portfolio
A typical BBU deal: a niche manufacturer with steady repeat sales. Not an AI story — simply predictable cash flow.

Antylia Scientific makes laboratory consumables: instruments, single-use materials, water testing kits. Its customers are pharma, biotech and environmental labs that buy continuously, regardless of the economic cycle. The deal price was not disclosed.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.4.tit: Antylia Scientific — an acquisition with CDPQ
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.4.why: A maker of laboratory equipment and consumables (pharma, biotech, water testing). Bought by the private equity arm (BBU) alongside the Canadian pension fund CDPQ.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.5.det: Where it sits in the portfolio
It extends BIP's digital infrastructure (towers plus data centres plus fibre) into a growing market. The logic is the same as in the AI programme: own the pipes the traffic runs through.

The tower business is simple: one tower is leased to several mobile operators at once, and they pay for years — moving a tower is expensive and pointless. India is one of the fastest-growing mobile internet markets in the world. The amount and structure of the deal were not disclosed.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.5.tit: American Tower India — an investor group buys the telecom towers
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.5.why: BIP and its partners are buying American Tower's Indian business — a portfolio of telecom towers. Towers rent space to mobile operators for a recurring fee.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.6.det: The Brookfield model in action: build or buy → raise the value → sell the mature asset → put the money into something new at a higher return. Selling at a good price confirms their asset marks are not inflated.
Saeta Yield is a Spanish portfolio of 745 MW of operating solar plants. Brookfield sold it to Masdar — Abu Dhabi's state energy company, which buys completed green assets worldwide.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.6.why: Selling a mature solar portfolio: the assets are built and have appreciated — the money is recycled into new X-Elio projects at higher returns.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.7.det: An exit from a mature asset at full price. The fund's profit is crystallised — meaning Brookfield receives fund profits in cash, not on paper.
Patrick Terminals is Australia's largest container port operator, which BIP had owned for years. Sold to a buyer group for A$2.5bn — a full exit.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.7.why: A full exit from the Australian ports business. The sale crystallises fund profits — and Brookfield takes its share of them.

**Structure.** BN is the listed parent. Through it an investor owns: (1) a stake in the BAM management company (>$1T of AUM; client money is excluded from BN's assets); (2) insurance / Wealth Solutions (BWS); (3) direct equity in the operating businesses — infrastructure (BIP), renewable power (BEP), private equity (BBUC), real estate (BPG). BN's real assets are its stakes in those vehicles plus carried interest and direct investments. Every figure below is blended (market + IFRS) at 31.03.2026, confirmed line by line against the BN Q1 2026 Supplemental, p.7 (opened and checked).

**Ring 1 — positions with a published valuation (blended, 31.03.2026)**

| Position | Vehicle / stake | BN value (blended) | oneLineDescription |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stake in the management company | BAM, ~74% | $52,030m | A listed stake in the alternative manager; fee-bearing capital $614bn, management fees $3.1bn over 12 months; annualised cash flow $1,953m |
| Carried interest (accrued + target), net | held by BN through BAM | $33,770m | BN's share of unrealised carry plus target carry; includes $6,420m net to BN of accrued carry |
| Direct investments | alongside the BAM funds | $10,816m | BN's direct commitments into BAM's flagship RE/credit/opportunistic funds |
| Wealth Solutions (insurance) | BWS, controlled | $30,420m | Insurance assets $143.5bn (→ $180bn after Just Group); investable assets $120bn |
| Real estate | BPG, controlled | $26,865m | Premium office/retail super-core plus assets held for monetisation plus development |
| Renewable power | BEP | $10,208m | Hydro, wind, solar; holds 51% of Westinghouse with partners; cash flow $485m |
| Infrastructure | BIP | $7,521m | Utilities, transport, midstream, data infrastructure; a perpetual capital vehicle |
| Private equity | BBUC | $2,810m | Business services and industrials; cash flow $24m |

Summary (Supplemental p.7, blended): Total investments $175,341m; Corporate and other −$430m; Capital $174,911m; Debt and preferred capital −$18,591m; **Capital, net $157,096m**; **per share $66.37** (this is management's own estimate). Every line has been confirmed against the primary PDF.

**Ring 2 — named, with no separate line-item valuation**
- **Westinghouse** — the nuclear reactor and fuel business; held through BEP with institutional partners (BEP + partners 51%, Cameco 49%); EV at acquisition (07.11.2023) US$7.9bn (confirmed by McCarthy Tétrault). BEP's own net economic share within that 51% is diluted by the LP partners and is not disclosed in the public primary sources — see gaps. There is no separate line in the Supplemental (it sits inside BEP / the private funds).
- **SpaceX** — a pre-IPO stake. **Disclosed verbatim** in the BN Q1 2026 Supplemental, p.16 (the "New Business Investments" block, $2.3bn of equity): "$2 billion of SpaceX shares at the current pre-IPO mark, of which approximately $1 billion is owned by Brookfield Corporation" — the whole group position is $2bn at the pre-IPO mark, of which **BN's own share is ~$1bn**.
- **AI investments**: Figure (humanoid robotics), The Deployment Company (a JV with OpenAI), Hark Labs (an AI platform). No valuations.
- **Just Group** (UK retirement) — the mandate began in Q2 2026; it added $40bn of fee-bearing capital and ~$100m of annual base fee for BAM (confirmed by BAM's Q1 2026 8-K).

**Concentration (by BN asset value).** The top 2 = BAM ($52,030m) + carried interest ($33,770m) ≈ 55% of Total investments of $175,341m (or ~59% measured against holdco assets of ≈$145bn, excluding consolidated fund assets). Concentration is high in the management company itself and the carry attached to it.

**Listed vs unlisted.** Listed: BAM, BIP, BEP, BBUC. Unlisted: Wealth Solutions, BPG real estate, direct investments, Westinghouse, carried interest.

**Geography.** Global, with the centre of gravity in North America; large RE assets in New York, London, Toronto, Berlin, Dubai, Tokyo and Sydney (a detailed named list of the top properties is not disclosed in the public Supplemental — see gaps).

**Themes.** (1) The power/AI build-out — Westinghouse AP1000 against data centre demand, BEP power contracts, the OpenAI JV, BAIIF; (2) credit as the largest fee-bearing segment ($282bn, including Oaktree and 17Capital); (3) insurance as a growing source of permanent capital.

co.brookfield.sections.3.bodyMarkdown:
BN's risk is not that the business breaks. The company is resilient: 95% of the debt is non-recourse to the holdco, and maturities to 2030 are covered by cash on hand. But the risk is not singular — it arrives from three different directions.

| Risk | Direction | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Debt and refinancing | how it is financed | 95% of the debt sits at the assets; if rates rise or an asset weakens, BN's stake in it gets cheaper — no bankruptcy required |
| AI infrastructure concentration | what the money is in | a bet on power and data centres (a $200bn pipeline); disappointment in AI returns and a capex squeeze hit the whole infrastructure book at once |
| Two marks — carry and insurance | how the value is counted | $60bn+ is valued by management itself (10x and 15x); the market pays zero for both |

At $44.08 the market is already priced where the valuation sits with carry and the insurance franchise written to zero — it is not paying for those marks. But that is only one of the three risks; the credit and asset risks need looking at separately.
co.brookfield.sections.3.deep.0.body:
First, what takes the panic out. BN is not facing bankruptcy: 95% of the debt ($249.5bn) sits against specific assets with no recourse to the holdco, and five years of maturities are already covered by cash on hand. In 2023 the group handed its Los Angeles towers, ~$1.1bn, back to the banks — and the loss stopped at fund level, never reaching the holdco. As a whole, the company is resilient.

But resilience is not the same as the absence of risk, and the risk here is not singular. It arrives from three different directions, and they are worth holding apart:

**How the company is financed.** Almost all the debt sits at the assets themselves. If rates rise or an asset weakens, refinancing gets more expensive, capital has to be injected into the asset, and BN's stake in it gets cheaper — no bankruptcy required.

**What the money is invested in.** Brookfield is betting heavily on AI infrastructure — power and data centres, a $200bn pipeline. If AI returns disappoint and hyperscaler capex contracts, the blow lands across the whole infrastructure and power book at once, not on a single asset.

**How the value is counted.** 59% of the assets ($102.8bn of $175.3bn) are marked by management itself; two of the large marks — future fund profits (carry) and the insurance franchise — the market does not recognise at all.

Each is taken apart below: what it is, what supports it and what breaks it.
co.brookfield.sections.3.deep.0.title: The thesis: no bankruptcy — but the risk is not singular
Of the group's $249.5bn of debt, only 5% ($14.3bn) has recourse to the holding company itself — which protects against bankruptcy, not against losses. The mechanism is quiet: a weak asset or higher rates → interest cover falls → refinancing costs more → capital has to be injected into the asset → BN's stake in it gets cheaper. No bankruptcy required. Today the position is healthy: maturities to 2030 ($3.66bn) are covered by cash on hand ($5.48bn), and the debt is long and fixed — 15 years, 4.8%, with 74% maturing after 2031.

The weak spot: on that 95% of the debt Brookfield discloses neither interest cover, nor a maturity schedule, nor the floating-rate share — it cannot be checked, and that is exactly where the shareholder's risk lives.
95% of the debt sits at the assets, not the holdco
The main bet right now is the physical infrastructure behind AI: power and data centres (Westinghouse, the 10.5 GW Microsoft contract, the Compass and Ascenty platforms, the $100bn programme with NVIDIA and the Kuwait fund). The risk is not in any one asset but in a single shared driver: if AI returns disappoint and hyperscaler capex contracts, demand for power and sites falls across the entire portfolio at once. There is already a first warning — New York's moratorium on data centres above 50 MW. On top of that sits a separate weakness: office and retail property ($26.9bn, 15% of assets), where segment earnings are already negative and a −20% move in building values erases ~$10bn of capital.
Watch: hyperscaler capex plans (Microsoft/Google/Amazon), data centre utilisation, new BEP power supply contracts.
a bet on AI power, a $200bn pipeline
$102.8bn of $175.3bn carries no market quote, and nearly 60% of that is two lines. The first is carry ($33.8bn): BN holds future fund profits at a 10x multiple and assumes they will deliver ~$2.7bn a year — while actual cash over the last year was just $528m, five times less than promised. The second is the insurance franchise ($30.4bn) at 15x on a thin 2.24% spread — exactly as regulators (the PRA before 31.07, NAIC on 11–14.08) have started scrutinising the "manager owns its own insurer" structure. The market today pays zero for both.
Watch: the "Realized carried interest, net" line over 12 months ($528m; the credibility threshold is >$1.5bn); the PRA/NAIC decisions; BWS's combined ratio (99% today).
Valuation: two marks the market will not recognise

co.brookfield.sections.3.deep.4.body: Hold. The risk in BN is not a broken business but a single question: are the two marks — carry and the insurance franchise — real. At $44.08 the market already pays zero for both, which is most of the discount and also what limits the downside: to fall meaningfully further, the market would have to start doubting what it does price — the real businesses and the BAM stake — and that is a break scenario, which is not present. Add if the 13.08 report shows carry accelerating towards $1.5bn or above. Reduce if the regulators (the PRA after 31.07, NAIC on 11–14.08) tighten capital against insurance: that is a permanent markdown of $30.4bn, not a one-off loss.

co.brookfield.sections.4.bodyMarkdown:
> Verified against primary sources 28.06.2026. HEADLINE: there are NO individual Form 4 filings in the SEC for purchases or sales of BN or BAM stock by senior management — and that is a structural fact, not a data gap (see below). The insider-confidence signal here is read not through Form 4 but through corporate actions: the buyback ($1bn+ YTD), the dividend increase (+17%) and the large personal holdings disclosed in the proxy.

**Form 4 / Section 16 — why there are no personal transactions**

BN and BAM are Canadian foreign private issuers (BN is incorporated in Ontario and headquartered in Toronto; its SEC category is large accelerated filer, forms 40-F/6-K). Their officers and directors are exempt from Section 16 and do NOT file Form 4 with the SEC for transactions in BN/BAM stock. Personal insider transactions are disclosed in Canada's SEDI system, and aggregate ownership in the annual Management Information Circular (proxy). That is why openinsider returns an empty table for the BN ticker (which its database maps to the delisted Banta Corp), and nothing with an issuer for BAM; openinsider/SEC Form 4 are uninformative for this company (checked: empty output).

IMPORTANT — reclassifying the previous claim: the 175 Form 4 filings under CIK BN (0001001085) and 10 under CIK BAM (0001937926) turn out, on parsing the XML, NOT to be transactions in BN/BAM stock but reports by BN/BAM as 10%+ owners of the non-traded **Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust** (Brookfield REIT) they manage. These are routine Class I subscriptions and redemptions at a NAV of ~$10.4 (code J), not trading in their own shares. The specific lines (SEC EDGAR Form 4, opened and parsed line by line):

| Transaction date | Filer | Issuer | Code | Buy/Sell | Shares | Price (NAV) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18.06.2026 | Brookfield Corp | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A (acquired) | 107,584 | $10.3874 |
| 20.05.2026 | Brookfield Corp | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A | 105,468 | $10.3689 |
| 20.04.2026 | Brookfield Corp | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A | 105,505 | $10.3726 |
| 31.03.2026 | Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | D (disposed) | 314,545 | $10.3726 |
| 20.02.2026 | Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A | 105,895 | $10.3778 |

The previous claim — "Bruce Flatt, Form 4 of 28.02.2026, ~107m shares, uninformative buy" — is withdrawn: the Form 4 nearest that date (filed 24.02.2026) is a BAM subscription into Brookfield REIT, not a Flatt transaction in BN stock. No personal Flatt Form 4 exists at the SEC (foreign private issuer).

**Management ownership (BN 2025 Management Information Circular, primary IR PDF, extracted with pdfplumber)**
- **Bruce Flatt (CEO):** holds **18,018,523** Class A and Exchangeable Class A shares directly and indirectly (note k of the circular). The widely quoted "~107–142m shares" from aggregators is NOT personal ownership but the block controlled through the Partners' collective vehicles (see below).
- **The Class B control block.** At 17.04.2025 BN had 1,647,462,652 Class A and just 85,120 Class B Limited Voting Shares (all privately held). The Class B shares sit in a trust; beneficial and voting interests are split one third each between Bruce Flatt, Jack L. Cockwell and, jointly, the five Partners (Kingston, Lawson, Madon, Pollock, Shah). The circular says verbatim: "no single individual or entity controls the Trust". Through the Class B shares (which elect half the board) the Partners hold strategic control on a small economic stake.
- **Partners Value Investments L.P. (PVI):** the Partners' listed partnership owns **~121m** BN Class A, ~31m BAM Class A and ~8m BWS Class A (fully diluted); the Partners hold ≥90% of PVI's units (circular). What it means for the decision: management's interests are firmly aligned with BN over the long run — large personal and collective capital in the stock, with no sales recorded.

**Buybacks (the corporate undervaluation signal)**
- **BN:** $470m repurchased YTD at ~$41 on average (≈37% below management's $66.37 estimate); over 12 months, 23.0m shares at a weighted average of $38.75 — confirmed in the Supplemental (p.8).
- **BAM:** $575m repurchased — confirmed in the 8-K/Supplemental. Together, BN+BAM is **>$1bn YTD**.
- **NCIB (mechanics, primary).** The TSX approved the renewal of BN's normal course issuer bid over **191,034,672** Class A shares = 10% of the public float; the period runs **27.05.2026–26.05.2027**; the daily TSX limit is 722,889 shares (25% of ADTV); purchases may be made on the TSX/NYSE/ATS; repurchased shares are cancelled or held in trust for the LTIP; an automatic purchase plan runs from mid-June 2026 (announced 25.05.2026). So the buyback is not a one-off but a renewable mandate.

**Dividend / share issuance**
- **BN:** the quarterly dividend was raised from $0.06 to **$0.07** per Class A share (an annual rate of **$0.28**, ≈+17%) — declared in February 2026, paid 31.03.2026 and 30.06.2026 (IR distributions page, opened). There have been no cuts; the policy remains a "modest dividend" with reinvestment through buybacks. Raising it in a year when the stock sits in the lower-middle of its annual range is a supportive signal.
- **BAM:** announced "record 2025 results and 15% dividend increase" (BAM IR press release; the headline was confirmed by web search, but the exact quarterly dividend of $0.5025 comes from an aggregator and was not re-opened against the primary source in this check — see gaps).
- **Preferred reset (06.2026):** BN fixed the reset rate on its Series 24 preference shares at 5.432% a year ($0.3395/quarter) for five years from 01.07.2026, with a right to convert into floating Series 25 (4.623% annualised); 10,808,027 Series 24 shares are outstanding — confirmed in BN's 6-K of 01.06.2026 (opened). This concerns the preferreds, not the Class A.
- **The BN+BWS merger** (26.05.2026): a 1-for-1 exchange, Brookfield Corporation Ltd., NYSE/TSX, tax-deferred, vote 16.07.2026 — confirmed by GlobeNewswire. Effect on the share count: BWS class A exchangeable shares convert 1-for-1 into BN.
- **BAM senior notes** (subsequent): $1.0bn ($550m @ 4.832% + $450m @ 5.298%) plus a $1.0bn CP programme — confirmed in the 8-K.

**Reading it for the decision (hold/add/cut).** There are by definition no personal Form 4 insider buys here, so we lean on corporate proxies: (1) a $1bn+ YTD buyback at ~$41 against management's $66.37 estimate — management clearly thinks the stock is cheap; (2) a +17% dividend increase; (3) very large personal and collective Partner ownership (Flatt personally ~18.0m Class A; PVI ~121m BN Class A) with no recorded sales. All three vectors point pro-hold/add. There is no value-destructive spin-off or issuance; the BN+BWS merger is 1-for-1 and non-dilutive. The structural drawback for tracking: personal insider transactions cannot be monitored through the SEC — only through SEDI (Canada).

co.brookfield.sections.5.bodyMarkdown:
We compare BN's management business (i.e. BAM) against the largest alternative managers. Every peer figure has been re-opened against the primary SEC 8-Ks (KKR, BX, APO — EDGAR; aggregators are no longer used).

| Metric | BAM (Brookfield) | Blackstone (BX) | Apollo (APO) | KKR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRE, quarter | $772m (+11%) | $1,548m (+23%) | $728m (+30%) | $1,016m (+24%) |
| Total AUM | >$1.0T | $1.30T | $1.03T | $758bn |
| Fee-paying AUM | $614bn (+12%) | $937.6bn | $836bn (FGAUM) | $615bn (+17%) |

**Important: the row above is FRE (fee-related earnings), not management fees.** It was previously labelled "fees": the figures are correct and comparable (FRE against FRE), but the label was wrong. Actual quarterly management fees are markedly higher — BX $2,133m, KKR $1,193m, APO ~$1.0bn, BAM $990m (consolidated).

Confirmed against the primary SEC 8-Ks: KKR — FRE $1,016m (+24%), AUM $758bn (+14%), fee-bearing capital $615bn (+17%). BX — FRE $1,548m (+23%), AUM $1.30T, fee-earning $937.6bn (BX labels all its Q1'26 figures "preliminary and unaudited"). APO — FRE $728m (+30%), AUM $1.03T, FGAUM $836bn.

⚠️ **These companies count AUM differently, and it is not directly comparable:** Apollo's AUM includes the Athene insurance balance sheet ($401bn ≈ 39% of AUM), and KKR's includes Global Atlantic ($220bn ≈ 29%). BX counts most conservatively. FRE is the only row in the table that is pre-tax for all of them and therefore genuinely comparable.

**Positioning:**
- **FRE size/pace:** BAM ($772m, +11%) trails BX and KKR in absolute terms and grows the slowest of the four (APO +30%, KKR +24%, BX +23%).
- **Capital mix:** BAM has the heaviest hard-asset tilt — $282bn of credit plus real assets (infrastructure/power/real estate) against BX's broader PE/credit mix and Apollo's insurance tilt.
- **What is unique to BN:** unlike the pure managers, a BN investor also gets direct capital in BIP/BEP/BBUC/BPG, carry on the balance sheet ($6.4bn net) and insurance (WS $30.4bn) — diversification that dilutes the purity of the fee-stream story.
- **Conclusion for the decision:** on fee-business growth BAM lags its peers, but BN offers upside through the discount to management's estimate ($66 vs ~$43), carry realisation and the Westinghouse option, none of which the peers have. The hold/add case rests on BN's discount and its optionality, not on BAM leading on FRE growth.

co.brookfield.sections.5.deep.2.title: What the portfolio is made of
co.brookfield.sections.5.deep.3.body:
**Brookfield** is the only owner-operator in the group: ~85,000 employees physically run assets, not money. Five names it is built from: **Westinghouse** (nuclear power), **Compass** (data centres), **Oaktree** (credit), **Clarios** (an operating business) and **Canary Wharf** (real estate). Its competitors manage capital — and a 10.5 GW contract for Microsoft cannot be delivered with a cheque; the generation has to be built and commissioned. The price of that: the slowest fee growth of the group (+11% against +23–30% for peers) and the worst AUM monetisation (61% against 72–81%). But that same slowness creates the ~35% discount to management's own estimate, and the hold case is that its operating edge in electrification closes it.

**Blackstone** is the largest by scale ($1.30T of AUM) and the most efficient at converting AUM into fees (72%). Its edge: an asset-light model that scales without freezing capital. Over 12 months it has quietly rebuilt its mix — 35% of AUM is now credit and insurance rather than classic real estate and buyout. The legacy: the BXMT mortgage REIT carries ~7% past due and pays dividends out of principal — not the main business, but an indicator that Blackstone has not fully exited the commercial property cycle.

**Apollo** grows fastest (+30% fees YoY) through one powerful channel: the Athene insurance arm raises its own capital through annuities, deploys it into loans ($71bn a quarter) and pays Apollo the fees on it. That closed loop delivers speed — and it is also first in line for the NAIC's 2026 review of capital requirements. If the regulator tightens the rules, growth stops abruptly rather than gradually, because there is only one channel.

**KKR** is the most diversified: private equity 30%, credit 43%, insurance through Global Atlantic, plus $18.3bn of deferred earnings in Strategic Holdings (direct balance sheet investments). On half Blackstone's AUM ($758bn) it monetises just as efficiently (81%) — earning a third more fees than Brookfield off the same base ($615bn against $614bn). The risk: its insurance channel runs the same model as Apollo's Athene — a regulatory hit to one touches both.

co.brookfield.sections.5.deep.4.takeaway: Brookfield's real edge is not size but the ecosystem: it owns every link in the chain and can therefore assemble, alone, a project its competitors cannot. Take an AI data centre campus: the power comes from its own generation (BEP's hydro and wind plus Westinghouse's nuclear), the site itself is built and operated by Compass, the compute is leased to developers by Radiant, and the whole thing is financed by Oaktree's in-house credit and the permanent capital of the insurance business. Neither Blackstone nor Apollo nor KKR has all of those pieces in-house — they would have to buy them in and share the profit with partners. The same linkage speeds up deals: when Brookfield buys an asset it immediately installs its own operators, refinances through its own credit and holds it on permanent capital — a closed loop. The other side of that: Brookfield is structurally behind in credit, buyout PE and tech, and over five years its stock has trailed KKR (~28%) and Apollo (~21%) with its own ~12%. The hold case: the ability to carry a full infrastructure project single-handed closes the ~35% discount.

co.brookfield.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
**Who owns what, and through what.** BN is the parent; inside it sit: (1) the stake in BAM (~74%, the listed manager); (2) Wealth Solutions/insurance (the BNT/BWS paired security); (3) the operating businesses directly (BIP, BEP, BBUC, BPG). IMPORTANT: Brookfield's 13F holdings are client money under management and are NOT included in the holding company's portfolio analysis.

**Management's edge thesis (Bruce Flatt, letter of 14.05.2026).** Operational scale, patient entry and permanent capital, rather than guessing the macro. Quotes (from the IR shareholder letter PDF — the letter's provenance comes from the agent; its text was not re-opened in this check, see gaps):
- "Macro Events Are Mostly Irrelevant to Long Term Investing… over the last 30+ years our shareholders have realized annual compound returns of 19%".
- "Price is influenced by capital flows, sentiment… Value is determined by the cash flows a business generates… they will always converge in the longer term".

**Capital allocation rules (confirmed in the Supplemental).**
- The objective is growth in distributable earnings (DE) per share and in management's estimate of value per share.
- Opportunistic buybacks: >$1bn repurchased YTD ($470m BN + $575m BAM) "when their prices sold off".
- Monetisation discipline: sales "substantially all at or above carrying values".
- Capital reserve: $188bn deployable ($74bn of cash/facilities + $114bn of uncalled fund commitments); average corporate debt maturity of 15 years.

**Layers of the strategy.**
1. **Three themes:** digitalization, decarbonization, deglobalization. Decarbonization has been reframed: "no longer one of energy transition, but rather energy addition… renewables, nuclear, storage".
2. **"Watch, Learn, Invest, Perfect, Scale"** — the process for entering a new asset class; "among the largest builders of data centers globally".
3. **Private credit with Oaktree:** "private credit is simply credit… We have no material exposure to software in our credit or equity strategies" — an answer to the fears around SaaS lending.
4. **Structural simplification:** merging BN and BWS into Brookfield Corporation Ltd. (1-for-1, vote 16.07.2026) to reach ~$145bn of permanent capital.

**Targets (Investor Day 10.09.2025 — the primary presentations were opened and checked).** BAM by 2030: fee-bearing capital $1.2T (from $563bn; slides 59/60/66); **FRE $5.85bn** (from $2,695m, 17% a year; slides 62/66); fee revenues $10.05bn (from $5,030m; slide 62); DE $5.9bn (slides 63/66). The main driver of fee-bearing capital growth is credit ($254bn→$640bn, slide 60).

BN by 2030: **management's estimate $68 → $140 per share** (slide 119); Total DE/share $2.31 → $6.95, ~25% a year (slide 118). All per-share figures are after the 3-for-2 split of 09.10.2025 (the basis is stated on p.2 of BN's presentation).

⚠️ This previously read "fees ~$5.8bn" — that was **a labelling error: $5.85bn is FRE, not fees**; fee revenues are twice that ($10.05bn). The "$176/$210" pairing that used to sit here mixed a **$176 target for 2029 from the 2024 presentation** with a December 2025 target on a different share basis — do not use it.
co.brookfield.sections.6.deep.0.body: Brookfield is the world's largest owner of real infrastructure: power plants, ports, data centres, pipelines. 250,000 employees run those assets directly — this is an operator, not just a fund. The strategy: buy physical assets with predictable cash flow, improve the operations, and hold for decades on permanent capital from the insurance business. The main bet right now is that AI requires enormous physical infrastructure (power plus data centres plus chips) — and Brookfield already owns the whole chain, from generating the electricity to the server racks and leasing the GPUs. Half of what they manage today did not exist as an asset class 15 years ago. The core advantage: Brookfield takes on projects purely financial funds cannot — a 10.5 GW contract cannot be delivered with a cheque; it has to be physically built and commissioned. Brookfield has engineers, operators and construction crews, not just capital — which opens deals to it that are closed to anyone holding only money.

Position: one of the largest data centre builders in the world — 150+ sites across 4 continents through the Compass, Data4 and Ascenty platforms. How it earns: it builds and leases capacity to the tech giants on long contracts (a $100bn programme with NVIDIA and Kuwait's fund), and through Radiant leases compute directly to developers. The edge: it owns the whole chain — the land, the construction, the power — so it can take on projects pure funds cannot carry.
Position: $365bn under management, targeting $640bn by 2030; the group's fastest-growing segment. How it earns: it has bought specialists for each type of credit — Oaktree (distressed debt, a $16bn fund, a record for the class), Castlelake (asset-based credit, aircraft leasing) and Angel Oak (mortgages). The edge: it lends when banks are afraid, and is waiting for a wave of expensive leveraged buyout refinancings in 2027–2028.

How it earns: it sells electricity directly on long contracts (Microsoft — 10.5 GW; Google — 3 GW from hydro) and builds reactors against government orders ($80bn, a $17.5bn DOE loan). The edge: AI demand needs all of it at once — renewables through Brookfield Renewable, and nuclear.
Position: it buys the best buildings in the world's main business districts and re-rates them through rents. How it earns: $60bn deployed over 5 years; Manhattan West in New York was built at $1,000 per sq ft and is now worth $2,500, with rents three times the first lease. The edge: the scale and quality of the assets let it lease faster than the market — the London tower One Leadenhall filled in six months, against overall occupancy of 96%.

How it earns: it gathers long-dated money by buying insurers — American Equity, Britain's Just Group, American National — and puts 30–40% into its own funds at a ~2 percentage point uplift. The edge: this capital does not have to be returned on a schedule, which makes it well suited to funding 30-year infrastructure.
Position: the seventh flagship fund (BCP VII) — a $6bn first close against a $12.5bn target. How it earns: it buys control of companies and grows their earnings itself. They watch an industry for years, learn its economics, enter cautiously, perfect the operations and only then scale. "We are not first in — but once we understand it, we move fast and at scale".
What they look for in an asset

A real physical asset with predictable cash flow, inflation protection and room for operational improvement. Quality and location matter more than a low price; they buy what can be held for decades, not flipped. Every asset must stand on its own, without leaning on the rest of the group.
The investment committee thinks almost entirely about not losing. Target returns: 6–8% in a bad case, 12–15% in a normal one, 20%+ in a good one. Every asset is financed separately — one asset's debt cannot drag the others down.
"Going against the crowd is hard — but it is the most profitable thing you can do". Manhattan West broke ground at the height of COVID, when nobody was building; rents there are now three times the first lease.
"You cannot compound at 17% for thirty years and make large mistakes — it is not possible". Hence long debt (15 years on average) and separate financing for every asset. A painting hangs in Brookfield's offices of a herd running off a cliff — a reminder not to follow the crowd.
"Over 30+ years shareholders have earned 19% a year, and macro events barely mattered". Tariffs, rates, geopolitics — "one day all of it will be forgotten". They earn on the cash flows of businesses, not on guessing cycles.
Buy back stock below value — an iron rule

They have repurchased more than $1bn year to date at ~$41 against their own $66 estimate (a ~40% discount). "We do not like issuing shares below their fair value". The dividend is kept minimal ($0.28/yr) — capital goes into buybacks and reinvestment.

**What they believe** (from the Q1 2026 letter / earnings call; provenance from VOICE, the text was not re-opened in this check):
- The macro is secondary to long-term returns: "macro events… tend to attract disproportionate attention relative to their long-term impact".
- A strong dollar is a positive: "operations predominantly in the U.S. or hedged to the U.S. dollar, we have benefitted commensurately".
- Capital is moving into quality: "capital increasingly shifting toward quality assets… underpinned by essential services and real assets".
- AI = structural demand for power: "The demand for energy is at an unprecedented high" (Connor Teskey, BAM Q1 2026 call).
- On power: "low-cost renewables, flexible gas, and dependable nuclear" (Teskey).

**What they avoid / the risk**
- Software/SaaS exposure in private credit: "no material exposure to software".
- The retail end of listed credit: "our products represent a disproportionately small component".

**What they are watching**
- How long the trade disruptions last; the path of rates and cut expectations; possible dislocation in credit as an entry point for opportunistic credit.

**Dated points from the investor letter (Q1 2026):**
1. 14.05.2026 — $67bn raised YTD; deployable ~$188–200bn (the Supplemental confirms $188bn).
2. 14.05.2026 — Just Group closed; total insurance assets → $180bn (+$40bn).
3. 14.05.2026 — the BN+BWS merger, to reach ~$145bn of permanent capital.
4. 14.05.2026 — Wealth Solutions: book equity $13.2bn, cash flow $2.0bn, ROE 15%, P&C combined ratio 99% (from the BN press release, not re-opened).
5. 08.05.2026 — Teskey: the infrastructure and PE flagships are "expected to be their largest vintages ever" (the 8-K confirms the launches).
6. 19.11.2025 — the Brookfield AI Infrastructure programme launched ($100bn of assets; NVIDIA and the Kuwait Investment Authority as partners; a $5bn framework with Bloom Energy) — from a BAM press release, not re-opened in this check.
$74bn of cash and credit facilities plus $114bn of commitments from fund investors not yet called
under management through Oaktree and the credit platforms — the group's largest asset class
Top sector by sales this year
the largest Q1'26 exit — sold "at or above carrying values", with the proceeds going into new construction
the programme with NVIDIA and Kuwait's fund — where most of the fresh capital is going right now
new capital YTD as of the 14.05.2026 letter — the freshest figure on money coming into the funds
They sell the mature and the finished — offices, completed data centres, solar and wind farms — and put the proceeds into construction: AI infrastructure, nuclear, credit platforms. In Q1'26 ~$17bn of assets were sold "at or above carrying values". For example: they sold the mature Data4 data centre platform for $3.6bn and put the money into building new ones through Compass.
The model: buy → improve → sell higher → recycle into the next thing
Physical infrastructure (power plants, ports, data centres, pipelines) delivers predictable cash flow and inflation protection. AI only reinforces that: it needs the physical world — electricity and data centres, not just software. For example: Westinghouse (nuclear) and Compass (data centres) are the physical layer under AI demand.
"The binding constraint on AI is not capital but access to electricity" — Flatt
They believe: real assets are the backbone of the economy
Banks are retreating from lending and private funds are taking the space. For Oaktree a crisis is not a threat but an entry point: it buys distressed debt when everyone panics and earns on the recovery. For example: Oaktree — $203bn of distressed debt, buying when others sell.
"The best returns come when liquidity is scarce" — Oaktree
They believe: private credit is replacing the banks
Insurance money (annuities, pensions) does not have to be returned to clients on a schedule — which makes it ideal fuel for 30-year infrastructure assets. Hence Brookfield's insurer acquisitions. For example: buying Just Group added +$40bn of long-dated money.
$180bn of assets; 30–40% invested back into its own funds
"We do not try to predict which AI models or chips will win". They avoid technology risk and speculative software lending — instead of betting on one company they own the infrastructure every player needs at once. For example: rather than betting on one AI model, they own the data centres every player leases.
"No material exposure to software credit" — their answer to the fears around SaaS
They do NOT believe in picking winners in technology
Three forces — digitalisation, decarbonisation, deglobalisation — converge on a single point: data centres and the electricity to run them. It is a bet on decades, not quarters; the aim is to compound capital at 15–19% a year, as over the past 30. For example: the 10.5 GW Microsoft contract is digitalisation (data centres) and clean power in one deal.
"Value is determined by a business's cash flow, not by rate cycles" — Flatt

co.brookfield.sections.8.deep.1.title: Calendar
Management values the company at $66.37 a share while the market pays ~$42.87 — a discount of about 35% (and management itself has been buying stock back at that same ~$41). That is the whole thesis: we are buying below what the company says it is worth. If the gap narrows towards 20% the bet pays off; if it widens past 45% while fees keep growing, buying gets more attractive still.
$11.8bn of fund profits are accrued on paper, but only $528m turned into actual cash over the last year. The market simply does not believe the paper will become cash — hence the entire discount. If the flow accelerates to $1.5–2bn a year the thesis is confirmed and it is worth adding; if it stays flat, the market is right not to pay for carry.
Fees are the group's most stable and most valuable income: $772m in the quarter (+11% YoY) and $3.1bn for the year (+18%). Healthy means growth of at least 11% a year. The moment fee-bearing capital grows below 8%, the machine is slowing — and that is a signal to reduce.
The company sold $17bn of assets in the quarter "at or above carrying values" — which proves the balance sheet marks are real rather than drawn. As long as sales clear at the marks, the balance sheet can be trusted; once assets start selling at a discount to it, the whole valuation comes into question.
The company may repurchase up to 191m shares (10% of the free float) over a year and has already spent $470m on BN (~$41 a share) and $575m on BAM. If management is buying, management thinks the stock is cheap. Accelerating the buyback at a low price is a strong signal; stopping it is a reason to take notice.
In the US the company does not disclose its executives' personal transactions (foreign private issuer); they appear only in Canada's SEDI database at sedi.ca. Large sales by executives are an early warning. So far the corporate signal points the other way: buybacks are running and the dividend was raised 17%.

co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.0.body: Brookfield is a bet that the physical world is worth more than the digital one. While the market pays 30-40x for a SaaS subscription, Brookfield buys the power plants, ports and data centres without which that SaaS does not run. $1T under management, $175bn of its own assets, 250,000 people on site — not a fund but an operator on the scale of a state. The thesis stands on three legs: a ~35% discount to management's own valuation (>$1bn of buybacks year to date at ~$41 — management thinks the stock is cheap), $11.8bn of unrealised fund profits (which turn into cash as assets are sold — $91bn was sold over the year at or above carrying values), and an AI/power option that is not in the price ($200bn of data centres, Westinghouse with the only licensed reactor in the US, the 10.5 GW Microsoft contract).
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essence
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.1.body: Concentration: 55-59% of BN's value is the management company plus future fund profits. A blow to one hits both. BAM's fees grow more slowly than peers' (+11% against APO +30%, KKR +24%). The insurance business is at the margin (a 99% combined ratio), and after the BN+BWS merger any losses move onto the parent balance sheet. The $11.8bn of carry is a promise, not a fact: only $528m turned into cash over 12 months. The main reason for the discount is that BN's accounting profit is falling ~35% a year on paper revaluations of buildings and funds. The multi-listing structure (BN, BAM, BIP, BEP) puts investors off — the market wants proof that fund profits become cash rather than staying on paper.
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
The merger is approved on 16.07.2026 and the discount narrows towards 20%. Carry starts converting: $2-3bn over 12 months instead of $528m. The AI programme lands its first construction contracts. The DOE documents the loan and Westinghouse re-rates towards $30bn+. Buybacks continue below intrinsic value. Flatt holds 18m shares personally, PVI 121m.
Rates stay higher for longer and asset sales freeze. Carry stays on paper for another 2-3 years. BAM loses share: fundraising slows and fee growth falls below 10%. The insurance business burns capital (a combined ratio above 100%). Westinghouse is a good business, but without new reactors it is not a transformation. The $26.9bn of real estate is marked down. Total DE keeps falling.
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.2.title: Two scenarios
Hold the position as a single line through BN (which already contains the stake in the BAM management company). Add on: a discount above 40% (a price below $40), or a quarter with carry accelerating after the BN+BWS merger closes; BAM fee growth of +15%+ YoY confirms the picture. Reduce on: an insurance combined ratio above 100%, or BAM fee-bearing capital growth below 8% YoY — which would mean the machine is losing market share.
16.07.2026 — the BN+BWS vote (the key one). 06.08.2026 — the Q2 report (the test: fees above $3.1bn over 12 months, carry accelerating). 2026 — DOE definitive financing for Westinghouse

co.brookfield.summary: Brookfield Corporation (BN) is the world's largest owner of real infrastructure. It manages ~$1T through funds and owns $175bn of assets outright: power plants, ports, data centres, real estate, pipelines. 250,000 employees run those assets directly — this is an operator, not just a fund. Fees are $3.1bn/yr (+18%). The main bets: AI infrastructure (a $200bn pipeline), nuclear power (Westinghouse) and private credit (Oaktree). It trades at a ~35% discount to management's own valuation.
co.brookfield.tagline: BN is the parent holding company: its stake in BAM plus accrued fund profits make up ~59% of asset value; the market holds it at a ~35% discount to management's own estimate ($66.37 vs ~$43).
co.brookfield.topBets.items.0.fact: It builds reactors and services operating nuclear plants for decades — a continuous income stream (co-owned with Cameco). The bet: only nuclear supplies round-the-clock clean electricity, and AI and data centres need ever more of it.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.1.fact: It builds vast data campuses on long leases to Microsoft and other giants — contracted money, not speculation. The bet: own the buildings AI runs in, rather than guess which AI company wins.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.2.fact: $209bn under management; the profile is distressed debt (the legendary Howard Marks), and earnings rise precisely in a crisis. The bet: private credit is replacing the banks and is the group's fastest-growing business.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.3.fact: Its battery is in one car in three worldwide, petrol and electric alike; ~80% of sales are replacements. The bet: steady cash flow that Brookfield makes more efficient.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.4.fact: 20m+ sq ft of offices and housing in London; Brookfield is reworking a district hit by remote working into housing and laboratories. The bet: quality property in a top location recovers.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.4.role: A business district in central London
co.brookfield.verdict.proofs.0: A ~35% discount to management's estimate ($66 vs ~$43) on quality assets
co.brookfield.verdict.proofs.1: The management franchise is growing: fees +18% YoY, fee-bearing capital $614bn
co.brookfield.verdict.proofs.2: Optionality on AI and power: 10.5 GW for Microsoft plus Westinghouse plus the $100bn AI programme
co.brookfield.verdict.rationale: A quality portfolio of real assets plus a growing management franchise, trading at a ~35% discount to management's own estimate — the asymmetry favours the upside.
co.brookfield.verdict.trigger: Add if the discount deepens past 40% or if the realisation of fund profits is confirmed; reduce if debt with recourse to BN rises or monetisations stall.

co.constellation.sections.0.bodyMarkdown:
Constellation is not a classic portfolio of stakes but a consolidated holding company. Its six core operating groups are aggregated into ONE reporting segment under IFRS 8 (since 2020), so revenue by group (Volaris, Harris, Jonas, Vela, Perseus) is **not disclosed** in the accounts — which is why line-by-line figures by group are unavailable in primary sources (see "Gaps"). Only Topicus, Lumine and Altera are disclosed as supplemental (source: the Q1 2026 MD&A [1]).

**Ring 1 — with a disclosed valuation or segment figures (Q1 2026 supplemental, $m, source: the Q1 2026 MD&A [1]):**

| Unit | Vehicle / CSI stake | Q1'26 revenue | Q1'26 net income | Valuation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSI ex-Topicus/Lumine | direct control (Volaris/Harris/Jonas/Vela/Perseus) | $2,466m | $318m | inside the CA$59.72bn market cap |
| Topicus.com (TSXV:TOI) | a super voting share (50.1% of the votes) plus ~31.3% of the economics; 48.6% subordinate voting | $507m | $63m | Listed, TSXV |
| Lumine Group (TSXV:LMN) | a super voting share (50.1% of the votes) plus 61.40% of the economics (157,553,539 subordinate voting shares) | $208m | $20m | Listed, TSXV |
| Altera | 100%, inside N. Harris | $147m | $7m | inside the market cap |
| Asseco Poland (WSE:ACP) | ~23.14% (an associate, equity method, a 3-month lag) | share of profit $11m | — | Listed, WSE |

The nine operating groups (source: CSI Operating Groups [10]):
- **Volaris** — "over 240 businesses", "more than 40 different vertical markets", "60+ countries", first acquisition 1995 (Ring 2)
- **Harris** (N. Harris Computer) — "Public Sector, Healthcare, Utilities, Private Sector and Insurance markets globally" (Ring 2)
- **Jonas Software** — "over 20+ years of experience", niche VMS (Ring 2)
- **Vela** — industrial and resource verticals (energy, marine, mining through acQuire) (Ring 2)
- **Perseus** — telecom, insurance, business software (Ring 2)
- **Topicus.com** — pan-European VMS (Ring 1, see the table)
- **Lumine Group** — "Since 2014", "30+ businesses", communications and media software (Ring 1, see the table)
- **Modaxo** — "people transportation" technology (Ring 2)
- **Andromeda** — a long-term holder of software businesses (Ring 2)

**Ring 2 (named, without a separate valuation):** Sygnity (Topicus Coop owns ~72.68%); inside Topicus — fintech, education (Eduarte), healthcare, public sector; inside CSI — dozens of niches across ~100+ verticals. Altera = the former Allscripts Hospitals & Large Physician Practices, bought by N. Harris on 02.05.2022.

**Concentration / geography / themes:** consolidated Q1'26 revenue of $3,181m; ~78% CSI core, ~16% Topicus, ~7% Lumine (calculated from the supplemental [1]). Geography: North America plus Europe (Topicus — the Netherlands/Germany/Scandinavia/Poland); ~100+ verticals reduce concentration in any one market. Themes: maintenance and recurring revenue is the main driver (maintenance organic growth +4% in Q1'26, [1]).

Revenue composition Q1 2026 (source: the Q1 2026 MD&A [1]):
- Maintenance and other recurring: ~$2,444m (~77% of revenue) — the core of the business
- Professional services: ~$546m; Hardware and other: ~$100m; Licences: ~$91m

co.constellation.sections.1.bodyMarkdown:
Q1 2026 deals: **$809m of total consideration** ($697m cash plus $112m of deferred payments) — a record for a first quarter (historically a quiet one) (source: the Q1 2026 press release [3], MD&A [1]). Cash outflow on businesses in investing activities was $766m, less $77m of acquired cash.

The largest deal of the quarter was **Synchronoss Technologies**, bought through Lumine Group and closed 13.02.2026: "aggregate cash consideration of $309.3 million" (source: the Lumine Q1 2026 press release [7]). Synchronoss is a SaaS personal-cloud platform for telecom operators; it was delisted from Nasdaq. The deal explains Lumine's +17% revenue growth on 0% organic growth and its −56% fall in FCFA2S (integration costs). NOTE: an earlier announcement carried an implied equity value of ~$116.4m / an EV of ~$258.4m — that was pre-closing framing; the final **cash consideration paid of $309.3m** is confirmed by Lumine's closing press release [7].

**Subsequent events (announced 12.05.2026):** acquisitions completed or contracted for $627m of cash at closing plus $159m of expected deferred payments = **$786m of total consideration** (source: the Q1 2026 MD&A / press release [1][3]). The verticals: local government, printing, financial services, healthcare, security, education, marketing, gaming, aviation, justice, manufacturing, mining, asset management, utilities, legal, defence, dealer, travel.

**Total capital deployed in H1'26 ≈ $1.6bn** ($809m in Q1 plus $786m announced), which management reads as an answer to the market's "AI fear" (context: levelheadedinvesting [16], flagged as secondary).

**Dry powder (at 31.03.2026, source: the Q1 2026 MD&A [1]):** cash $3,010m, debt $3,990m, net debt ~$979m. The CSI Facility is an unsecured revolving line with a $1,085m limit (expanded from $840m in January 2024). ~$1,095m of the cash is "trapped" in Topicus, Lumine and subsidiaries with non-recourse debt and cannot be freely distributed up to CSI.

Additionally: DerbySoft through Vela/Juniper Group — agreed 14.04.2026, closing 01.06.2026 (a majority stake; the price is not disclosed, source: CSI press releases [12]).

**PENDING:** $786m of subsequent-event deals (some closed, some open commitments) — see s04.

co.constellation.sections.3.bodyMarkdown:
**1. AI disruption of niche VMS (high, playing out in the price).** The trigger: the market assumes generative AI will devalue legacy VMS (hence the −42.6% over the year). Management's counter-argument: prices for private assets at the "lower end" have not fallen (CIO Anzarouth, secondary context [16]). The trigger metric: accelerating churn in maintenance revenue (organic maintenance growth is still +4%, [1]).

**2. Slowing organic growth (medium-high, partly realised).** FX-adjusted organic growth is only +2% (Q1'26) / +3% (FY2025); licences −13% FX-adjusted. The growth rests on acquired growth (source: [1][6]).

**3. Falling deal ROIC as sizes and competition rise (medium).** Growing capital to deploy ($1.6bn in H1'26) against a fixed hurdle rate may force larger and more expensive deals (Altera, Synchronoss, Asseco are all larger than the historic bolt-ons).

**4. Key person / succession (medium-high, near term).** Mark Leonard stepped down as President (September 2025) and did not stand for re-election to the board after the AGM of 15.05.2026 (source: the press release of 27.03.2026 [5][12]); he remains an adviser on PEMS. The President is Mark Miller. The risk is to the capital allocation culture after the founder's departure.

**5. Integration risk on large turnaround assets (medium).** Altera (organic −13%), Synchronoss (Lumine FCFA2S −56%).

**6. Structural / liquidity (low-medium).** ~$1,095m of cash is trapped in Topicus, Lumine and non-recourse subsidiaries; net debt is $979m ([1]).

**7. Revaluation volatility in earnings (medium).** The IRGA/TSS membership liability and the Asseco/Sygnity revaluation produce non-cash swings in net income (a $252m charge in FY2025; a +$76m reversal in Q1'26) — which distorts net income as a metric ([6][1]).
co.constellation.sections.3.deep.0.body: Constellation has two kinds of risk: risks to the **model** (scale starting to work against it, hurdles eroding, AI undermining niche software) and risks of **transition** (Leonard has gone, disclosure has been reduced, the spin-outs complicate the structure). The model risks are slow, but if they materialise they break everything. The transition risks have already partly materialised (the stock is −50%), but the mitigants are strong (Miller, the culture, record deployment).

Deployment consistently below $1.5bn a quarter; rising special dividends
Average deal size rising; average IRR falling (proxied through TOI/LMN)
FX-neutral organic growth below 2% for several quarters
Operating presidents leaving; insider purchases falling away
New covenant breaches; rising non-recourse debt
Impairments above $200m a year; a widening gap between IFRS net income and FCFA2S

co.constellation.sections.3.deep.1.title: The risk matrix
co.constellation.sections.3.deep.2.items: On a base of $11.6bn, 15% growth requires ~$1.7bn of new revenue a year. Organic growth (~2%) delivers ~$230m — the rest ($1.4–1.5bn) has to come from acquisitions. At multiples of 1.5–2.5× that means deploying $2–3.5bn. The mechanism: either you lower the hurdle (ROIC erosion), or deal sizes rise (PE competition), or you return cash to shareholders.
So far Q1'26 ($809m) and the ~$1.6bn year to date refute the thesis

VMS moats rest on switching costs, regulatory embeddedness and the uneconomics of rewriting. AI genuinely lowers the cost of building replacement software — a threat to "thin" SaaS (Perseus, Jonas). What AI does NOT erode: data gravity, compliance certification, integration (Harris utilities, Topicus public sector).
Leonard (the AI webcast): AI threatens "thin" SaaS more, and deep bundled VMS less

The President's Letter (with the combined ratio and IRR vintages) has not been published since 2021 — that is precisely the disclosure now unavailable. Large deals (Altera, Synchronoss) are done at the lower 20% hurdle, which mechanically drags the average ROIC down. PE is pushing entry multiples up.

Other listed comparables (the Scandinavian serial acquirers — Vitec, Lifco, Lagercrantz) are not verified in this dossier. Conclusion for the decision: CSU trades on a de-rating (P/E 57.6, P/FCFA2S ~23x — at the bottom of its own history) while still growing revenue and FCFA2S at a double-digit rate; the argument leans to hold/add for a long-term holder who believes VMS is durable against AI.
co.constellation.sections.5.deep.0.title: Comparison with competitors
co.constellation.sections.5.deep.1.body:
**The advantage:** 30 years of compounding — 1,000+ acquisitions, not one of them sold. Every business sits on a captive maintenance base with ~0% churn and an annual price increase (CPI-linked). A decentralised culture and mandatory share ownership keep managers in place. Nobody else has that combination of scale, discipline and culture in VMS.

**The proof:** a combined ratio above 30% for more than ten consecutive years; revenue from $25m (2006) to $11.6bn (2025); FCFA2S +44% in Q1'26 with the stock at its cheapest in four years. Competitors (Roper, Enghouse) are either smaller in scale or less disciplined (Roper has lowered its IRR to ~15%).

**Why it is hard to replicate:** it takes 30 years to build trust in niche verticals ("we will never sell your business"). It takes a culture you cannot buy — only grow. And it takes the scale for large carve-outs (Altera, Synchronoss) that smaller acquirers cannot reach.

**The honest trade-off:** the model works while there are enough VMS targets. The law of large numbers presses: on a $12bn base you need $2–3bn of deployment a year. Disclosure is thin — one segment, and no combined ratio since 2021. Leonard has gone — a culture-versus-system test. AI may erode the moats of the "thin" VMS businesses.

**Conclusion for the decision:** is a stock 50% off its peak an entry into a proven compounding machine, or the start of a regime shift? EV/EBITDA of ~13× against a historic 30–60×. The answer depends on whether Miller keeps the discipline while accelerating deployment. The FY2026 annual report (March 2027) is the moment of truth.

co.constellation.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
**Who they are.** Constellation Software Inc. (TSX:CSU) is a serial acquirer of vertical market software (VMS): it buys, holds forever and develops small niche software businesses.

**Management.** Mark Leonard stepped down as President on 25.09.2025 on health grounds; the President is Mark Miller (source: MIC-EN-2026 [5]; the press release of 27.03.2026 [12]). Leonard did not stand for the board at the AGM of 15.05.2026. From 01.01.2026 Mark Miller has voluntarily given up salary and bonus (as Leonard did in 2023–2025) — a strong alignment signal: senior management earns only through the share price (source: MIC-EN-2026 [5]).

**The edge thesis (Leonard's letter of 15.02.2021 [4]).** Verbatim: "Most of our competitors maximise financial leverage and flip their acquisitions within 3-7 years. CSI ... We are permanent and supportive stakeholders in the businesses that we control". The advantage is permanent ownership plus decentralisation: "We allow tremendous autonomy to our business unit managers"; the groups grew "without succumbing to the siren song of increased centralisation, bureaucracy, and control".

**Capital allocation rules (the letter of 15.02.2021 [4]; the Q1 2026 MD&A [1]).**
1. The objective is to reinvest all FCFA2S into deals that clear the hurdle rate: "our objective is to invest all of our FCFA2S in acquisitions which meet our hurdle rate".
2. Hurdle rate discipline matters more than volume: "perennial inability to invest all of the cash that we generate".
3. Special dividends have stopped; the regular quarterly dividend ($1.00/quarter) is retained, but "will also be sacrificed" if better uses for the cash appear.

**Three layers of the strategy (the letter of 15.02.2021 [4]).**
1. **Small and mid-sized VMS** — the core. Most FCFA2S goes here, at the highest deal tempo.
2. **Large VMS** (cheques in the hundreds of millions): historically "less than 10% of our FCFA2S ... only three large VMS acquisitions during our entire 26 year history". CSI knew ~80% of the large VMS businesses that came up for sale and was invited into 16% — it is building a dedicated head office team.
3. **Outside the VMS circle of competence** (PEMS — Permanent Engaged Minority Shareholder): the newest and riskiest; "highly contrarian thinking". Topicus's Asseco investment is the model in action.

**The specific hurdle rates are NOT confirmed in primary sources.** The IRRs by deal size (~30%/25%/20%) circulate in secondary sources (In Practise [17]) and in Leonard's early letters; no primary filing carrying those numbers has been opened. The 2021 letter confirms only the structure (see "Gaps").

**The AI lens.** All year the market has valued CSU as if AI would hollow out VMS (the "SaaSpocalypse"). Management answered with action — accelerating capital deployment in Q1 2026. There is no explicit AI strategy stated in the public primary filings — it is a management narrative from the earnings call, not a filing quote.
co.constellation.sections.6.deep.0.body: Constellation is the world's largest disciplined serial acquirer of niche vertical market software (VMS): it buys mission-critical software across 100+ verticals, holds it forever and runs it decentrally. Six operating groups (Volaris, Harris, Topicus, Vela, Jonas, Perseus) work as "mini-Constellations" — each with its own CEO, its own deal authority and its own P&L. The head office sets the hurdle rate (IRR) and allocates capital, but does not interfere in operations. The key difference from PE: Constellation holds businesses indefinitely — competitors "maximise financial leverage and flip within 3--7 years" (Leonard, 2021). Financial policy: all FCFA2S (~$1.9bn TTM) is reinvested into deals above the hurdle; the dividend is minimal ($1 a quarter since 2016, unchanged); there are no buybacks; and the shares have never been split (21.2m of them at C$2,800). The engine runs on negative working capital — subscription revenue is collected in advance, and VMS businesses operate with negative net tangible assets. The two carved-out listed subsidiaries -- Topicus (TSXV:TOI) and Lumine (TSXV:LMN) -- are part of a spin-out playbook: CSU keeps control through a super voting share, while the managers get their own "currency" for deals. The key question now: the machine is designed not to depend on any one person, but Mark Leonard has gone (September 2025, on health grounds) and did not stand for re-election to the board (March 2026) — for the first time in 30 years Constellation is running without its founder.

scaling

The playbook can repeat: when an operating group grows large enough to deploy capital independently, it can be carved out. No new carve-outs have been announced, but Juniper Group (under Vela) is an example of a sub-structure forming.
Carving out subsidiaries (the spin-out playbook)

CSU shareholders receive shares in the subsidiary as a dividend in kind (tax-efficiently); the subsidiary gets its own "currency" for deals; CSU keeps consolidation and control through a super voting share; this also creates a growing NCI block ($692m of equity)

Healthcare, homebuilding and other verticals. Its approach is distinctive: it does not consolidate businesses but keeps them at their original scale. Potentially the most exposed to AI alongside Jonas — "thin" SaaS businesses with few people and little support.

co.constellation.sections.6.deep.3.title: The operating groups — how the machine works inside
co.constellation.sections.6.deep.4.items: The "never sell" doctrine: Constellation does not sell businesses as a matter of principle, even shrinking ones — all that matters is their ability to generate the required IRR. Unlike PE with a 3–7 year horizon, that lets it buy declining businesses if the IRR is adequate. "We are permanent and supportive stakeholders in the businesses that we control."
Never lower the hurdle — it drags everything down

Leonard analysed 20 years of deal vintages and concluded that lowering the hurdle rate "magnetically" drags down the expected IRR of every subsequent deal, so the company resists lowering it even when surplus cash accumulates. Better to return money to shareholders than to dilute the discipline.
Decentralisation is architecture, not a slogan

A thin head office; the CEO of each operating group works as a mini-CEO of Constellation, with deal authority and their own P&L. Large acquisitions are approved by the board, but operational decisions sit at business unit level. The groups grew "without succumbing to the siren song of increased centralisation, bureaucracy, and control" (Leonard, 2021).
Managers are tied in with shares

Bonuses are calculated from net income for bonus purposes and Average Invested Equity Capital; a meaningful share must be invested in CSU stock and held for years (escrow). Leonard voluntarily gave up salary and bonus in 2021–2025; Miller did the same from 2026. Senior management earns only through the share price.
Negative working capital as a structural advantage

"Our VMS businesses operate with negative working capital — management anticipates that it can continue to grow the business organically without any additional funding." Subscription revenue is collected in advance: the business funds itself and needs no external capital for organic growth.
Dividends are an admission of failure, not a goal

Special dividends were used as a release valve when capital could not be deployed at the hurdle rate; the practice has stopped. The regular quarterly dividend ($1.00/share) "will also be sacrificed" if better uses for the cash appear. Everything is subordinate to reinvestment.
AI is an opportunity, not a threat

Miller (Q1 2026 earnings call): AI is a greater threat to "thin" SaaS businesses (few people, sold over the internet, little support), while bundled software plus services in deep niche verticals is protected. In practice Constellation accelerates deployment into the AI panic — it sees deals above the hurdle and does not consider the VMS niche to be under threat.

**What they believe (from primary sources [4][1]).**
- Permanent ownership beats PE's flip model (competitors "maximise financial leverage and flip ... within 3-7 years").
- Reinvestment beats returning capital: dividends are an admission of an inability to deploy all the cash, not a goal.
- Hurdle rate discipline matters more than size.
- **Negative working capital as a structural advantage** (Q1 2026 MD&A): "our VMS businesses operate with negative working capital ... management anticipates that it can continue to grow the business organically without any additional funding" (maintenance is collected in advance).

**What they avoid.** Centralisation, bureaucracy, leverage for flipping, share dilution (21.2m unchanged), and lowering the hurdle rate in the small and mid-sized segment.

**What they watch (per their own disclosures).** Organic growth (the weak spot: FX-adjusted +2% in Q1'26; maintenance +4%, licences −13%, professional services −5%, hardware −7%); large VMS deals (they are invited into 16%); stakes in listed securities through Topicus (Asseco ~23.14% equity method; Sygnity) — whose share prices drive the IRGA revaluation.

**A signal in actions rather than words.** Amid the AI fears of 2026 the company raised deployment to a record level for a first quarter ($809m in the quarter plus $786m of commitments) — meaning it sees deals above the hurdle rate and does not consider the VMS niche to be under threat (the figures are from [1][3]; the AI context is secondary [16]).

co.constellation.sections.7.deep.1.items: deployment

A record acquisition pace precisely as the stock fell and AI panic set in. Q1'26 was $809m (six times Q1'25); a further $786m is contracted. The focus is widening: to the small bolt-ons (the core) they are adding large carve-outs (Synchronoss $309m, DerbySoft) and minority stakes in listed companies (Asseco/Sygnity through Topicus — $530m in FY2025).
A signal in action: they accelerate buying when the market is afraid — meaning they see deals above the hurdle rate
Where the money is moving
the thesis

"Most competitors maximise leverage and resell within 3-7 years." Constellation never sells a business — not even shrinking ones (Altera, -13% organic). That gives it unique access to VMS sellers: they prefer a permanent owner to a PE fund, because they know the business will not be broken up and resold.
"We are permanent and supportive stakeholders in the businesses that we control" — Leonard, the 2021 letter
They believe: permanent ownership beats PE's flip model

The AI webcast (September 2025) was a rare public appearance for Constellation. The position: AI is a greater threat to "thin" SaaS businesses (few people, sold over the internet), and a weak threat to bundled software plus services in deep verticals. VMS moats — switching costs, regulatory embeddedness, accumulated workflow data — are not broken by AI. The hurdle rate is the margin of safety: even with heightened uncertainty, a 20-30% hurdle absorbs the error.
Miller (Q1'26): "I look at AI as a chance to do more for customers, not to do the same thing more efficiently"
They believe: deep VMS is protected from AI
discipline

Leonard analysed 20 years of deal vintages and concluded that lowering the hurdle "magnetically" drags down the IRR of every subsequent deal. Three levels: 30% (small), 25% (medium), 20% (large). Dividends are not a goal but an admission of an inability to deploy all the cash: they "will be sacrificed" if better uses for capital appear. Special dividends have stopped — reinvestment takes priority.
The historic combined ratio (ROIC plus organic growth) stayed above 30% for more than a decade
They believe: hurdle rate discipline matters more than volume
what they avoid

The market sold the stock down more than 50% on fear that AI would devalue a thousand niche software businesses. Management's answer: prices for private VMS assets have not fallen, deal volumes have not shrunk, and the pipeline is alive. Baksh: "nothing has changed — the same volume in the market we have always seen". Constellation deliberately buys deeply embedded, mission-critical systems with high switching costs — not "thin" SaaS.
Baksh: "This is a great buying opportunity... We still buy shares in the market"
They do NOT believe AI will destroy the VMS model
the view

The company is opportunity-constrained, not capital-constrained: there is more free capital than there are suitable deals. The answer is to widen the perimeter: from strict VMS into hybrid businesses (hardware+software, data+software) and into the PEMS model (a permanent minority shareholder — Asseco being the example). Growth through carve-outs: Topicus and Lumine trade separately but are consolidated, creating "currency" for deals and motivation for the group managers.
Leonard: "narrowing the aperture is a bad idea"; the aim is to deploy all FCFA2S above the hurdle rate
