co.kkr.sections.5.deep.3.body:
**KKR** is the only large manager in the group that has both its own insurance balance sheet (Global Atlantic, wholly owned, ~$170bn+ of assets) and direct core PE capital on its balance sheet (Strategic Holdings). Proof of the efficiency: on half Blackstone's AUM ($758bn against $1.30T) it monetises just as well (81% against 72%) and collects two thirds of its fees — fee-related earnings (FRE) of $1.0bn against $1.55bn, with FRE per share +23% YoY. The honest negative: fundraising lags — inflows of ~$28bn in the quarter against ~$115bn at Apollo and ~$68.5bn at Blackstone; and Global Atlantic shares with Athene the risk of the NAIC tightening in 2026. The decision: a compressed multiple (the stock is ~−30% over the year), management buying the drawdown and the Strategic Holdings upside outweigh that → **hold/add**; the trigger against is inflows failing to recover while the NAIC tightens.

**Blackstone** is the largest by scale ($1.30T of AUM) and the most efficient at converting AUM into fees (72%, FRE $1.55bn). The asset-light model scales without freezing capital. Over 12 months it rebuilt its mix — 35% of AUM is now credit and insurance. The legacy: the BXMT mortgage REIT carries ~7% past due and pays dividends out of principal — an indicator that it has not fully exited the commercial property cycle.

**Apollo** grows fees fastest (+30% YoY) through a single channel: the Athene insurance arm raises capital through annuities, deploys it into loans and pays Apollo the fees (FPAUM $836bn, +40%). The closed loop delivers speed, but it is first in line for the NAIC's 2026 review of capital requirements — if the regulator tightens the rules, growth stops abruptly rather than gradually, because there is only one channel.

**Brookfield (BAM)** is the only owner-operator in the group: ~85,000 employees physically run assets, not money. The price of that is the worst AUM monetisation (61%) and the slowest fee growth (+11% against +23–30% for peers), but that same slowness creates the ~35% discount to management's estimate and the option on power for AI.

co.kkr.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
**Management's edge thesis (Q1'26 call, 05.05.2026):**
- Durability and diversification of earnings. CFO Rob Lewin: "We benefit from real stability and durability of earnings and increased visibility on how they will grow". In Q1'26 "85% of segment earnings are from the more durable and recurring portions" (FRE + insurance OE + Strategic Holdings OE) — ~$1.3bn of the $1.5bn of segment earnings.
- A 50-year record. The CEO in the release: "On May 1st, KKR celebrated its 50th anniversary... a half century of navigating cycles".
- AI as a cross-portfolio lever: 150+ portfolio companies are deploying AI (applicable to Asset Management and Infrastructure, not to Insurance or the roll-up).

**Capital allocation rules (Lewin, Q1'26 call):** "how we take our marginal dollar of cash flows and drive the most amount of recurring durable and growing earnings per share". There is no rigid formula — the decision is made at the margin on risk-adjusted return. Q1'26 priorities: (1) a $317m buyback (3.5m shares at $91.08); (2) M&A (Arctos closed 04.05.2026); (3) recapitalising Insurance as spreads widen; (4) growing Strategic Holdings. Employees own ~30% of KKR's stock (per the call) — the foundation of its long-term orientation.

**Layers of the strategy (2024 Investor Day, 10.04.2024, plus Q1'26):**
- 2026 targets: FRE/share above $4.50; TOE/share above $7; ANI/share $7-8 (revised on the Q1'26 call to "more likely below $7").
- Long term: ANI/share of $15+ within 10 years; AUM of $1T by 2030.
- Strategic Holdings OE: $350m+ in 2026 → $700m+ by 2028 → $1.1bn+ by 2030.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.0.body: KKR is a manager that has learned to own, not only to collect fees. The model rests on three economies that feed each other. The first is asset management: $758bn under management produces fee-related earnings (FRE) of $3.9bn a year, and it is the most predictable part. The second is insurance: KKR wholly owns Global Atlantic, which gathers annuity and retirement money; that is "permanent capital" ($326bn) — long-dated money that does not have to be returned to investors on a schedule and can be invested in KKR's own funds. The third is Strategic Holdings: KKR holds stakes in its best portfolio companies directly on its own balance sheet, not only in client funds, and collects rising dividends from them. The core advantage lies not in any one of the three but in how they interlock: fees fund growth, insurance capital provides the fuel and cheap long-dated liquidity, and the balance sheet stakes turn the funds' success into KKR's own profit. That is why all three metrics grow in step at ~20% a quarter (Nuttall, call of 05.05.2026). The other side: the balance sheet component makes results sensitive to the exit environment — when selling assets is unattractive, realised carry (a share of fund profits) and adjusted net income (ANI) sag, as happened with the 2026 target, which management lowered to "more likely below $7" a share, shifting some exits into 2027.

co.kkr.sections.6.deep.3.items.0.v: Position: six global data centre platforms plus an entry into the generation that feeds them (a JV with SK in Korea, $1.3bn, KKR 51%, 1.7 GW operating, targeting 10 GW by 2031). How it earns: it builds and leases capacity to hyperscalers on long contracts; $40bn+ deployed into digital infrastructure at an IRR above 20%. co.kkr.sections.6.deep.3.items.1.v: Position: $15bn of new capital into credit in a single quarter — the largest inflow of any strategy; direct lending is $39bn. How it earns: it lends around the banks and through secured portfolios (ABF); one example is the A$400m (~US$275m) Ampol financing of July 2026. The edge: the banks are retreating from lending, but KKR keeps the riskier retail credit small (the private BDC at 0.4% of AUM, FSK under 2%) — growth without concentration.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.3.items.2.v: Position: a wholly owned insurer, book value $11.66bn, Q1 operating earnings $260.3m. How it earns: it gathers long-dated annuities (80% of Q1 originations at 7+ years) and invests them in KKR's own funds. The edge: permanent capital for infrastructure; the risk has materialised — in Q1'26 the bond book took a GAAP investment loss of −$652.7m (10-Q), alongside tight spreads and fierce competition for liabilities (both acknowledged outright by management).
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.3.items.3.v: Position: the K-Series platform at $38bn (+80% YoY), with Q1 inflows of $4bn against $250m of redemptions; plus a dedicated Asian flagship (India, Japan). How it earns: it sells private markets products to private investors and across Asia. The edge: the two fastest-growing sources of new capital now that the institutional channel is saturated.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.3.items.4.v: Position: stakes in core PE companies on KKR's own balance sheet rather than only in client funds (6 of ~18 are named: USI, 1-800 Contacts, Heartland Dental, Internet Brands, Mills Fleet Farm, BMC Software). How it earns: it takes rising dividends from those stakes — segment operating earnings of $178.9m over 12 months, targeting $350m+ in 2026 and more than $1bn by 2030. The edge: it turns the funds' success into KKR's own profit — something the pure managers do not have.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.3.items.5.v: Position: Karo Healthcare €2.65bn (from EQT, consumer health); Biotage $1.22bn (Swedish life sciences); 51% of Thomson Reuters' Global Print business (~$500m); the Allyntra platform built around Precipart (medtech, launched July 2026). How it earns: control of companies plus improving their earnings directly. The edge: scale and sector teams give access to deals closed to purely financial funds. IMPORTANT: KKR's own equity share in each is not disclosed — only the fund deal sizes are public.

Each feeds the others: fees fund growth, insurance capital provides long-dated liquidity, and the balance sheet stakes turn the funds' success into KKR's profit. The interlock is the real edge.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.4.items.2.v: The structural target (Investor Day 2024): roughly 70% of pre-tax earnings from recurring sources (fees plus insurance economics), so the result depends less on one-off exits. That is also what makes FRE ($3.9bn a year) the anchor of the valuation.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.4.items.3.k: Do not sell a good asset into a bad environment

co.kkr.sections.6.deep.4.items.4.v: 80% of Q1 insurance originations ran 7+ years, against 37% for the whole of 2024. The logic: long-dated liabilities are an ideal match for 30-year infrastructure; but management is candid that spreads are tight and competition for liabilities is fierce.
co.kkr.sections.6.deep.4.items.5.v: The private BDC is 0.4% of AUM and the listed FSK under 2%. co.kkr.sections.6.deep.4.items.6.v: The dividend was raised to $0.78 — a seventh consecutive year. Buybacks are opportunistic: $317m year to date at ~$91. Capital goes into growing the business and into permanent capital rather than into an inflated dividend.

co.kkr.sections.7.bodyMarkdown:
**What they believe (Q1'26 call, 05.05.2026):**
- Long-duration insurance: 80% of Q1'26 originations had a duration of 7+ years (against 37% for the whole of 2024) — a bet on higher ROE once spreads normalise. Lewin: "$6 billion of dry powder equity... translates into $60-plus billion of buying power" in a dislocation.
- Digital infrastructure / the AI build-out is the main secular theme: $40bn+ deployed (KKR plus partners), a gross IRR above 20%, six global data centre platforms.
- Perpetual capital as a stabiliser: $326bn (43% of AUM, 51% of FPAUM — primary).

**What they avoid:** retail credit while spreads are compressed. Lewin: "Spreads are as tight as they've been in a very long time". They do not force exits in a weak monetisation window — they defer them rather than cancel them.

**What they watch:** the monetisation window (normalisation is the trigger for ANI); volatility as a signal for buybacks and for deploying insurance dry powder; the wealth channel (they expect a Q2 slowdown amid the noise around private credit redemptions).

**Recent dated points:**
1. **11.06.2026 (BusinessWire):** the launch of **Helix Digital Infrastructure** — $10bn+ of long-duration capital; anchor investors KKR, the Kuwait Investment Authority, NVIDIA and Vistra; CEO Adam Selipsky, formerly head of AWS. A direct AI lens.
2. **25.06.2026 (BusinessWire, intra-quarter update):** Q2'26 capital markets transaction fees are expected at ~$175m, with some transactions shifted from Q2 into Q3'26 — confirming the thesis that monetisations are being delayed.

co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.0.v: The stock is ~$100.94 (a ~$90.6bn market cap) — −34% over the year from a 52-week high of $153.87. Meanwhile management has repurchased $317m year to date at an average of ~$91, and the buyback mandate tops up automatically (+$500m when the remainder falls to ≤$50m). If KKR is buying, KKR thinks the stock is cheap. Accelerating the buyback at a low price is a strong signal; stopping it is a reason to take notice. (The price comes from market aggregators as at 22.07.2026, not from KKR's own filings.)
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.1.k: Carry realisation (the share of fund profits)
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.1.v: $18.3bn of embedded gains are accumulated on the balance sheet, but Q1 turned $720m of that into cash as realised carry (+120% YoY), with more than $900m monetised since 31.03 against a forward guide of more than $1.2bn — "the largest in the company's history" (Lewin). That is the whole ANI thesis: if the flow accelerates the $7 target is reachable and it is worth adding; if it stalls, the market is right to discount deferred exits.
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.2.k: Growth in management fees and FRE
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.2.v: Fees are the group's most stable income: management fees of $1.2bn in the quarter (+30% YoY) and fee-related earnings (FRE) of $3.9bn over 12 months at a ~69% margin. Healthy means the key metrics growing ~20% a quarter (Nuttall: "all of our key metrics grew about 20%"). The moment fee-paying AUM (FPAUM, $615bn today, +17%) grows below 8%, the machine is slowing — a signal to reduce.
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.3.v: Q1 raised $28bn (of which $15bn into credit), and $127bn over 12 months; uncalled investor commitments of $125bn sit at an all-time high. The fastest new channel is K-Series retail: $38bn (+80% YoY), with Q1 inflows of $4bn against redemptions of just $250m. While inflows grow, the fuel for future fees is there; slowing fundraising is an early signal for the whole model.
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.4.v: KKR's largest balance sheet position: book value rose from $9.48bn to $11.66bn over the year, with Q1 operating earnings of $260.3m. But in the same quarter the segment posted net investment-related losses of $652.7m (a GAAP line driven by marks and spreads) — read it alongside the positive operating earnings rather than as a net loss. Management acknowledges outright that "spreads are as tight as they've been in a very long time" (Lewin). Further compression of investment income is a direct risk to the main balance sheet bet.
co.kkr.sections.8.deep.2.items.5.v: The listed BDC managed by KKR is a direct read-through on the credit quality of the portfolio. In Q1 its NAV fell to $18.83 (−9.9% QoQ), non-accruals rose to 4.2% at fair value / 8.1% at cost (from 5.5%), and the distribution was cut from $0.48 to $0.42. KKR has responded with a $600m plan and a fee waiver for four quarters. Further growth in non-accruals is a warning; NAV stabilising after the $150m injection would confirm the bottom is in.

co.kkr.sections.9.bodyMarkdown:
*The analyst's interpretation based on disclosed facts. Not a valuation, and no DCF.*

**What the recent events mean:**
- The gap between FRE and ANI is structural rather than a crisis. FRE +24% and management fees +30% YoY show the fee base growing towards the $4.50+ target. Lowering the ANI guide below $7 and shifting capital markets fees to ~$175m with deals moving into Q3 is a problem of monetisation-window timing, not deteriorating fundraising. The "quality" of the earnings is protected; only the carry and realisation component is volatile.
- Helix ($10bn+, KKR/KIA/NVIDIA/Vistra) turns the AI thesis into a distinct capital pool. It supports FPAUM growth and future management fees.
- FSK (the BDC) is the main negative signal out of the ecosystem. NAV −9.9% in the quarter, non-accruals up to 4.2% at fair value, a distribution cut and an emergency $300m package — visible deterioration in credit quality at the lower end of direct lending. The direct effect on KKR's holdco is small (FSK is a vehicle, not KKR's balance sheet), but it is (a) a reputational and fundraising headwind for credit and the K-Series wealth channel, and (b) an early indicator of stress in private credit.

**Structural impact:**
- Strategic Holdings is back-end-weighted towards the $350m+ target; the EBITDA contribution (KKR's share, ~$1.1bn LTM) delivers rising dividends regardless of the exit window. Positive for durability.
- Insurance (GA, book value $11.66bn) — the pivot into long duration (80% of originations at 7+ years) plus $6bn of dry powder is an option on ROE rising as spreads widen; the current ROE is below the low-double-digit target — a headwind.

**Signals (triggers, not valuation levels):**
- **HOLD / ADD triggers:** (1) Q2'26 confirming capital markets fees of ≥$175m and Strategic Holdings OE heading to $350m; (2) the $1.2bn+ of forward monetisations actually closing; (3) spreads widening → insurance ROE turning up; (4) Helix scaling with new investors.
- **TRIM / CUT triggers:** (1) non-accruals rising further at FSK → systemic rather than idiosyncratic credit stress; (2) monetisations deferred again → the ANI target at risk for two consecutive quarters; (3) the K-Series wealth channel slowing while redemptions continue; (4) insurance OE stagnating with the dry powder undeployed despite volatility.
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.0.body: KKR is a manager that has learned to own, not only to collect fees. While the market pays 30x for software, KKR builds power plants and data centres and lends to companies around the banks — and keeps part of it on its own balance sheet. $758bn under management, fee-related earnings (FRE) of $3.9bn over 12 months, and its own insurer Global Atlantic (book value $11.66bn) — not a fund but a machine of three economies: asset management, insurance permanent capital and the balance sheet stakes of Strategic Holdings. The thesis rests on three pillars. The first is the de-rating: at $100.94 the stock is 34% below its $153.87 peak and trades at ~19.8x adjusted net income (ANI of $5.10 over 12 months) against ~30x at the peak — while the business grew ~20% in the quarter. The second is $18.3bn of embedded gains: unrealised carry (a share of fund profits) that turns into cash as exits happen — realised carry in the quarter was $720m (+120% YoY). The third is an AI and power option that is not in the price: $40bn+ deployed into digital infrastructure at a gross IRR above 20%, six data centre platforms, and an entry into the generation that feeds them (a $1.3bn JV with SK in Korea, a 51% stake, targeting 10 GW by 2031).
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essence
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.1.body: The exit environment is weak — and it already shows in the numbers. Total investing earnings fell to $932m over 12 months from ~$1.2bn, management lowered the 2026 ANI target to "more likely below $7", and some monetisations have slipped into 2027. That is not a break in the fee model but realised carry (a share of fund profits) moving in time — yet the market pays for the fact, not the promise. Global Atlantic, the largest balance sheet position ($11.66bn), posted −$653m of net GAAP investment losses in Q1'26 (alongside $1.9bn of positive net investment income) — part of those valuations are mark-to-model rather than market, and management acknowledges outright that spreads are tight and competition for insurance liabilities is fierce. The managed BDC FSK is visibly degrading: NAV/share $18.83 (−9.9% QoQ), non-accruals of 4.2% at fair value / 8.1% at cost, and the distribution cut from $0.48 to $0.42 — KKR is propping it up with its own money ($150m of convertible preferred plus a $150m tender at $11.00) and by waiving 100% of the incentive fee for four quarters. Add the divergence between GAAP earnings and ANI, key-person risk (Kravis/Roberts) and dilution from the Series D mandatory convertible ($2.59bn, 6.25%). Until carry turns into cash, the multiple stays at ~18–19x.
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.desc: The Q2'26 report (30.07–04.08) shows the turn: total investing earnings return to $1.2bn+ and 12-month ANI breaks through $7. Realised carry accelerates — the $1.2bn+ of forward monetisations after 31.03 close out ("the largest forward guide in the company's history", Lewin). The multiple recovers towards the ~$125.53 consensus (~24.6x). Global Atlantic stabilises its marks and the −$653m GAAP loss does not recur. The buyback continues below intrinsic value ($317m year to date at ~$91), and the dividend rises for a seventh consecutive year to $0.78. The long-run path to $15+ ANI a share is reaffirmed.
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.title: Bull
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.2.items.1.desc: Rates stay higher for longer, exits freeze and carry stays on paper into 2027. 2026 ANI falls short of $7. FSK degrades further: non-accruals above 5% of fair value, and the $300m of support is not enough. Global Atlantic takes new GAAP investment losses after the −$653m, spreads stay tight and competition for liabilities squeezes returns. The multiple sticks at ~18x or de-rates towards the 52-week low of $82.67. Total investing earnings keep falling from $932m.
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.2.items.1.title: Bear
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.2.title: Two scenarios
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.3.items.0.v: Hold the position as a single line through KKR & Co. (which contains asset management, Global Atlantic and the Strategic Holdings balance sheet stakes). Add on: a quarter in which monetisations turn — total investing earnings returning to $1.2bn+ and 12-month ANI above $7; realised carry accelerating above $720m a quarter confirms the picture. Reduce on: FSK non-accruals above 5% of fair value, or new GAAP investment losses at Global Atlantic after the −$653m — which would mean the balance sheet side is burning capital rather than compounding it.
co.kkr.sections.9.deep.3.items.1.v: 30.07–04.08.2026 — the Q2'26 report (the key test: total investing earnings above $1.2bn, ANI/share heading to $7, realised carry accelerating). 2026 — the legal close of the Korean SK JV (power for AI); the roll-out of the $600m FSK support plan. Medium term — the path to $15+ ANI a share (Investor Day 2024).

co.kkr.summary: KKR is one of the world's largest alternative asset managers: it runs $758bn of other people's money for a fee plus a share of its funds' future profits. On the balance sheet sits its own insurer, Global Atlantic ($220bn of assets), a source of permanent capital. Money flows in two directions: into private credit (the listed fund FSK — also the main stress signal) and into infrastructure for AI — the Helix data centres alongside NVIDIA. Fees grow at a double-digit rate, but profit rose only 5%: the window for selling assets has shifted to 2027. The stock is 34% off its peak, and both co-CEOs bought the dip.
co.kkr.tagline: A global alternative asset manager (AUM $757.9bn): the fee base is growing (FRE +14% LTM, a 69% margin), but ANI rose only 5% because monetisations slipped — a problem of exit-window timing, not of the base; the stock is 41% off its peak, and both Co-CEOs bought the dip.
co.kkr.topBets.items.0.fact: KKR's largest own position: book value $11.66bn, assets $220bn — a general account backing annuities and life insurance (fixed income and structured credit, not corporate equity stakes). In Q1'26 the portfolio posted a $652.7m GAAP investment revaluation loss in a single quarter. The bet: permanent insurance capital provides long-dated money for KKR's strategies — but the bond concentration is now measurable as a risk rather than a hypothesis.

co.kkr.topBets.items.1.fact: A new $10bn+ company for AI data centres; partners NVIDIA, the Kuwait Investment Authority and Vistra (50 GW, the preferred power supplier); CEO Adam Selipsky, formerly head of AWS (launched 10.06.2026). A fund asset, not KKR's balance sheet — KKR's economics are fees plus carry (a share of fund profits) plus a thin co-invest. The bet: pull KKR's $40bn+ of digital infrastructure into a single hyperscale vehicle aimed at AI demand, owning the buildings rather than guessing which AI model wins.
co.kkr.topBets.items.1.role: Builds hyperscale data centres for AI
co.kkr.topBets.items.2.fact: A managed BDC: a $12.3bn portfolio, NAV/share $18.83 (−9.9% on the quarter), non-accruals of 4.2% at fair value; the distribution cut from $0.48 to $0.42, with KKR injecting ~$300m of support (convertible preferred plus a tender). The only vehicle that discloses every portfolio company — and the clearest indicator of stress in the private credit ecosystem. The bet: private credit is replacing the banks, but early stress is already visible in the numbers.

co.kkr.topBets.items.3.fact: Direct dividend-paying core PE stakes: USI Insurance, 1-800 Contacts, Heartland Dental, Internet Brands, Mills Fleet Farm and BMC Software (6 of ~18 are named; individual values are not disclosed). Look-through adjusted EBITDA is ~$1.1bn today; operating earnings (OE) are planned to grow from $178.9m over 12 months to $1.1bn+ by 2030. The bet: a structural difference from peers — not just fees, but direct cash flow from companies KKR owns outright.

A fund asset (capital from KKR Asia-Pacific infrastructure), not KKR's balance sheet. The bet: take operating control of the power supply to data centres and semiconductor plants across Asia.

co.softbank.sections.0.bodyMarkdown:
**The NAV base** (primary — SOTP page [3] and the December FY2025 deck [1], at 31.03.2026): equity value of holdings **¥48.26T**, net debt **¥8.21T** → **NAV ¥40.06T**, **NAV/share ¥7,029**, **LTV 17.0%**. Pro forma NAV is **¥47.7T** ($303.2B) at prices as of 12.05.2026 [1]. All figures are post-split (4-for-1, effective 01.01.2026). Shares excluding treasury ≈ **5,699m**; USD/JPY 159.88. [3]

The portfolio is organised by economic structure: consolidated operating assets (Arm, SoftBank Corp.), managed vehicles (SVF1, SVF2, the LatAm Funds) and other direct or balance sheet stakes. Within each vehicle come the sector and the asset; a real figure is given wherever it is disclosed line by line, and otherwise marked "not disclosed".

**Positions with a published valuation (equity value, ¥T, at 31.03.2026):** [3]

| Position | Vehicle | Stake / detail | Equity value (¥T) | % of NAV equity | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arm Holdings | direct + consolidation | ~87% (secondary, see gaps); listed on Nasdaq (ARM) since Sep-2023 | **19.15** (adj.) | ~40% | A CPU architecture designer; record revenue of $4.92B (+23%), market cap ~$221B at 12.05.2026, ~4.2x the IPO. [1; 13] |
| SVF2 | LP interest + GP | dominated internally by OpenAI | **17.19** | ~36% | Vision Fund 2; the core asset is OpenAI preferred stock; the SVF segment turned positive for the first time. [1] |
| SVF1 | LP interest + carry | a mature portfolio | **3.38** | ~7% | Vision Fund 1; net equity IRR ~4% (blended 5%); cumulative return $103.6B on cost of $87.2B. [1] |
| SoftBank Corp. (SBKK, 9434) | direct | ~40% (secondary, as of May 2026) | **2.85** (adj.) | ~6% | The Japanese telecom operator, a dividend cash flow, building in-house AI data centres. [1; 14] |
| LatAm Funds | LP interest + carry | — | **1.04** | ~2% | The Latin American funds; net blended IRR −2%. [1] |
| T-Mobile US | direct (under a collar) | almost fully monetised in FY2025 | **0.05** (adj.) | ~0% | The US operator; the remainder sits under a prepaid forward. [1] |
| Others | direct + SB Northstar | — | **4.61** | ~10% | Other listed and unlisted stakes, SB Northstar, Ampere (consolidated), Intel and others. [1] |

**The key point:** Alibaba and Deutsche Telekom have DROPPED OUT of the NAV table at 31.03.2026 (they were present at 31.03.2025) — Alibaba was physically settled through the prepaid forward (see 02), and DT was sold ($2.74B) plus a collar settlement. [1; 11]

**Named, but without a separate public line-item valuation (they sit inside SVF/Others):**
- **OpenAI** — SVF2's and SBG's largest AI position; a $730B pre-money (Feb 2026); SBG's planned stake is ~13% after the $30B follow-on; held indirectly inside SVF2's ¥17.19T. The developer of ChatGPT and Codex; its valuation went $260B→$730B in a year. No separate line-item valuation is disclosed. [4; 1]
- **Stargate / PORTS Technology Campus (Ohio)** — AI infrastructure (10GW of power plus 10GW of data centre), a government partnership with DOE/DOC/SB Energy/AEP Ohio; capex is not disclosed as a single figure. [1; 8 — partner primary]
- **Ampere Computing** — consolidated (100%, closed 25.11.2025, $6.5B), Arm server CPUs; sits inside "Others". [1; press 26.11.2025]
- **Robo HD** — a holding company for ~20 robotics companies (SVF2 58.7% / SBG 41.3%), a Physical-AI portfolio of 30+ companies. No valuation disclosed. [1]
- **Cruise** — mentioned in the brief as an AI name; not confirmed as a separate line or valuation in primary sources → gaps.

**Concentration:** Arm + SVF2 = **~76% of equity value** — extreme. **Geography:** Japan (SBKK), the US (the Arm listing / T-Mobile / OpenAI / Stargate), the UK (Arm plc), LatAm. **Listed vs unlisted:** listed — Arm, SBKK, T-Mobile; the largest unlisted — OpenAI and the Physical-AI portfolio. **Themes:** AI models (OpenAI), AI chips (Arm, Ampere), AI infrastructure (Stargate/SB Energy), Physical AI.

| Scenario | Level | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI IPO delay** | High (playing out) | On 26.06.2026 the stock fell 12.5% (−¥5.6T) on a report the IPO would slip to 2027 → deferred realisation plus the problem of refinancing the $40B bridge (March 2027). [18 — Bloomberg search; 17] |
| **Arm + SVF2 concentration (~76%)** | High | A fall in the Arm ADS (−20% in Dec-2025 per the press) or a mark-down of OpenAI collapses NAV; Arm is a single point of failure. [3] |
| **An OpenAI mark-down / fundraising failure** | High | If the $730B pre-money is not confirmed, SVF2's ¥17.19T and the planned $30B get marked down; the tranches are conditional on OpenAI continuing to raise. [4] |
| **Leverage against AI capex** | Medium-high | Bridge loans plus $38.5B of commitments at 17% LTV; a rise towards the 25% ceiling if monetisation slows. |
| **AI bubble / the theme re-rating** | High | Son himself raised the bubble question at the AGM; a correction in AI multiples hits Arm, OpenAI and Ampere at once. |
| **Liquidity of the unlisted NAV** | High | The growth of the unlisted OpenAI stake lowers the listed share; OpenAI is hard to pledge as collateral, which complicates refinancing the $40B bridge. |
| **FX (USD/JPY)** | Medium | Most of the assets are in USD (Arm, OpenAI, T-Mobile); NAV is struck at ¥159.88 (March); a stronger yen reduces the yen NAV. |
| **Key person (Masayoshi Son, 32.73%)** | Medium-high | Concentration of decisions and of ownership; succession is not disclosed. [5] |
| **The discount to NAV does not close** | Medium | The ~49% discount persists despite the buyback; market distrust of the holdco structure and of the level-3 valuations. |
co.softbank.sections.3.deep.0.body:
First, what takes the panic out. SoftBank Group is not facing bankruptcy: ¥3.5T of cash covers two years of bond maturities (¥1.6T) twice over, and LTV of 17% is formally below the 25% threshold. FY2025 net income of ¥5,002.3bn was a record for corporate Japan. As a whole, the company is resilient.

But resilience is not the absence of risk, and here it arrives from two different directions worth holding apart:

**What the money is invested in (positioning).** The portfolio is extremely concentrated: Arm plus OpenAI ≈ 65% of the ¥48.3T portfolio value. OpenAI ($79.6bn, ~25% of NAV) is marked at the last round price ($730bn pre-money) — $45bn of unrealised revaluation that the market has never once confirmed. 85% of the SVF's unrealised portfolio is private (Level 3, model-valued). The listed share has fallen over the year from 75% to 53%.

**How the model works.** The holding company funds its AI expansion with a $40bn bridge loan (due 25 March 2027) on negative operating cash flow of −¥428.8bn. S&P revised the outlook on its BB+ rating to Negative (3 March 2026). Inside the portfolio there is clear circularity: SVF2 (funded by SBG) invests in OpenAI, which leases capacity at Stargate (funded by SBG), and OpenAI's mark raises SBG's NAV, on which its creditworthiness depends. SBG itself leads OpenAI's round at a higher valuation — and that same valuation re-marks the stake it already holds, while the rise in NAV widens its financing capacity. Masayoshi Son controls ~34% of the shares, with veto rights.

Each is taken separately below: origin, scale and what breaks.
co.softbank.sections.3.deep.0.title: The thesis: no bankruptcy — but the risk is twofold
co.softbank.sections.3.deep.1.groups.0.i: Two assets make up ~65% of the ¥48.3T portfolio value. The $20bn Arm margin loan is fully drawn (a ¥3,168.5bn balance) — if Arm's multiple compresses, collateral cover falls, and the specific LTV triggers are not disclosed by the lender. Arm has already fallen 20% in December 2025.
OpenAI: valued at the last round

Marked at a $730bn pre-money (a $122bn round, February 2026). Unrealised revaluation of +$45bn — against a gap in cash realisations: nothing has come back from OpenAI. S&P called OpenAI the asset of "the weakest credit quality" in the portfolio. A confidential S-1 was filed on 8 June 2026, but press reports suggest the IPO is leaning towards 2027.
SVF Level 3: a private portfolio valued on models

85% of the combined SVF funds' unrealised value is private companies valued on models. SVF2 was historically loss-making and only turned positive thanks to OpenAI (cumulative gains of $21.0bn on cost of $97.7bn).
The growth of the unlisted OpenAI stake squeezed the listed share from 75% (March 2025) to 53%. Unlisted assets are harder to pledge as collateral, which complicates refinancing the bridge loan.
co.softbank.sections.3.deep.1.groups.0.l: Positioning — what the money is invested in
co.softbank.sections.3.deep.1.groups.1.i: The largest loan in SBG's history ($20bn drawn, $10bn to draw in July and $10bn in October 2026). It carries LTV covenants whose definition is "completely different" from the LTV SBG discloses. Repayment comes from an OpenAI IPO (which is slipping) or from financing against existing assets.

The ¥5T of profit is an unrealised revaluation of Arm and OpenAI. The real sources of cash are SBKK distributions and monetisations. The gap between the holdco's needs (¥602.4bn of interest, ¥1.6T of maturities, $20bn of OpenAI capital calls) and its recurring inflows is covered by monetisation and debt.

SBG leads an OpenAI round at a higher valuation → the same valuation re-marks the stake it already holds → unrealised gains rise → NAV rises → financing capacity widens. In parallel: SB Energy builds capacity for OpenAI (funded by SBG), and under Crystal Intelligence SBG/SBKK pay OpenAI ~$3bn annualised, which feeds into OpenAI's ARR and therefore its valuation.

A downgrade mechanically raises the cost of senior debt and narrows access to it. Moody's has it at Ba2 (unsolicited, and SBG disputes it). Returning to Stable requires a successful IPO of key assets and keeping LTV below the ceiling.
Son: key person plus conflicts of interest

co.softbank.sections.3.deep.5.body:
**Hold.** SoftBank's risk is not a broken business but a single question: will the market confirm OpenAI's $730bn mark. At ¥3,555 the market already strips out the entire unrealised OpenAI gain ($45bn) and adds a holdco/governance/leverage discount — even writing OpenAI to zero leaves a residual NAV (¥4,796/share) 35% above the market price, which caps the downside: to fall meaningfully further the market would have to start doubting the value of Arm and SBKK, and that is a break scenario, which is not present.

Add if the OpenAI IPO is confirmed at ≥$730bn and the $40bn bridge is refinanced. Reduce if the IPO slips beyond 2027 while Arm falls more than 25%: that is a double hit to NAV and to the margin loan's collateral cover.

**Numerical review thresholds:** LTV above 20% is a warning, above 25% changes the thesis. Cash below 2x annual maturities (under ¥1.6T over two years) is a warning. The Arm price — monitor it against the margin loan's LTV trigger (the $20bn facility, a ¥3,168.5bn balance). An OpenAI mark below cost ($34.6bn) means a NAV re-rating. A listed share below 50% means the portfolio's liquidity is deteriorating. The bridge: less than 50% refinanced by December 2026 is pressure. S&P: any action on the BB+ Negative is a signal.

| Metric | SoftBank Group (9984) | Berkshire Hathaway (BRK) | Prosus / Naspers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type | Vision-fund holdco + consolidated Arm | Diversified holdco + insurance float | Tech holdco (ex-Tencent stake) |
| Discount to NAV | ~49% (¥3,555 vs ¥7,029) | ~at or above book (a premium / small discount) | wide (often 30-45%) |
| Concentration | Arm+SVF2 ~76% — extreme | diversified (Apple is the largest, not >50%) | Tencent dominates — comparable |
| Leverage (LTV) | 17.0% net debt / equity value | low net debt, a large cash pile | moderate |
| Buyback against the discount | ¥330.3bn executed (2024-25), none since | systematic, below intrinsic value | aggressive |

**Reading it:** SBG is closer to Prosus/Naspers (a wide holdco discount plus concentration in a single tech asset) than to a diversified Berkshire. What distinguishes SBG is consolidating an operating asset (Arm) plus large unlisted AI exposure (OpenAI), which makes NAV harder to value (Level 3) and partly justifies the discount. *The Berkshire/Prosus peer figures are general industry context, not from primary filings → directional, see gaps.*

**Conclusion for the decision:** against its peers SBG is the most aggressive and least diversified exposure to AI; a wide discount to raw NAV (~49%) plus the live catalyst of the OpenAI IPO delay argue for **hold** until (a) the OpenAI IPO timing and (b) the refinancing of the $40bn bridge (March 2027) are clear. Adding is justified if the discount widens further and the listed share stabilises with LTV below 20%.

co.softbank.sections.5.deep.3.body:
**SoftBank** is the only holding company in the group with negative operating cash flow (−¥429bn in FY2025) alongside record net income of ¥5T. All of that profit is an unrealised revaluation of Arm and OpenAI; ¥3.5T ($22bn) of cash covers two years of bond maturities, but the $40bn bridge loan due in March 2027 changes the liquidity picture radically. The ~49% discount to NAV is the deepest in the group, and the market justifies it with four things: (1) OpenAI is marked at a $730bn round, not at a market price — an unrealised revaluation of +$45bn; (2) the $40bn loan is a one-year instrument; (3) operating cash flow is negative; (4) every decision runs through Son (~34% of control). The only catalyst for closing the discount is an OpenAI IPO; the ¥93bn of buybacks over the year is token against ¥40T of NAV.

**Berkshire Hathaway** is SBG's opposite. It trades at a premium to book value (~$630bn), because it has spent 60 years proving it can convert cash into above-market returns. Its $330bn+ of cash — the largest in the corporate world — lets Buffett buy back stock below intrinsic value and invest in a crisis. The portfolio contains not one pre-IPO tech asset, which simultaneously rules out AI upside and insures against model-valuation risk. The one structural question: Greg Abel as Buffett's successor — the market has not yet priced Berkshire without its founder.

**Prosus / Naspers** is SBG's closest structural analogue: a holding company with a large tech stake (~80% of NAV in Tencent), trading at a 35–40% discount. The key difference: Tencent is a mature, profitable, listed asset with dividends of its own. Prosus closes its discount with aggressive buybacks funded by Tencent sales; SBG directs its monetisations into OpenAI rather than into buybacks. For an SBG investor, Prosus is a useful benchmark: if a listed core asset and aggressive buybacks still leave Prosus at a 35–40% discount, then SBG's ~49% with an unlisted OpenAI and no buyback is not an anomaly.

**Investor AB** is the model of a predictable discount: a 10–15% gap on maximum diversification (no asset above 25% of NAV), 100+ years of Wallenberg stewardship and a steady dividend stream from the portfolio. An investor choosing SBG over Investor AB is buying asymmetric upside (an OpenAI IPO, Arm's growth) at the price of asymmetric downside (a credit crunch, a margin call on Arm). The difference in discount (~49% vs ~12%) reflects exactly that difference in risk profile.

co.softbank.sections.5.deep.4.body: SoftBank is the only large holding company to have assembled the two most valuable AI assets at once: a processor architecture (Arm, a ~90% stake, market cap ~$221bn, record revenue of $4.92bn for the year) and the largest generative model (OpenAI, ~11% through SVF2, a $730bn pre-money, >900m weekly users). The proof: NAV rose 56% over the year (¥25.7T to ¥40.1T), Arm posted record revenue (+23%), and OpenAI tripled its valuation in 12 months ($260bn to $730bn). It cannot be replicated: Berkshire will not touch pre-IPO tech on principle, Prosus is tied to a mature Tencent, and Investor AB works the industrial cycle. No other holding company owns chips (Arm + Ampere), models (OpenAI), infrastructure (Stargate, SB Energy, DigitalBridge) and robotics (ABB, Robo HD) at once, under the strategic control of a founder with ~34% of the votes. The other side: a $40bn bridge loan on a one-year term (due March 2027), 65% of NAV in two assets, OpenAI marked at its last round (with no cash realisation at all), negative operating cash flow (−¥429bn), and every decision running through Masayoshi Son. The ~49% discount is not a market error but the price of that combination of risks. The decision: does the investor believe the OpenAI IPO will price at no less than $730bn and the bridge loan will be refinanced within 12–18 months — in which case SBG turns out to be the only holding company owning the key links of the AI stack, and the discount compresses.

co.softbank.sections.5.deep.5.takeaway: SoftBank's real advantage is neither scale nor diversification (it loses on both to Berkshire and Investor AB), but unprecedented vertical integration of the AI stack. SBG is the only holding company that owns a processor architecture (Arm, ~90%), server CPUs (Ampere, 100%), a model company (OpenAI, ~11%), AI infrastructure (Stargate, SB Energy, DigitalBridge) and robotics (ABB, Robo HD) all at once. Neither Berkshire (which will not touch pre-IPO tech on principle), nor Prosus (tied to a mature Tencent), nor Investor AB (the industrial cycle) could assemble the same structure. SBG pays for it with the deepest discount in the group (~49%): the market sees a $40bn bridge loan on a one-year term, an unrealised OpenAI revaluation, negative operating cash flow and everything resting on one person. The hold case: the discount is justified by the risks, but if the OpenAI IPO prices at $730bn+ and the loan is refinanced, SBG will be the only holding company with the full AI stack, and the discount will compress.

co.softbank.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
Masayoshi Son positions SoftBank as a holder of stakes along a single axis — artificial superintelligence (ASI), the "No.1 ASI Platform Provider" with all four layers (the 46th shareholders' meeting, 24.06.2026; December FY deck pp. 6-8, 67):
1. **AI Model** — OpenAI (~13% through SVF2). [4]
2. **AI Chip / Semiconductor** — Arm (consolidated), Ampere.
3. **AI Infrastructure / power** — Stargate, SB Energy.
4. **Robot / Physical AI** — ABB Robotics ($5.375bn), Robo HD. [7]

The AGM's "goose and golden eggs" metaphor: the market sees the "eggs" (market cap) while undervaluing the "goose" (the ASI NAV machine). Son called the bubble talk "an insult" ("The AI revolution has only just begun"). [s03 VOICE; Axios/Outlook Business — secondary validation; the AGM PDF extracted with font corruption, see gaps]

**Capital allocation rules (verbatim, December FY deck p.66):** "Maintain LTV below 25% in normal times (upper threshold of 35% even in times of emergency)" and "Maintain at least 2 years' worth of bond redemptions in cash position". The actual LTV is 17.0% (down from 18.0%); cash is ¥3.5T; non-recourse project finance for power and data centres; a bridge-to-takeout for OpenAI ($40bn, due 25.03.2027). [1; 17]

**Layers of the strategy:** (1) monetise mature assets (T-Mobile/DT/NVIDIA/the Alibaba settlement) → redeploy into AI; (2) concentrate in OpenAI ($30bn follow-on, three $10bn tranches in Apr/Jul/Oct 2026, → $64.6bn/~13%, a $730bn pre-money); (3) vertically integrate AI chips (Arm + Ampere); (4) buybacks as a residual instrument (FY2025 was only ¥93.2bn). [1; 4]

The NAV target of **¥1 quadrillion by 2042** is a forward-looking management ambition from a verbal presentation (secondary sources Axios/TradingView), not an audited fact and not the current NAV; see gaps.
co.softbank.sections.6.deep.0.body: Since its founding SoftBank Group has believed technology is the key to a more connected and fairer world. It began as a pioneer of the information revolution: personal computers → the internet → broadband → smartphones. At every shift SBG adapted its business model. Now comes the next chapter of that transformation: the AI revolution, which management believes will bring more innovation and disruption than the previous 300 years. The way we live will change: how we travel, work, detect and treat disease, build cities and grow food. SBG positions itself as a "Vision Capitalist" — an investor that funds and connects a network of innovative technology companies shaping the future through computing power and memory. The philosophy: Information Revolution → Happiness for Everyone. The vision: to become the corporate group that supplies the world's most important technologies. The strategy: a Strategic Synergy Group — an ecosystem of portfolio companies with industry technologies, financial capital and human capital.
co.softbank.sections.6.deep.0.title: Vision & Strategy: 300 years of growth
co.softbank.sections.6.deep.1.body: SoftBank Group is an investment holding company that Masayoshi Son is rebuilding into a vertically integrated AI platform. The aim is to become the number one supplier to artificial superintelligence (ASI) by owning every layer of the stack: chips (Arm, Ampere, Graphcore), models (OpenAI, ~13%), infrastructure (Stargate — $500bn / 10 GW, SB Energy, DigitalBridge), robots (ABB Robotics, Robo HD) and distribution (SBKK, PayPay). The logic is an analogy with Apple's ecosystem: whoever owns the whole stack controls demand at every level. The financial mechanism: systematically monetising mature assets (T-Mobile $17.9bn, NVIDIA $5.8bn, Deutsche Telekom $2.7bn) and redeploying into AI — $44bn was invested in FY2025. The balance sheet is formally disciplined (LTV 17%, cash ¥3.5T), but ~65% of NAV sits in Arm (~40%) and OpenAI (~25%), and the main funding channel is a $40bn bridge loan due in March 2027. Everything hinges on the OpenAI IPO (which would confirm the $730bn mark and provide the liquidity to repay the loan) and on Arm holding its multiple (the main collateral for the $20bn margin loan). The strategy works as a HOLD case while the IPO has not fallen through and LTV stays below 25%; it becomes a CUT trigger if both go the other way at once.

The AI-oriented share of NAV rose from 18% (three years ago) to above 60%. Son treats the mature telecom assets as a source of capital for the AI stack.

co.softbank.sections.6.deep.5.items.1.v: The formal rule: LTV below 25% in normal times, a 35% ceiling in a crisis. The actual position at 31 March 2026: LTV 17.0% (down from 18.0% a year earlier), cash of ¥3.5T ($22bn) against ¥1.6T of bond maturities over two years — cover of more than 2x. The discipline holds, but a $40bn bridge loan on a one-year term creates a mismatch between long-dated assets and short-dated debt.
co.softbank.sections.6.deep.5.items.2.k: Arm forever, everything else is a source of capital
co.softbank.sections.6.deep.5.items.2.v: Arm is a permanent platform, not for sale (~40% of NAV, a ~90% stake). SBKK, T-Mobile, Alibaba, NVIDIA and Deutsche Telekom are monetisation sources, sold to fund AI. Every dollar raised from a mature asset goes into the AI stack or into buybacks.

Management's analogy is Apple's ecosystem: the user cannot do without SoftBank at any level.
co.softbank.sections.6.deep.5.items.4.v: The priority is NAV growth, then buybacks, with dividends minimal. FY2025 saw just ¥93.2bn repurchased against ¥40T of NAV. The ¥11-a-share dividend has been frozen for 13 years. Management chooses to put $64.6bn into OpenAI rather than close a 49% discount — NAV growth matters more than capital return.

Son took OpenAI's share of NAV from 2% to ~25% in a single year, while selling NVIDIA ($5.8bn) despite the AI rhetoric. Effective control of ~34–35% of SBG's shares (per Bloomberg's calculation; with veto rights over special resolutions) lets Son ignore market pressure — including Elliott's demand for a $15bn buyback.

In FY2025: T-Mobile $17.9bn, NVIDIA $5.8bn, Deutsche Telekom $2.7bn — ~$27bn of monetisations in total. In return: OpenAI $32.4bn, Ampere $6.5bn, Intel $2.0bn. Alibaba, the largest asset three years ago, has been removed from the NAV table entirely.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.0.fo: The model: sell the mature → redeploy into AI → fund through the bridge and bonds
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.1.de: Son flatly denies a bubble and calls the talk of one "an insult". The vision: artificial superintelligence (ASI) will require ~200m chips, ~$9T of capital and ~400 GW of power by around 2035. The specific goal is to be "the number one platform for ASI". They are building vertically: from chips (Arm, Ampere) through models (OpenAI) to physical robots (ABB, Robo HD).
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.1.ti: They believe: the AI revolution has only just begun
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.2.de: Unlike Brookfield (infrastructure that is agnostic to the AI model), SoftBank deliberately backs specific winners and builds ecosystem lock-in on the Apple analogy. Four layers: (1) chips — Arm + Ampere, (2) models — OpenAI, (3) infrastructure — Stargate + SB Energy + DigitalBridge, (4) physical AI — ABB Robotics + Robo HD (~20 companies). The server CPU TAM was raised from $50bn to $100bn+.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.2.fo: CFO Govil on the call (13.05.2026): the analogy is Apple's lock-in — control from the chip to the end product
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.2.ti: They believe: own the whole stack, not one layer
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.3.de: Stargate: a $500bn / 10 GW programme, announced at the White House on 21.01.2025 with Trump, Altman and Ellison. SB Energy is building 1.2 GW of solar (Milam County, Texas; $1bn from OpenAI and SoftBank). Seven US sites. Funded through non-recourse project finance — with no effect on the holding company's LTV.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.3.ti: They believe: power is AI's bottleneck
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.4.de: SoftBank deliberately runs in the opposite direction from diversification: Arm plus OpenAI is ~65% of the portfolio. Telecom (T-Mobile, DT), general-purpose chips (NVIDIA) and China (Alibaba) have all been sold or reduced to residuals. Management considers the ~49% discount to NAV unfair: head of IR Okayama said outright that "the stock is very cheap if you value it off our stakes".
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.4.ti: They do NOT believe diversification protects you
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.5.de: At the annual meeting of 24.06.2026 Son named a target of ¥1 quadrillion of NAV (from today's ~¥74T) — implying ~18% growth a year for 16 consecutive years. Son's metaphor: the market sees the "eggs" (market cap) while undervaluing the "goose" (the value-creation machine through ASI). This is the founder's personal position, not audited guidance — but ¥40T→¥74T in three months (March→June 2026) shows how fast NAV can move when Arm rises.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.5.fo: Son's personal target; it implies a ~18% CAGR — comparable to Brookfield's history (19%), but at incomparably higher concentration
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.1.items.5.ti: How they see the world: 14x NAV over 16 years

co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.1.k: OpenAI: $32.4bn over the year, plus a further $30bn follow-on
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.1.v: SBG's largest concentrated bet. Its OpenAI stake was ~11% at the end of FY2025, rising to ~13% by October 2026. Valued at the last round price (a $730bn pre-money) — S&P called it the "weakest credit quality" asset in the portfolio.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.2.k: A $40bn bridge — the largest loan in SBG's history
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.2.v: A one-year loan (due 25.03.2027) funding the OpenAI tranches. $20bn was drawn in April 2026. The takeout runs through bonds and asset-backed financing. It carries LTV covenants whose definition is "completely different" from the LTV SBG discloses.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.3.v: NVIDIA was sold in October 2025 (32.1m shares). T-Mobile went in block sales of 75.4m shares for $16.2bn plus a hedge. Deutsche Telekom $2.7bn. The capital was redeployed into AI. CFO Goto: "We want to provide investment opportunities for investors while maintaining financial strength."
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.4.k: Ampere Computing — vertical integration into server CPUs
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.4.v: A 100% acquisition for $6.5bn, closed November 2025. Arm server processors. Combined with Arm and Graphcore into the AI Computing segment. Rene Haas (formerly CEO of Arm) became operating head of SoftBank Group International from April 2026.
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.5.k: Son is building control: a ~34–35% stake with veto rights
co.softbank.sections.7.deep.4.items.5.v: Holding more than one third gives veto rights over special resolutions. Through MASA USA LLC, Son takes 17.25% of SVF2's profit above a 130% MOIC (not yet reached). Every strategic decision is concentrated in one person.

co.softbank.sections.8.bodyMarkdown:
**Reporting calendar (estimated from history):**
- **Early–mid August 2026** (~5-7 Aug): FY2026 Q1 earnings. The exact date was NOT published on the IR calendar as of 28.06.2026 (a gap). [5/IR calendar]
- **Mid-November 2026:** FY2026 Q2. **Mid-February 2027:** Q3. **Mid-May 2027:** FY2026 full year. **Late June 2027:** the 47th AGM.

**Transaction triggers:**
- **01.07.2026:** the second OpenAI tranche, $10bn. [4]
- **01.10.2026:** the third OpenAI tranche, $10bn; cumulative → $64.6bn. [4]
- **25.03.2027:** the $40bn bridge falls due — the takeout refinancing window. [17]
- **H2 2026:** the closings of ABB Robotics ($5.375bn) [7] and DigitalBridge (~$4.0bn) [10].
- OpenAI IPO signals (the tranches could accelerate; SVF2's preferred shares convert into common).

**Filing windows:** EDINET (the securities report, code 9984) — late June / early July (the exact shareholder register and Son's stake). EDGAR is uninformative (SBG is exempt under Rule 12g3-2(b); the 13F tells you little). For Arm, Form 20-F (EDGAR CIK 1973239) gives SBG's exact stake.

**Feeds:** NAV/SOTP https://group.softbank/en/ir/stock/sotp · IR News https://group.softbank/en/ir/news · Ownership https://group.softbank/en/ir/stock/ownership. **Numbers:** LTV against 25% (17.0%); OpenAI's pre-money ($730bn); Arm's ADS / market cap (~$221bn); cash covering at least two years of maturities (¥3.5T).
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.0.items.2.no: a takeout through senior bonds, asset-backed financing and disposals
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.0.items.3.no: price ¥3,555 vs NAV/share ¥7,029; a LongYield calculation, not an SBG disclosure
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.0.de: The second drawdown from the $30bn follow-on. Funded from the $40bn bridge loan. Once done, SBG's cumulative OpenAI position reaches ~$54.6bn. If the tranche slips or the terms change, that signals problems at OpenAI or with the bridge lenders.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.1.de: The thing that matters: actual LTV after the bridge drawdown and the new investments. If LTV has risen to 20% or above, management is exhausting its stated headroom (a 25% ceiling). Plus: the listed share of assets (Mar-26 = 53%, with the alarm threshold below 50%) and an updated OpenAI mark.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.2.de: Awaiting regulatory approvals in the EU, China and the US. ABB Robotics revenue is $2.3bn (2024) with a 12.1% operational EBITA margin. A delayed close would point to antitrust problems — complicating the Physical AI strategy.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.3.de: Shareholders approved it on 23 April 2026. Awaiting regulatory approvals. AUM ~$108bn. It gives SBG a ready-made data centre management platform, but adds ~$3.1bn to cash outflows. Marc Ganzi retains independent management.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.4.de: The final drawdown; SBG's cumulative OpenAI position reaches $64.6bn, a ~13% stake. After it the $40bn bridge loan is fully drawn. From October the takeout countdown begins: five months to the bridge's repayment on 25 March 2027.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.5.de: By then the bridge is fully drawn. The key question: how much of the $40bn has been refinanced, with what instrument (senior bonds, asset-backed financing, project finance) and at what rate. April's takeout tranche priced at 8.2% in USD / 6.9% in EUR — if the cost rises, it pressures the P&L.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.6.de: A confidential S-1 was filed on 8 June 2026 at a valuation above $850bn (press reports, not an SBG disclosure). If the IPO prices at ≥$730bn, SVF2's mark is confirmed by the market and the preferred shares convert into common. A slip into 2027 is the main risk catalyst: it complicates the bridge takeout and fixes the unrealised nature of the $45bn gain.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.7.de: Repayment falls on 25 March 2027. The takeout mechanisms: senior bonds (April 2026 already raised $3.5bn at 4x oversubscription), asset-backed financing (the Arm margin loan, the SBKK margin loan) and disposals. The threshold: if less than 50% of the drawn amount is refinanced by December 2026 and S&P downgrades below BB+, the thesis turns negative.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.8.de: The outlook has been Negative since 3 March 2026. S&P called OpenAI the weakest-credit-quality asset in the portfolio. A downgrade below BB+ mechanically raises the cost of, and narrows access to, senior debt — critical for the bridge takeout. Returning to Stable requires a successful IPO of key assets and a stable LTV.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.8.ti: S&P action on the BB+ rating
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.9.de: The $20bn facility is fully drawn (a ¥3,168.5bn balance). Arm is the core collateral asset (~40% of NAV). The specific margin loan LTV triggers are not disclosed, but a fall in Arm's price reduces collateral cover → the risk of a top-up. A fall in Arm of more than 25% from the peak hits NAV and loan cover at the same time.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.items.9.ti: Arm's price against the margin loan trigger
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.1.title: Calendar
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.0.v: Management discloses LTV every quarter (17.0% at 31 March 2026, pro forma ~15% at 13 May). The policy: below 25% in normal times, a 35% ceiling in a crisis. While LTV is below 20% the balance sheet is fine. A rise towards 20% is a warning; breaking 25% changes the thesis — management would have broken its own rule. The $40bn bridge loan carries separate LTV covenants (defined differently from the LTV SBG discloses — the exact triggers are not published).
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.1.v: Cash of ¥3.5T ($22bn); bond maturities over two years of ¥1.6T ($10bn) → cover of more than 2x. The policy is to hold at least two years of maturities in cash. Cover falling below 2x would break its own rule and signal liquidity stress. Separately: the $38.5bn of committed investments at 31 March 2026 is funded by the bridge loan, not from cash.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.2.k: OpenAI's mark and the path to an IPO
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.2.v: Marked at the last round price: a $730bn pre-money, a cumulative cost of $34.6bn for SBG's position and a fair value of $79.6bn (an unrealised revaluation of +$45bn). Zero cash realisations from OpenAI. If the next round or an IPO prices below $730bn, NAV is marked down and SVF2 (¥16.3T) takes the hit. A confidential S-1 was filed on 8 June 2026 at a valuation above $850bn (press reports). An IPO slipping beyond 2027 while the bridge expires is the critical scenario.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.3.v: At 31 March 2026 it was 53% (down from 75% a year earlier). The fall is driven by the growth of the unlisted OpenAI position. S&P noted the deterioration in portfolio liquidity. The threshold: a sustained fall below 50% would mean the portfolio depends on model and last-round valuations rather than market prices — reinforcing the case for the discount to NAV.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.4.k: The bridge takeout: the pace of refinancing
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.4.v: Of the $40bn bridge loan, by April 2026 $3.5bn of senior notes and ¥418bn (~$2.6bn) of hybrids had been issued — a takeout of ~15% in the first month, at 4x oversubscription. The remaining ~$34bn must be refinanced within 11 months (by 25 March 2027). Every quarterly report is a progress check. The threshold: if less than 50% is refinanced by December 2026 and S&P downgrades, the thesis turns negative.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.5.v: S&P BB+ with a Negative outlook (since 3 March 2026). JCR A (the Japanese agency). Moody's Ba2 — unsolicited and disputed by SBG. The April senior note priced at 8.2% (USD) / 6.9% (EUR). An S&P downgrade below BB+ raises the cost of the bridge takeout and narrows the investor pool. A return to Stable would signal falling risk.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.6.v: ~49% (¥3,555 against NAV/share of ¥7,029). The discount is structural: the market does not believe Arm and OpenAI will be monetised at NAV, plus key-person risk (Son at 34.2%) and the opacity of Level 3 valuations. The buyback is token (¥93.2bn against ¥40T of NAV). The discount will not close on its own — it needs a liquidity catalyst (an OpenAI IPO, an Arm re-rating). A discount widening beyond 50% with LTV stable below 20% is the ADD zone; narrowing below 35% with no liquidity event is the TRIM zone.
co.softbank.sections.8.deep.2.items.7.v: Son controls ~34.2% (with veto rights over special resolutions). The last buyback (Aug 2024 — Aug 2025) was ¥330.3bn / 42m shares. FY2025 saw only ¥93.2bn repurchased. A new large buyback programme would be a potential catalyst. Management's priority is NAV growth (investing in OpenAI), not capital return. No personal purchases or sales by Son were recorded in FY2025.

co.softbank.sections.9.bodyMarkdown:
*(Interpretation, kept separate from the primary sources above.)*

**Reconciling the NAV basis — the main conclusion:** the brief assumed two divergent bases (SOTP at a ~12% discount vs the AGM at ~50%). **The primary sources do NOT support that framing.** The official SOTP page (RE-CHECKED by WebFetch, 31.03.2026): NAV ¥40.06T, NAV/share ¥7,029, price ¥3,555, 5,699m shares (post-split), USD/JPY 159.88 → a discount of **49.4%**, stated on the page itself. The AGM deck uses the same NAV/LTV definition; ¥13,000/share and a ~12% discount do not appear in the extractable text. No separate basis producing a ~12% discount was found; ¥74T / ¥13,000 / ¥1 quadrillion are either Son's verbal aspirational targets or pre/post-split confusion. For decision purposes there is **one basis: a ~49% discount.**

**What the events mean:**
- A ~49% discount at LTV of 17% and cash of ¥3.5T is a classic holdco discount, not a balance sheet stress signal. It persists structurally: the market does not believe SBG will monetise Arm and OpenAI at NAV, plus key-person risk (Son at 32.73%) and the opacity of Level 3 valuations.
- Concentration in OpenAI ($64.6bn by Oct-2026, ~13%) alongside a token buyback (¥93.2bn) means management chooses to raise its AI bet rather than close the discount. The discount will not close on its own; the only catalyst is a liquidity event (an OpenAI IPO, an Arm re-rating).

**The AI lens (where it is real):** Arm (¥19.15T, a direct revaluation lever), OpenAI (entered at a $730bn pre-money, with no liquidity before an IPO; SVF2's ¥17.19T is a proxy for OpenAI), Stargate, Ampere, SB Energy. **Where not to stretch it:** SoftBank Corp (telecom), T-Mobile (hedged) and part of SVF1 — those are cash and balance sheet, not AI upside.

**Decision signals (NOT investment advice; levels in post-split ¥):**
- **HOLD by default:** a 40-50% discount, LTV below 20%, cash covering at least two years of maturities — the current configuration.
- **ADD zone:** a discount above 50-55% (a price of ≲¥3,200-3,500 with NAV stable), LTV below 20%; an OpenAI IPO at ≥$730bn.
- **TRIM/CUT zone:** the discount narrowing below 35% with no liquidity event; the IPO slipping beyond 2027 plus widening spreads on SBG bonds; falling Arm data centre royalties; problems with the bridge takeout by March 2027; LTV above 25-30%.
- **Review triggers:** the OpenAI tranches (01.07 / 01.10.2026); OpenAI IPO signals; FY2026 Q1 earnings (~Aug 2026); a change in Son's stake (EDINET).
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.0.body: SoftBank Group is neither a fund nor an operator but Masayoshi Son's concentrated NAV bet on AI. Two assets -- Arm (~40% of NAV, ~90% owned, consolidated) and OpenAI (~25%, through SVF2, marked at the last round of $730bn) -- make up ~65% of the ¥48.3T portfolio. NAV is ¥40.1T (~$251bn), and the stock trades at a ~49% discount to NAV/share of ¥7,029 (a market calculation, not a company disclosure). Profit of ¥5,002bn (+334%) is a record for corporate Japan, but it is paper: a revaluation of Arm and OpenAI on operating cash flow of -¥429bn. LTV is 17%, but behind it sit a $40bn bridge loan on a one-year term (March 2027) and a $20bn margin loan against Arm shares (fully drawn). The interpretation: a ~49% discount creates asymmetry -- if the OpenAI IPO prices at >==$730bn the mark is confirmed, the loan is refinanced and the discount narrows; if the IPO slips, the mismatch between a one-year loan and multi-year infrastructure is exposed. Son (~34% of the shares including controlled vehicles -- Bloomberg) is raising the bet to $64.6bn in OpenAI by October 2026.
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essence
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.1.body: Two thirds of the value sits in two assets. Arm: collateral for the $20bn loan (fully drawn), with the collateral triggers undisclosed — a fall in Arm's price squeezes cover. OpenAI: marked at the last round price ($730bn); SBG itself led that round, creating circularity — SBG's investment raises OpenAI's valuation, the revaluation raises NAV, and NAV provides financing capacity for the next investment. S&P called OpenAI the asset with "the weakest credit quality" and moved the outlook to Negative (3 March 2026). The $40bn bridge is one-year funding against multi-year AI infrastructure; press reports (not company-sourced) say the OpenAI IPO has slipped to 2027 — and the stock fell 12.5% (−¥5.6T) on 26 June. 85% of the Vision Funds' value is private positions (valued on models). The end buyer of Stargate's capacity is a loss-making OpenAI. Of the ¥5T of profit, nothing has been realised from OpenAI.
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.de: An OpenAI IPO in 2026 at >==$730bn — the mark is confirmed by the market and SVF2's preferred shares convert into common. The $40bn bridge is refinanced (April's $3.5bn bond takeout drew 4x oversubscription — an indicator). Arm keeps growing: royalties +11%, the server CPU TAM raised to $100bn+. The discount narrows towards 30-35%. Pro forma NAV ¥47.7T, NAV/share ~¥8,400. Son (~34%) raises his personal bet.
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.2.items.1.de: The OpenAI IPO slips to 2027 (already signalled by non-company sources) or prices below $730bn — the +$45bn unrealised revaluation is erased. The $40bn bridge is not refinanced by March 2027 — forced sales or an expensive takeout. S&P downgrades below BB+ — the cost of debt rises. An AI correction compresses Arm's multiple — pressure on the $20bn collateral. A double hit to NAV, and the discount widens towards 55-60%.
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.2.title: Two scenarios
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.3.items.0.v: Hold the position through 9984.T (TSE); the SFTBY ADR is not officially supported by SBG. The current configuration (a ~49% discount, LTV of 17%, cash covering more than 2x maturities) is a hold. Add on: a discount above 50% with LTV below 20% and a confirmed 2026 OpenAI IPO window, or more than 50% of the bridge taken out by December 2026. Reduce on: the OpenAI IPO slipping beyond 2027 combined with Arm falling more than 25% from the peak; or LTV above 25%; or an S&P downgrade below BB+. This is interpretation, not investment advice.
co.softbank.sections.9.deep.3.items.1.v: 01.07.2026 — the second $10bn OpenAI tranche. 01.10.2026 — the third $10bn tranche (cumulative $64.6bn / ~13%). ~Aug 2026 — the Q1 FY2026 report (the test: LTV, cash, the bridge takeout). H2 2026 — the ABB ($5.375bn) and DigitalBridge (~$4bn) closings. 25.03.2027 — repayment of the $40bn bridge (the key one).

co.softbank.summary: SoftBank Group (9984.T) is Masayoshi Son's Japanese investment holding company, concentrated in two bets: Arm (~40% of NAV, consolidated, ~90% owned) and OpenAI (~25% of NAV, through SVF2). NAV is ¥40.1T, but the stock trades at a ~49% discount — the market does not trust the model valuation of OpenAI and doubts the refinancing of a $40bn bridge loan. Money flows from monetisations (NVIDIA sold for $5.8bn, T-Mobile for $16bn) into AI bets (OpenAI $32bn, Ampere $6.5bn). The key risk is concentration: Arm plus OpenAI is ~65% of NAV, and both depend on the AI cycle.
co.softbank.tagline: SBG is an investment holding company whose equity value of holdings is ~76% concentrated in Arm (¥19.15T, consolidated) and Vision Fund 2 (¥17.19T, dominated internally by OpenAI); the stock trades at a ~49% discount to a raw NAV/share of ¥7,029, and a possible slip of the OpenAI IPO into 2027 is a live catalyst that tips the decision to hold until the IPO timing and the refinancing of the $40B bridge loan are clearer.
co.softbank.topBets.items.0.fact: A ~90% stake, ~40% of holding company NAV (¥22.3T). Arm-architecture processors sit in every smartphone and increasingly in servers and AI accelerators. Listed on NASDAQ, consolidated into SBG's accounts. The main anchor of value, and the collateral for the margin loan.
co.softbank.topBets.items.0.role: The processor architecture for the whole world
co.softbank.topBets.items.1.embodies: A bet on the AI platform
co.softbank.topBets.items.1.fact: A ~11% stake through SVF2, valued at ~$300bn → a stake worth ~$79.6bn (~25% of NAV). $32.4bn deployed. Valued on a model, not at a market price. An IPO is the key catalyst: at a valuation of ≥$730bn it would close the entire discount to NAV.
co.softbank.topBets.items.2.fact: A joint venture with Oracle and OpenAI: $500bn / 10 GW of AI data centre capacity. SBG leads it. If it is built, it creates the physical infrastructure the AI economy runs on.
co.softbank.topBets.items.3.fact: Bought for $6.5bn in April 2025. Vertical integration: Arm (architecture) → Ampere (server CPUs) → Graphcore (accelerators). It competes with Intel and AMD in servers.
co.softbank.topBets.items.4.fact: SVF1 ($99bn, ~130 companies, mature and harvesting) and SVF2 ($56bn, dominated internally by OpenAI). Its assets include ByteDance, Coupang, DiDi, Grab and PayPay. SVF1's cumulative return is 1.01× — effectively flat — but SVF2 pulls the segment up through OpenAI.
co.softbank.topBets.items.4.role: Two funds holding dozens of AI companies
co.softbank.verification: Re-checked directly by WebFetch in this pass (primary sources): the SOTP page — NAV ¥40.06T, equity value ¥48.26T, net debt ¥8.21T, NAV/share ¥7,029, share price ¥3,555, a 49.4% discount, 5,699m shares, USD/JPY 159.88, with a line-by-line position breakdown [3]; the Ownership page — Son 32.73% / 1,865,511 thousand shares, top 10 at 66.08% [5]; the Alibaba release — ¥546.1bn non-consolidated intra-group, "no shares bought or sold in the market", no consolidated gain, 304m shares / 38m ADRs [11]; the OpenAI follow-on — $30bn / three tranches in Apr-Jul-Oct / $64.6bn / ~13% / $730bn / preferred shares [4]; the AGM index — a ¥11/share dividend, with no extractable NAV figures [6]; FY2025 net income ¥5,002.3bn (+333.7%) — search validation [12]. Three discrepancies with the brief were caught and resolved: (1) the discount — the primary source gives ~49%, NOT ~12%; (2) Son's stake — 32.73%, NOT ~35%; (3) the Alibaba "~425x / full market exit" — NOT confirmed by primary sources, and flagged. Reconciling the NAV basis: there is one primary basis (SOTP, a ~49% discount); ¥74T/¥13,000 cannot be extracted from the AGM PDF and are flagged in the gaps. Overall confidence: high on Tier-1 substance and the key reconciliation (NAV, ownership, Alibaba, OpenAI — primary sources confirmed directly by WebFetch); medium on the AGM narrative, the exact Arm/SBKK stakes and the peer context (secondary sources / corrupted PDFs). No DCF or fair value estimates were used — only disclosed facts and historical anchors.

co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.0.detail.rea: TPG's largest deal shows the scale of its capital under management: the platform can carry an $18bn take-private with an equal partner. The CVR shifts part of the valuation risk back to the seller. For a TPG shareholder this is a source of future carry (a share of fund profits), not an asset on TPG's balance sheet.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.0.detail.wha: TPG and Blackstone are buying listed Hologic (medical diagnostics and equipment) outright: $76 in cash per share plus up to $3/share as a CVR — a contingent payment linked to breast-health revenue for FY26/27. ADIA and GIC come in as minority co-investors. Announced 21.10.2025, shareholder vote 05.02.2026, deal closed (José Almeida appointed CEO).
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.0.title: Hologic — an $18.3bn take-private alongside Blackstone
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.0.why: TPG's largest move of the period. A buyout of the medtech manufacturer at $76/share plus up to $3/share of deferred payment (a CVR) tied to breast-health revenue in FY26/27.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.1.detail.rea: A bet that the shortage of AI compute infrastructure is structural, and on Indian demand. For TPG this is a business line rather than a one-off deal: fee-earning capital (FPAUM) grows as the platform is built out.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.1.detail.wha: TPG is committing up to $1bn (up to ₹8,820 crore) to HyperVault — a data-centre platform for AI workloads being built jointly with TCS. TPG's stake will be 27.5–49% (the combined TCS+TPG commitment is up to ₹18,000 crore, ~$2.03bn).
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.1.title: TCS HyperVault — up to $1bn into AI data centres in India
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.1.why: TPG is entering AI data centres in the fast-growing Indian market. The final stake is 27.5–49% of the joint platform with TCS.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.2.detail.fac: immediately accretive to FRE and DE
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.2.detail.rea: A classic purchase of a management platform: TPG is buying a fee stream rather than an asset. Immediate accretion to FRE/DE is a direct argument for HOLD for a TPG shareholder.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.2.detail.wha: TPG is buying Peppertree Capital — a manager of wireless tower infrastructure — for up to $660M plus up to $300M of deferred payment (an earn-out), up to $960M in total. The deal closed on 01.07.2025 and adds $7.7bn to assets under management.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.2.title: Peppertree Capital — buying a wireless tower platform
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.2.why: It adds $7.7bn of assets under management immediately and, TPG says, lifts fee-related earnings (FRE) and distributable earnings (DE) straight away.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.3.detail.rea: A niche Growth/Capital deal: predictable software cash flow. It does not change the thesis on its own — one item in the pipeline of mid-size deals that fill the funds.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.3.detail.wha: TPG is buying Proficy — GE Vernova's industrial software division (software for managing manufacturing and energy assets) — for $600M. Signed 11.09.2025, closing in H1 '26.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.3.title: GE Vernova Proficy — buying industrial software for $600M
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.3.why: TPG is buying the Proficy industrial software business. Closing is expected in the first half of 2026.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.4.detail.rea: The payoff from the 2023 integration: the credit/real estate platform raises large capital in its own right. It diversifies fee-related earnings (FRE) beyond private equity.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.4.detail.wha: TPG Angelo Gordon closed its fourth European real estate fund (Europe Realty IV) at ~$2.5bn — the platform's largest European fund. This is the credit and real estate division integrated into TPG in 2023.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.4.source: TPG Angelo Gordon press release, May 2025
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.4.title: TPG AG Europe Realty IV — a $2.5bn fund close
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.4.why: The largest European real estate fund on the TPG Angelo Gordon platform — proof that the 2023 credit/real estate integration attracts capital.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.5.detail.rea: A small bolt-on in the infrastructure strategy. The undisclosed amount signals a deal that is small relative to $306bn of AUM; no impact on the thesis.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.5.detail.wha: Through its Transition Infrastructure strategy, TPG is acquiring waste operators Waste Eliminator and Liberty Waste. Financial terms are not disclosed.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.5.title: Waste Eliminator + Liberty Waste — Transition Infrastructure deals
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.5.why: TPG is adding waste businesses through its Transition Infrastructure strategy. The amount is not disclosed — which is itself a fact, not a gap.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.6.detail.rea: A small growth investment. Noted for completeness of the feed; it carries no weight of its own in a HOLD/ADD/CUT decision.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.6.detail.wha: TPG Growth is investing in Smith + Howard — a professional services (audit and advisory) firm. The amount and structure are not disclosed.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.6.title: Smith + Howard — a TPG Growth investment
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.6.why: An investment by the TPG Growth division in professional services. Terms are not disclosed.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.7.detail.fac: de minimis or negative under Up-C/TRA — the exact figure is not disclosed in the available primary sources
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.7.detail.rea: TPG returns capital through the dividend rather than buybacks — the usual model for a manager that earns on fees. Negative or near-zero GAAP equity per share is an artefact of the Up-C/TRA structure, not a sign of weakness: a shareholder's economics are set by FRE, DE and carry, not by book equity.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.7.detail.wha: TPG is paying a variable dividend of $0.59 for Q1 '26 (declared with the FY2025 results — $2.06/share; $1.98 was paid in cash in calendar 2025). Share buybacks are negligible. The Up-C structure / tax receivable agreement (TRA) means most of the loss goes to non-controlling interests: a consolidated GAAP net loss of −$123M, but only −$1.5M attributable to Class A.
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.7.title: Dividends: $0.59 for Q1 '26, a ~5% yield — against negative GAAP equity
co.tpg.changesDeep.timeline.7.why: TPG returns capital through a variable dividend (~5% yield) with almost no buyback. The GAAP net loss for the quarter was −$123M (consolidated), but only −$1.5M of it falls to Class A.

co.tpg.recentMoves.0.detail: TPG and Blackstone are taking medtech company Hologic (diagnostics, women's health) private at $76 a share plus up to $3 a share in contingent payments tied to 2026–2027 revenue. ADIA and GIC are minority co-investors. Announced 21.10.2025, approved by shareholders 05.02.2026, the deal has closed. The surgical division (>$4bn) is already up for sale.
co.tpg.recentMoves.0.signal: TPG's largest capital deployment: it spends part of the dry powder and builds future carry. An early sale of the surgical unit above $4bn would accelerate the return of cash to the fund.
