co.tpg.recentMoves.1.signal: It lifts management fees immediately — not a promise but an addition to the fee base from day one. It extends TPG into digital infrastructure.
co.tpg.recentMoves.1.title: Peppertree Capital — a communications tower platform

co.tpg.recentMoves.2.signal: A direct bet on the shortage of AI compute capacity and on Indian demand. Small relative to $306bn of assets, but it sets the direction of growth.
co.tpg.recentMoves.2.title: AI data centres in India alongside Tata

TPG is a holdco: its only material asset is a stake in the TPG Operating Group; an Up-C structure with "controlled company" status under Nasdaq rules (the FY2025 10-K). The holding company earns by managing capital rather than by holding corporate positions, so its "portfolio" here means AUM across six platforms, with the funds as the "positions". The 13F portfolio is client assets in managed accounts and is EXCLUDED from the holdco valuation by methodology.

**AUM by platform at 31.03.2026** (source: the Q1 2026 10-Q, AUM table — checked line by line through SEC EDGAR):
- Credit — $95,196m ($95.2bn; +30% YoY from $73,430m)
- Capital (private equity) — $89,732m ($89.7bn; from $76,016m)
- Real Estate — $39,246m ($39.2bn)
- Growth — $32,366m ($32.4bn)
- Impact (Rise/climate) — $31,551m ($31.6bn)
- Market Solutions — $18,091m ($18.1bn; from $7,668m — the effect of consolidating Peppertree)
- **Total AUM — $306,182m ($306.2bn)**; FAUM — $175,372m ($175.4bn; from $142,794m)

**AUM by platform at 31.12.2025** (the FY2025 10-K; the segments here are in size order): Credit $93.1bn, Capital $90.9bn, Real Estate $38.2bn, Growth $32.2bn, Impact $31.2bn, Market Solutions $17.4bn — a total of $303.0bn; FAUM $170.1bn. (The segment totals differ between the 10-K at Dec-31 and the 10-Q at Mar-31 because of the date — both figures are primary, and there is no contradiction.)

**The largest funds as "positions"** (the FY2025 10-K fund performance table, Total Value):
- TPG IX (2022 vintage) — $12,014m committed, Total Value $15,383m.
- TPG X (2025 vintage, activated in Q3'25) — $10,858m committed (early; NM).
- The Rise Climate Funds — $16,014m committed in total (Rise Climate I 2021 plus II/Global South/TI 2025).
- TPG Direct Lending (MMDL, aggregate) — Total Value $14,792m.
- TPG VII (2015) — Total Value $24,825m; TPG VIII (2019) — $20,252m.

**Named portfolio companies** (named without a separate disclosed valuation in the holdco filings): Hologic (closed 07.04.2026, a Blackstone plus TPG deal at up to $18.3bn / $79 a share — counterparty IR), Surescripts, Viking Cruises, DirecTV, OneOncology (exited → Syncora), Intersect Power (Rise Climate, the digital power exit → Google), Sabre Industries (Rise Climate), Curium (a continuation vehicle), and the direct Anthropic / OpenAI / SpaceX positions in Tech Adjacencies / T-POP.

**Capital structure by duration** (the Q1'26 earnings release): long-dated 10+ year funds = $204.5bn (67% of AUM); perpetual capital = $49.7bn (16% of AUM).

**Holdco capital structure** (the Q1'26 earnings release / the annual meeting 8-K, record date 08.04.2026): ~160.46m Class A common shares (153.78m at the annual meeting record date); ~223.85m Common Units convertible into Class A → TPG Inc accounts for ~41% of the units in the Operating Group (160.46m / 384.31m = 41.7%).

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total AUM, $bn | 221.6 | 245.9 | 303.0 | 306.2 |
| FAUM, $bn | — | 141.3 | 170.1 | 175.4 |
| Management fees, $m | 1,178.7 | 1,625.7 | 1,800.1 | 475.1 |
| Fee-related revenues, $m | 1,337.3 | 1,831.5 | 2,109.3 | 557.2 |
| Fee-related earnings (FRE), $m | 606.3 | 764.2 | 952.6 | 246.9 |
| FRE margin | 45% | 42% | 45% | 44% |
| Distributable earnings (DE), $m | 627.9 | 894.6 | 1,042.1 | 296.0 |
| After-tax DE, $m | 585.3 | 837.3 | 973.5 | 281.6 |

The pace: FRE compounded at a ~25% CAGR from 2023 to 2025; management fees at a ~24% CAGR. LTM FRE passed $1bn for the first time after Q1'26 ($1,018m).

**GAAP (FY2025, 10-K):** total revenues $4,670.2m (against $3,500.1m, +33%); net income $599.6m (against a loss of $(76.9)m in FY2024). **GAAP Q1'26: a net loss of $(123.3)m**, but only $(1.5)m of it attributable to TPG Inc. — most sits with non-controlling interests; the cause of the loss is an unrealised capital allocation-based loss. GAAP EPS tells you little in an Up-C structure — look at DE per share.

**LTM management fees by platform** (the Q1'26 earnings release): Capital $525m, Credit $356m, Real Estate $339m, Impact $286m, Growth $236m, Market Solutions $120m. Real Estate is the only platform where management fees fell quarter on quarter ($95m→$83m).

**Fee income structure:** the weighted average management fee rate is ≈1.1–1.2% of FAUM (the FY2025 10-K). FRE is the most stable part; performance allocations are volatile.

**Balance sheet / liquidity (the Q1'26 earnings release):** cash $89m; net debt $2.3bn; debt obligations $2,343m; available liquidity $1.7bn; an undrawn revolver of $1.6bn. Borrowings: $2.0bn of senior plus subordinated note principal (including the 2034 senior notes of $600m at 5.875% and a 2064 subordinated note of $400m at 6.95%); $250m of secured note principal (collateral $496m) — if not redeemed by 20.06.2028 the coupon steps up by 4.0%. Credit ratings: Moody's A3 / S&P BBB+ / Fitch A-. **Available capital (dry powder, 31.12.2025): $72,436m** — Capital $21,776m, Credit $18,268m, Real Estate $12,293m, Impact $9,564m, Growth $7,050m, Market Solutions $3,485m.

**Dividend:** $0.59 per Class A share for Q1'26 (record 11.05.2026, payable 26.05.2026; press release). The payout is at least 85% of TPG Inc's share of after-tax DE.

co.tpg.sections.3.bodyMarkdown:
TPG's risk is not its debt. Net debt is only $2.3bn, the credit ratings are A3/BBB+/A-, dry powder is $72.4bn, and operating management has not made a single open-market sale in 2026 (Form 4, EDGAR). But a resilient balance sheet is not the absence of risk — the risk sorts by origin into two groups.

| Risk | Group | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Credit and real estate (Angelo Gordon) | positioning | the newest and largest platform: Credit at $95.2bn (31% of AUM), bought 02.11.2023 for ~$2.7bn; private credit plus real estate are exposed to a "private credit winter" and the CRE cycle — a fall in NAV hits the fee base |
| The flagship fund marks | positioning | $1.28bn of unrealised carry (a share of fund profits) is concentrated in Capital ($581m) and in the 2020-and-earlier vintages ($809m); if exits freeze (FY2025 realisations of $23.4bn were flat YoY) it does not get monetised; the weak vintages weigh: LSI net −25%, Asia I −10%, AION −11% |
| Carry timing against stable FRE | business model | fee-related earnings (FRE) of $1.02bn LTM are growing and predictable, while realised carry over 12 months was only $232.8m and is volatile — the market pays for FRE and discounts carry |
| The Up-C/TRA structure plus the dividend | business model | GAAP is distorted: the Q1'26 net loss was $(123.3)m, but only $(1.5)m of it sits at TPG Inc (the rest is NCI); the dividend is at least 85% of distributable earnings (DE) at a payout of ~300–630% of GAAP EPS; it is variable and falls with DE |

At $43.74 (a P/DE of ~15x on LTM after-tax DE of $2.81 a share) the market has already taken −38% off the 52-week high of $70.38 — most of that risk. Each group is taken apart below: what supports it and what breaks it.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.0.body:
First, what takes the panic out. TPG is a manager with a light balance sheet: bankruptcy and solvency are not the question here. There is no asset-level debt as there would be at a property owner; equity attributable to TPG Inc is positive at $1.13bn (SEC XBRL, 31.03.2026), and 12-month fee-related earnings (FRE) passed $1bn for the first time ($1,018m). As a business the company is resilient.

But resilience is not the absence of risk, and the risk here is not singular. It arrives from three different directions, and they are worth holding apart:

**What the money is invested in.** 31% of all assets ($95.2bn of $306bn) is the Angelo Gordon credit platform, only integrated on 02.11.2023 for ~$2.7bn. It is the youngest and most credit-cycle-sensitive part: if the cycle turns, its margin and fees compress at once.

**How the value is counted.** Accrued carry (a share of fund profits) is $1.2bn on the balance sheet, but only ~$233m came through as cash over 12 months. A fivefold gap — value held on paper and dependent on the flagship funds' exits.

**How the company is structured.** The Up-C structure and the tax receivable agreement (TRA) route tax benefits and part of the cash to pre-IPO unit holders. The dividend ($2.06 over 12 months, ~5.1%) rests on distributable earnings (DE), not on GAAP — and is paid over a GAAP loss (−$123m, of which only a fraction reaches TPG Inc, in Q1 2026).

Each is taken apart below: what it is, what supports it and what breaks it.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.0.title: The thesis: no bankruptcy — but the risk is not singular
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.0.desc: TPG bought Angelo Gordon on 02.11.2023 for ~$2.7bn (~$900m in cash plus up to 70m TPG Operating Group units plus a $400m earnout). The credit and real estate platform is $95.2bn of $306bn of AUM — 31% of the whole base. It is the youngest part of the portfolio and the most sensitive to the credit cycle: if the cycle turns, both asset valuations and the fees charged on them fall together. The risk is not in any single fund but in one shared driver — the state of the credit markets.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.0.foot: The weak spot: the separate disclosure of Credit AUM ($73.4bn→$95.2bn) in the 10-Qs is not confirmed in primary sources — it can only be checked through net accrued carry in Credit ($484m). The stress metrics (non-accruals ~1%, redemptions 1.3%) come from affiliated vehicles' data rather than TPG's own 10-Q.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.0.title: Concentration in Angelo Gordon's credit
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.1.desc: Accrued carry (a share of fund profits) was ~$1.2bn at 31.03.2026, already down from $1.3bn at the end of 2025. But only ~$233m turned into cash over 12 months ($68m realised in Q1 2026). A fivefold gap — value held in marks that only materialises when the flagship funds exit. By segment the accruals are: Credit $484m, Growth $189m, Impact $155m. The market pays grudgingly for that gap today.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.1.foot: Watch: the "Realized performance allocations" line — $68m in Q1 2026 (confirmed in primary sources); the credibility threshold is sustainably above $500m a year. The $233m over 12 months is an aggregation, not a separate line in the accounts.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.1.title: Carry is held on paper, not in cash
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.1.value: $1.2bn of accrued carry against ~$233m realised over 12 months
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.2.desc: TPG pays $0.59 per Class A share a quarter ($2.06 over 12 months, ~5.1% at a price of $43.74), variably — at least 85% of distributable earnings (DE) per share. But Q1 2026 produced a net GAAP loss of −$123m, part of it attributable to TPG Inc. The dividend is covered by DE rather than by GAAP: against GAAP EPS (~$0.46 over 12 months, a P/E of ~95x) the payout is ~448%. The Up-C structure and the tax receivable agreement (TRA) route tax benefits and cash flow to pre-IPO unit holders, which leaves the equity attributable to TPG Inc thin — +$1.13bn, a book value of ~$3.00 a share.
co.tpg.sections.3.deep.1.items.2.foot: PROVENANCE FLAG: the negative balance of −$2.69 a share from the original brief is NOT confirmed in primary sources — SEC XBRL (31.03.2026) gives equity attributable to TPG Inc of +$1.13bn (positive, but thin). The real structural flag is that the dividend rests on DE rather than GAAP, is variable, and is the first thing cut if realisations fall.

co.tpg.sections.3.deep.4.body: Hold. TPG is a manager with a light balance sheet: bankruptcy and solvency are not the question — equity attributable to TPG Inc is positive (+$1.13bn), and 12-month fee-related earnings (FRE) passed $1bn for the first time ($1,018m). The risk is not on the balance sheet but in three places: a young concentration in Angelo Gordon's credit (31% of AUM, integrated on 02.11.2023 for ~$2.7bn), carry held on paper ($1.2bn accrued against ~$233m realised over 12 months), and the Up-C/TRA structure, in which the dividend rests on distributable earnings (DE) and is paid over a GAAP loss (−$123m, of which part reaches TPG Inc, in Q1 2026). Add if the Q2/H2 2026 reports show realised carry accelerating towards $500m+. Reduce if the credit cycle hits the Angelo Gordon platform, or a GAAP loss forces a cut to the variable dividend: that would strike the only stable support under the price. PROVENANCE FLAG: the negative balance of −$2.69 a share from the original brief is not confirmed in primary sources — equity attributable to TPG Inc is positive but thin (~$3.00 a share). The CFO change (Weingart → André) takes effect on 27.07.2026; no open-market insider transactions are recorded.

co.tpg.sections.4.bodyMarkdown:
**Form 4 — opened through EDGAR XML (CIK 0001880661).** No open-market purchases or sales by operating management are recorded in 2026. Every transaction is an annual grant (Code A), tax withholding on vesting (Code F), or a movement of Operating Group units (Code J). There is no code P (purchase) or code S (open-market sale) by serving management in 2026.

| Date | Insider | Role | Code | Volume | Price | Holding after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11.02.2026 | Winkelried, Weingart and others | annual grants to senior management | A | as a block | — | — |
| 01.04.2026 | Jennifer L. Chu | Chief Legal Officer & GC | F | −22,079 | $40.51 | 196,974 |
| 14.04.2026 | David Trujillo | director | F | −8,379 | $39.42 | 237,297 |
| 12.05.2026 | William H. McRaven | director | A | +7,434 | — | a director award |
| 16.06.2026 | Kelvin L. Davis | director | J | +41,661 units | $42.48 | 11,602,827 |

The Form 4 conclusion: there are no bearish signals through sales; it is all routine vesting and tax withholding. The last genuine on-exchange sale by a senior figure was Jon Winkelried on 29.02.2024 (~1.05m shares, ~$43.8m); the CEO has made no on-exchange transactions since. **Neutral.**

**Buybacks.** TPG does not run a separate value-driven buyback programme. Across 2024–25 the company repurchased ~$250m of stock — an anti-dilutive buyback offsetting the dilution from employee equity grants, not a purchase of a "cheap stock" below its own valuation like Brookfield's or KKR's systematic buybacks. TPG returns capital through the dividend, not through buybacks.

**The dividend — variable, tied to distributable earnings (DE).** The policy: a payout of at least 85% of after-tax DE. For Q2'26 it declared $0.59 a share (record 11.05.2026, payable 26.05.2026). Through 2025 it moved quarter by quarter: $0.53 → $0.41 → $0.59 → $0.45 (a 2025 total of $1.98). Over the last 12 months it is ~$2.24, a ~5% yield at a price of ~$43.74. This is not a fixed, rising rate like KKR's $0.195 (raised every year since 2018) but a floating function of realised carry and FRE.

**The control structure — Up-C.** Class B common stock carries 10 votes a share and no economic rights; voting control sits with GP LLC and the pre-IPO partners. Per the latest 13D/A, James G. Coulter (co-founder) and Jon Winkelried (CEO) are deemed to own ~58% (Coulter ~220.2m, Winkelried ~218.7m, against a 377.7m Class A base). Economically the pre-IPO partners hold ~58% of the Operating Group through exchangeable units — so only ~42% of DE accrues to the public Class A. Alignment here is structural (the partners are locked into units) rather than signalled through on-exchange purchases.

**Issuance.** Equity has been issued for growth deals: Angelo Gordon (2023, up to 62.5m units) and Peppertree (2025, up to $418m) — which dilutes the Class A economics but funds growth in AUM and fees.

**A management change.** The CFO transition: Jack Weingart → Axel André (effective 27.07.2026).

co.tpg.sections.4.deep.0.takeaway: The thing that matters here is the ABSENCE of transactions, not their direction. Unlike KKR, where the serving Co-CEOs bought the drawdown, TPG has not had a single open-market purchase or sale by operating management in 2026: only annual grants (code A) and tax withholding on vesting (code F). The one large on-exchange sale by a senior figure in two years was Winkelried in Feb'24 (~$43.8m, ~1.05m shares), before the current drawdown. The company repurchased ~$250m across 2024–25, but that is an anti-dilutive buyback against grants, not the purchase of an undervalued stock. Alignment at TPG rests on something else: the pre-IPO partners are locked into ~58% of the economics through Up-C units and cannot simply sell them on-exchange. Weighted by who is trading, the verdict: neutral, closer to hold.

(The TPG figures come from the Q1'26 8-K/10-Q. The peer numbers come from BX/ARES/CG's own earnings releases via aggregators, and are not reconciled line by line with TPG's primary sources; the ARES/CG FPAUM figures are approximate.)

**Relative positioning (decision-grade):**
- **Scale:** TPG is the smallest listed manager in the set ($306bn against Blackstone's $1.30T, Ares's $644bn and Carlyle's $475bn).
- **Growth:** but the fastest on fees — FRE +36% YoY, while Carlyle's FRE actually fell (−4%). AUM +22%, FAUM +23%.
- **Valuation:** the cheapest and highest-yielding — a forward P/E of ~14 on a ~5% yield; and the stock is −21% over the year against the S&P's +18%.
- **What is unique to TPG, and the risk:** the Up-C — the public Class A receives only ~42% of distributable earnings (DE), with the rest going to the pre-IPO partners; and the credit platform (Angelo Gordon, ~$95bn) is younger than Blackstone's, Ares's or Apollo's.

**Hold/add/cut conclusion:** fast fee growth plus a high yield plus a compressed valuation after a drawdown → the relative-value profile is closer to hold/add; the main negatives against BX and ARES are smaller scale, a young credit franchise and the structural Up-C discount. The trim signal is FRE growth slowing below ~15% while realisations fail to recover.

co.tpg.sections.5.deep.2.title: What the portfolio is made of
co.tpg.sections.5.deep.3.body:
**TPG** is the smallest in the group ($306bn of AUM) but grows fastest: fee-related earnings (FRE) +36% YoY, with the 12-month figure passing $1bn for the first time ($1,018m). It is a pure manager on fees and carry (a share of fund profits) — without the insurance balance sheet or the owner-operator model that distinguish KKR and Brookfield. The multi-strategy platform is assembled from six businesses: Capital ($89.7bn), Credit through Angelo Gordon ($95.2bn, integrated since 2023), Real Estate ($39.2bn), Growth ($32.4bn), Impact / Rise ($31.6bn) and Market Solutions ($18.1bn). Accrued unrealised carry is $1.2bn. Two features drive the decision: TPG is cheaper than its peers (a forward P/E of ~14) and more generous on dividends (a ~5% yield, the highest in the group), but the Up-C structure gives Class A holders only ~42% of distributable earnings (DE) — the other ~58% goes to the pre-IPO partners through exchangeable units. The hold case: a cheap valuation and fast growth close the gap, but what you buy is 42% of the economics.

**Blackstone** is the largest by scale ($1.30T of AUM) and the most efficient at converting AUM into fees (72%). Its edge is an asset-light model that scales without freezing capital. Over 12 months it quietly rebuilt its mix: 35% of AUM is now credit and insurance. The legacy of the property cycle is the BXMT mortgage REIT at ~7% past due — not the main business, but a reminder that Blackstone has not fully exited commercial real estate.

**Ares** is a credit specialist growing almost as fast as TPG (+26% fees YoY), with quarterly management fees passing $1bn for the first time. Its core is direct lending (~65% of AUM and above), and it is the structural leader there. The price of that focus: concentration in a single asset class late in the credit cycle — if defaults rise, the blow lands squarely on the core.

**KKR** is the direct benchmark for TPG. On $758bn of AUM it monetises 81% against TPG's 57% and collects four times the quarterly fees ($1,016m against $247m) on a base only 2.5 times larger. It is diversified: private equity 30%, credit 43%, plus the Global Atlantic insurance balance sheet and $18.3bn of deferred earnings in Strategic Holdings. TPG's gap to KKR is the price of youth (the Angelo Gordon credit platform dates from 2023), smaller scale and the absence of permanent insurance capital. KKR's risk is that same insurance channel, under NAIC capital review in 2026.

co.tpg.sections.5.deep.4.takeaway: TPG's real advantage is not scale (it is the smallest in the group) but the combination of "a dedicated impact franchise plus the fastest fee growth plus the cheapest valuation". TPG Rise and Rise Climate together form the largest specialist impact investment platform in private markets ($31.6bn) — a dedicated business rather than an overlay on the core, as it is at competitors. Plus a multi-strategy platform of six businesses, into which the Angelo Gordon credit franchise was integrated in 2023 ($95.2bn, already 31% of AUM). The other side shows in the same table: TPG lags structurally in credit scale (Angelo Gordon is young), it has no permanent insurance capital with which KKR and Apollo turn spread into profit, and the Up-C structure leaves Class A holders only ~42% of distributable earnings (DE). The hold case: cheapness (a forward P/E of ~14), a ~5% yield and leadership in impact, against a discount for youth, the absence of an insurance block and diluted Class A economics.

co.tpg.sections.6.bodyMarkdown:
**The edge thesis — scale plus diversification plus cross-platform deal sourcing.** Jon Winkelried (CEO), press release of 01.05.2026 (verbatim): "TPG's strong first quarter performance reflects the significant momentum across our global platform, as the scale of our franchise and consistent execution continue to translate into powerful results… Our resilient business model is intentionally built to navigate complexity and capitalize on opportunity".

Measurable confirmation: LTM FRE passed $1bn for the first time, at a 44% FRE margin for the quarter (+620 bp YoY); Q1'26 management fees were $475.1m (+15% YoY).

Cross-platform sourcing (transcript): Curium was "sourced and completed through the close collaboration of TPG's investment professionals across four platforms and three geographies" — one deal drawing on both TPG GP Solutions and Life Sciences.

**Capital allocation rules (the 10-K plus the earnings release):**
- A target dividend payout of at least 85% of TPG Inc's share of after-tax DE; Q1'26 was $0.59 per Class A share.
- GP commitments are funded in cash, not by deferring fees (the 10-K).
- The clawback / contingent repayment obligation was $7.9m at 31.12.2025 (the 10-K).
- Balance sheet investments are deal-specific (for example $500m into Jackson, funded by a $500m senior note issue) rather than a general increase in leverage.
- The composition of pre-tax DE: 83% from FRE in Q1'26 (against 97% in Q4'25).

**Layers of the business mechanics:**
1. Management fees — the predictable base ($475m in Q1'26; growing across 5 of 6 platforms, with Real Estate the only decline). $33bn of capital already raised but not yet earning fees is embedded FAUM growth.
2. Fee-related performance ($8.2m in Q1'26) plus transaction, monitoring and other fees, net ($73.9m, +30% YoY) → fee-related revenues of $557m.
3. Realised performance allocations (carry): $67.7m net in Q1'26; $232.8m LTM. The Q1'26 drivers: TPG IX, THP II (Capital), Rise Climate I (Impact) and Growth V.
4. Private wealth: T-POP (a perpetual PE evergreen) reached $2.1bn of AUM in ~10 months ($545m of inflows in Q1; the private wealth channel is +130% YoY). Weingart moves to CEO of Global Wealth Solutions to run it.
5. Credit (after Angelo Gordon): the largest platform by AUM. Twin Brook (direct lending): 310+ companies, an average LTV at origination of 42%, interest cover above 2x, non-accruals "just above 1%", and ~50% of deals add-ons.

By duration: performance-eligible AUM ≈$253bn; performance-generating AUM ≈$208bn; net accrued performance $1.19bn (Q1'26); available capital $72.8bn (dry powder).
co.tpg.sections.6.deep.0.body: TPG is a multi-strategy asset manager: six platforms under one roof — private equity (Capital, $89.7bn / 29% of assets), credit (Credit, $95.2bn / 31%), real estate (Real Estate, $39.2bn / 13%), growth investing ($32.4bn / 11%), impact (Rise, $31.6bn / 10%) and Market Solutions ($18.1bn / 6%). Total assets under management (AUM) were $306.2bn at 31.03.2026 (+22% YoY). Unlike KKR, TPG has NO insurance balance sheet of its own (KKR's is Global Atlantic), and unlike Brookfield it has no owner-operator infrastructure model. What distinguishes TPG comes down to three things. First, buying Angelo Gordon in 2023 made credit its largest segment ($73.4bn → $95.2bn, +30% YoY) and the main engine of its fee base. Second, the retail evergreen fund T-POP ($2.1bn, with private wealth inflows +130% YoY) is being built as a substitute for the permanent or insurance capital it does not have. Third, the Up-C corporate structure with a tax receivable agreement (TRA): despite a pre-tax GAAP loss (−$123m in Q1'26), TPG pays out ~85% of distributable earnings (DE) as a dividend. TPG's own economics are (1) fee-related earnings (FRE) on assets under management, (2) carry (a share of fund profits) plus balance sheet allocations, and (3) the TPG Angelo Gordon credit platform. IMPORTANT: the funds' portfolio companies (Hologic, Curium, Anthropic and others) are CLIENT fund assets, not TPG's own balance sheet; the company does not disclose its own equity share in them.

Notable: the 2023 integration turned TPG from a PE house into a multi-strategy one — this segment now carries the bulk of fee growth.

co.tpg.sections.6.deep.4.items.4.v: TPG has no insurance balance sheet of its own (unlike KKR's Global Atlantic). It is building a substitute for permanent capital through the T-POP retail evergreen fund ($2.1bn, private-wealth inflows +130% YoY) — the fastest-growing source of new money.
co.tpg.sections.6.deep.4.items.5.k: Capital return: ~85% of distributable earnings paid out as dividend

A structural quirk for valuation: the Up-C corporate structure with its tax receivable agreement (TRA) produces a pre-tax GAAP loss (–$123M in Q1 '26) alongside positive DE — so valuing TPG on a GAAP P/E is wrong; look at DE and FRE instead.
co.tpg.sections.6.deep.4.items.6.k: Provenance: client funds ≠ TPG's balance sheet
co.tpg.sections.6.deep.4.items.6.v: The headline names (Hologic, Curium, Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX) are assets of CLIENT funds, not TPG's own balance sheet. The firm does not disclose its own stake in them; TPG's own economics are fees (FRE), carry and balance-sheet allocations — not the value of the portfolio companies.

co.tpg.sections.7.bodyMarkdown:
**What they believe (earnings call transcript 01.05.2026, verbatim attribution):**
- **A difficult environment = a window of opportunity.** Winkelried: «Our business is intentionally built to be resilient through cycles… The current environment is an opportunity… We've never felt more confident in the positioning of our franchise».
- **PE on the cusp of a strong cycle + AI as a tool.** James Coulter (Founding Partner & Executive Chairman): «I personally believe this will be the most positive weapon that we've seen in a long time in private equity».
- **The current PE portfolio is resilient.** Todd Sisitsky (President): «This is a portfolio across private equity, I think we'd be excited about in any environment».
- **Private credit — structural growth; an institutional focus as the defence.** TPG separates itself from retail credit funds with their 'elevated redemptions'; TCAP redemptions are 1.3%.
- **AI — driver and risk.** Direct positions in Anthropic / OpenAI / SpaceX in the Tech Adjacency fund and T-POP (with no disclosed valuation); ~80% of staff use AI tools daily.

**Where they are cautious:** part of TPG VIII is classified as carrying AI-disruption risk in software (to be mitigated); the new funds (IX, X) make AI part of underwriting. PE valuation was −1% in Q1 '26 on multiple compression (Capital: earnings +$1.2bn, multiples −$2.4bn) — a mark-down from the multiple market, not from operational deterioration.

**What they are watching:** the IPO window for the large private AI companies («1 to 3 of the large companies to go public over 18 months»); portfolio software bookings +20% YoY; the Jackson Financial ABF $2bn of initial commitments 'tracking ahead of plan'.

co.tpg.sections.8.deep.2.items.0.v: Fees are a manager's steadiest income: $246.9M for the quarter (+36% YoY), a 44% margin against 38% a year earlier, and over 12 months FRE passed $1.0bn for the first time. Management targets 47% for 2026. While the margin is climbing towards 47% the thesis is working and adding is justified. If it sticks below 42% while fee-earning capital growth slows, the machine is stalling — a reason to trim.
co.tpg.sections.8.deep.2.items.1.v: $1.19bn of fund profits is accrued on paper (net accrued performance), but only $233M turned into hard cash over the last year ($67.7M in the quarter). The market does not believe the paper will become cash — hence part of the discount. If realisation accelerates above $300M a quarter the thesis is confirmed; if it stands still, the market is right not to pay for the carry.
co.tpg.sections.8.deep.2.items.2.v: TPG has no insurance balance sheet of its own, as KKR does with Global Atlantic — the substitute is T-POP retail evergreen capital: $2.1bn under management, $545M of inflows in the quarter, the private-wealth channel +130% YoY. This is the most valuable kind of money — it cannot be withdrawn on demand. Sustained inflow growth is a leading signal for future fees; a halt in inflows hits the whole model.
co.tpg.sections.8.deep.2.items.3.v: Over 12 months: $55.9bn raised ($10.3bn in the quarter, +75%), $58.9bn deployed ($14.4bn, +96%), $27.8bn returned to investors ($8.7bn, +103%); dry powder of $72.8bn. Faster realisations are the direct route to converting carry into cash. If sales stall while deployment rises, fee-earning capital grows but distributable earnings lag.
co.tpg.sections.8.deep.2.items.4.v: The TPG Angelo Gordon credit platform holds $95.2bn of assets (+30%). Twin Brook direct lending: more than 310 companies, average LTV 42%, non-accruals 'a little above 1%'. While non-accruals sit around 1% the platform is healthy and compounding fees. A move past 2–3% is an early signal of mid-market stress and a reason to trim.
co.tpg.sections.8.deep.2.items.5.v: A $0.59 dividend against distributable earnings (DE) of $0.70 a share — a payout of around 85%; a ~5% yield, with negligible buybacks. The Up-C structure and the tax receivable agreement (TRA) mean that under US GAAP Class A carries a loss even though TPG Inc's equity is positive (+$1.13bn). Capping the payout (below 80%) would free up cash; keeping it at 85%+ on top of a paper loss is a risk factor to keep in view.

co.tpg.sections.9.bodyMarkdown:
> An analyst's interpretation built from verified primary facts. NOT company disclosure and not a valuation.

1. **The FRE machine passed $1bn LTM at a 44% margin (quarter) / 46% (LTM) against a 47% target** — a qualitative shift towards predictable income. Supports: $33bn of capital already raised but not yet earning fees (built-in FAUM growth); management fees +15% YoY with growth in 5 of the 6 business lines. Watch point: real estate management fees are falling ($95M→$83M for the quarter).
2. **GAAP net loss vs cash earnings is accounting noise.** Q1 '26 GAAP net loss $(123)M, of which only $(1.5)M is attributable to TPG Inc.; after-tax DE +51% to $282M. Signal: look at DE/FRE, ignore the GAAP volatility.
3. **The flagship track record (10-K, verified) sets the 'gravity' of the carry:** future monetisation rests on TPG IX (net 24%, $14.2bn unrealised), THP II (net 29%), Rise Climate I (net 15%, $7.9bn unrealised) — specific funds with large unrealised tails. The $1,280M net accrued is concentrated in the 2020 & prior ($809M) and 2022 ($280M) vintages.
4. **The AI lens is real and cuts both ways.** Positive: direct positions in Anthropic/OpenAI/SpaceX, the $6bn Tata data centre, Intersect → Google as an exit premium, an IPO window for AI companies. Negative: AI risk in the mature TPG VIII; PE valuation −1% in Q1 '26 from multiple compression. Do NOT stretch the AI story over real estate / mortgage REITs (TRTX/MITT) — those are interest-rate and CRE-cycle stories.
5. **Management transitions against aggressive guidance.** Weingart → Global Wealth Solutions (T-POP $2.1bn, private wealth +130%); CFO André (RGA/Jackson) — a twin priority on insurance capital. Risk note: the CFO changes at exactly the moment of a 47% FRE margin target and a >$50bn fundraise.

**Insiders/holders (Form 4 — verified):** no open-market sales by operating management in 2026 year to date; everything is routine vesting (Code F) and director grants (Code A); Davis Kelvin — a unit acquisition (Code J), not a sale. Neutral.

**Hold / add / trim signals for the TPG Inc holdco position (NOT the share price):**
- **Base case: HOLD / ADD on confirmations.**
- **ADD triggers:** (1) Q2 FRE margin ≥46% and cumulative fundraising ≥$25bn towards >$50bn; (2) final closes of TPG X / Healthcare Partners III above the previous vintages (TPG IX was $12.0bn committed); (3) T-POP AUM >$3bn; (4) the quarterly depreciation in Capital/Growth turning positive.
- **TRIM / caution:** (1) TCAP non-accruals above ~2% or redemptions jumping above ~2–3%; (2) rising reserves/delinquencies at TRTX (CRE stress); (3) a downgrade below A3/BBB+/A- against net debt of $2.3bn; (4) a guidance miss in the new CFO's first quarter; (5) reclassification of most of TPG VIII as 'material AI risk'; (6) Code S appearing among operating management.
- **Operational markers:** FRE margin <43% for two consecutive quarters = the operating-leverage thesis has reversed; LTM realised carry <$200M (currently $233M) = weakening monetisation; available capital <$60bn (currently $72.4bn) without offsetting fundraising; a continued decline in real estate management fees.
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.0.body: TPG is a bet on a multi-strategy asset-management platform that has just passed $1bn of fee-related earnings (FRE) over 12 months for the first time. It manages $306.2bn (+22% YoY), of which $175.4bn is fee-earning (FPAUM, +23%). Unlike Brookfield there are no power plants or ports of its own here; unlike KKR there is no insurance balance sheet (Global Atlantic in KKR's case). TPG's distinguishing feature is the multi-strategy machine plus the Angelo Gordon credit platform, bought in November 2023 for ~$2.7bn and contributing $95.2bn of assets (31% of total AUM). The thesis rests on three pillars: (1) fee-related earnings (FRE) of $246.9M in Q1 (+36% YoY), a 44% margin with a 47% target for 2026 — steady cash flow growing faster than at most peers; (2) the Angelo Gordon credit platform as the growth engine — $95.2bn of assets, +30% YoY; (3) an unrealised share of fund profits — carry of $1.19bn on the balance sheet against only ~$233M realised over 12 months: an option that converts into cash as assets are exited, and one not priced into the ~$44 share price against a 52-week high of $70.38.
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essentials
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.1.body: The main reason for the discount is accounting. In Q1 '26 TPG reported a consolidated GAAP net loss of −$123M (only −$1.5M of which falls to Class A shareholders — the rest goes to non-controlling interests because of the Up-C structure). The $0.59 quarterly dividend ($2.06 declared for FY2025, a ~5% yield) is paid on top of a GAAP loss: it is covered by distributable earnings (DE), not by accounting profit — an ~85% payout of DE, but several times GAAP EPS (~$0.46 over 12 months). The Up-C structure creates a tax receivable agreement (TRA) obligation to the pre-IPO holders — a cash outflow not reflected in the margin. PROVENANCE FLAG: the negative book value of −$2.69 a share claimed in the brief is NOT confirmed by primary data — on XBRL as at 31.03.2026 the equity attributable to TPG Inc is positive but thin: +$1.13bn (BVPS ~$3), with total equity including non-controlling interests at $3.72bn. The $1.19bn of carry is a promise, not a fact: only ~$233M was realised over 12 months, and the accrued carry itself is down from $1.3bn at end-2025. The public free float is younger and smaller than KKR's or Brookfield's — worse liquidity and index weight, which deepens the discount.
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.desc: The FRE margin reaches the 47% target for 2026 (44% in Q1) and LTM FRE settles above $1bn. The Angelo Gordon credit platform holds +30% YoY. Carry starts converting: realisation accelerates from ~$233M towards $500M+ over 12 months as fund exits come through. T-POP retail permanent capital ($2.1bn, inflows +130% YoY) scales as a substitute for the insurance balance sheet TPG does not have. The discount to the $70.38 high narrows.
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.title: Bull case
co.tpg.sections.9.deep.2.items.1.desc: Fundraising slows and fee-earning capital (FPAUM) growth falls below +10% YoY (from +23%). Carry stays on paper for another 2–3 years, with realisation stuck around ~$233M. GAAP losses continue, the ~$2 dividend is sustained only by DE at an 85% payout, and the TRA obligation presses on cash. The Angelo Gordon integration fails to deliver margin synergies. The CFO change (André from 27.07.2026) adds uncertainty. The price tests the 52-week low of $36.95.

Add: the FRE margin confirms progress towards the 47% target (44% in Q1) OR a quarter in which carry realisation accelerates above ~$60M, after ~$233M over 12 months — a signal that the accrued $1.19bn has begun converting into cash. Trim: fee-earning capital (FPAUM) growth below 10% YoY (from +23%) — the platform is losing momentum; OR a dividend cut — meaning distributable earnings (DE) no longer cover the 85% payout.

co.tpg.summary: TPG (NASDAQ: TPG) is one of the largest private investment firms in the US: $306bn under management across six strategies. Its main earnings come from fees for managing other people's money — these have passed $1bn a year for the first time and are growing faster than anyone else's in the industry — plus a share of the profits from successful funds. The largest business line is credit (the Angelo Gordon platform), followed by buyouts: the latest deal is Hologic at $18bn alongside Blackstone. The dividend is variable (~5%), and the shares sit near their 52-week low despite record assets — because of the Up-C structure, under which public holders receive only ~42% of the profits.
co.tpg.tagline: > A listed alternative asset manager with $306.2bn of AUM (31.03.2026); its income increasingly rests on predictable management fees — LTM FRE passed $1bn for the first time, at a 44% FRE margin for the quarter. The decision on the position rests on the durability of the fee base in Credit ($95.2bn, +30% YoY), on executing the fundraising target of more than $50bn in 2026, and on the CFO transition arriving in the middle of tight guidance.
co.tpg.topBets.items.0.fact: A credit platform with $95.2bn under management — 31% of all TPG assets and the largest segment (a year ago, $73bn). The core is Twin Brook: 310+ mid-market borrowers, LTV ~42% at origination. Bought in 2023 for ~$2.7bn and the main driver of asset growth ever since, as well as the steadiest fee base (management fees of $356M over 12 months, +30% YoY). Castlelake — lending against real assets and aircraft (Brookfield owns 51% of the fee income)
Angel Oak — US mortgage and consumer credit
Primary Wave — investments in music rights (song royalties)
port.brookfield.allocation.byTheme.2.pla: Brookfield lends to companies and investors through the firm it bought, Oaktree — the world's specialist in distressed and opportunistic debt. It is the largest segment by size under management; management specifically stresses that it barely lends to software companies, to avoid the fashionable risk.
port.brookfield.holdings13F.note: Brookfield Corp's public 13F portfolio is mostly its own stake in the manager Brookfield Asset Management (BAM, 71%) plus positions in pipelines, power and utilities (Cheniere, Williams, NextEra) and in other listed Brookfield entities (BEP, BBUC, BIP). It is only a small, publicly traded slice of Brookfield's assets — the bulk sits in private infrastructure outside the 13F. 47 of 153 are shown. Source: fintel.io / SEC 13F-HR (31.03.2026).
port.brookfield.notDisclosed: Brookfield does NOT disclose by name: (1) BPG's top real estate assets — the "139 properties" case: BN's and BAM's public quarterly filings carry no line-by-line list with a valuation for each office, retail or multifamily building; only a few recent transactions are named (prime office Tokyo, mixed-use Paris, US senior living). (2) BEP's net economic share within the 51% of Westinghouse after the LP partners — the effect on NAV cannot be quantified. (3) Individual data centre sites inside BIP (disclosed in aggregate: >150 data centres, 1.3 GW). (4) Specific Oaktree/credit positions — these are client assets and are not disclosed. (5) Individual valuations for particular BEP hydro, wind and solar assets (disclosed by country and region). (6) BN's SpaceX and AI investments (Figure, The Deployment Company with OpenAI, Hark Labs) — no line-item valuation in the Supplemental. On accounting: Brookfield's 13F holdings are client money under management and are NOT included in the holding company's portfolio.
port.brookfield.sectors.0.name: Asset management
port.brookfield.sectors.0.plain: This is Brookfield's own management business (BAM): it manages external investors' money through a series of flagship funds, each focused on a specific asset class. Fees of ~$3.1bn a year plus a share of the profits of the successful funds.
port.brookfield.sectors.0.subsectors.0.c: The world's largest infrastructure fund. It owns ~$100bn of assets: pipelines (Inter Pipeline), telecom towers (Heartland, ~200k), logistics (IPL) and data centres (>150 sites, 1.3 GW). Brookfield holds a ~27% economic interest.
The main beneficiary of AI demand, through data centres and power grids. Brookfield's largest and most liquid fund.
The flagship infrastructure fund — ports, pipelines, towers, data centres

One of the world's largest owners of renewable generation: ~34 GW of capacity (hydro, wind, solar, distributed, storage). Also a controlling stake in Westinghouse Electric (nuclear fuel and services). Brookfield holds ~48%.
A bet on decarbonisation plus nuclear power. Westinghouse gives unique exposure to the nuclear renaissance.
The flagship renewable power fund — hydro, wind, solar, nuclear (Westinghouse)

An asset-light management platform, carved out of BN in 2022. It collects management fees (~$3.1bn a year) and a share of the carry ($33.8bn accrued). It runs more than $1T across ~40 funds. Brookfield holds 75% of the shares.
The only pure fee-revenue company in BN's structure. The market values BAM above the whole of BN — an anomaly the thesis is built on.
A market cap of ~$22bn (with BN holding 75%)
The listed management company — it collects the fees from every Brookfield fund
port.brookfield.sectors.0.subsectors.1.c: An unlisted division: 139+ properties, including prime offices (Canary Wharf, Brookfield Place NYC), shopping centres and multifamily. Individual valuations are not disclosed — only the aggregate.
The riskiest segment — offices have been under pressure since the pandemic. Also the most undervalued if they turn.
Real estate funds — offices, shopping centres, housing, warehouses

One of the world's largest credit managers. Its specialism: distressed and opportunistic credit, and special situations. Brookfield bought 68% in 2019. These are client assets — they are not in BN's portfolio directly, but they generate fees.
The fastest-growing segment by fundraising. It gives Brookfield exposure to the credit cycle without balance sheet risk.
The largest credit platform — distressed debt, special situations

Brookfield's insurance and retirement platform: American Equity (annuities, $70bn+) and AEL (UK annuities). It raises permanent capital through insurance products and reinvests it into Brookfield's strategies. The fastest-growing part of AUM.
A permanent capital engine — the money does not have to be returned to clients, which gives stable long-term fees. The main driver of AUM growth.
The insurance and retirement platform — annuities and permanent capital
port.brookfield.sectors.1.name: Insurance and retirement
port.brookfield.sectors.1.plain: Brookfield gathers money through insurance companies and retirement products (annuities), then invests it into its own strategies — producing long-term capital that does not have to be returned to clients immediately.
port.brookfield.sectors.1.subsectors.0.c: AEL is one of the US leaders in fixed and fixed-indexed annuities (retirement savings products), distributed through 40,000+ independent agents and licensed in all 50 states. Brookfield owns 100% (fully bought in by May 2024 for ~$4.3bn, at $56.50 a share).
A major source of long-term insurance money invested into Brookfield's strategies.
A US leader in fixed and indexed annuities

American National is a large life, annuity and property & casualty (P&C) insurer headquartered in Galveston, Texas. Brookfield owns 100% (a $5.1bn deal closed in May 2022). The P&C arm was later folded into the Argo platform.
Another large supplier of permanent insurance capital to the platform.
A large life, annuity and property insurer

Just Group is the UK leader in pension risk transfer (where a company hands its pensioner obligations to an insurer) and individual annuities: 700,000+ customers and ~£30bn of pension savings. Brookfield owns 100% (a £2.4bn / ~$3.2bn deal closed 01.04.2026), adding ~$40bn of assets under management.
A recent large acquisition that takes insurance assets to ~$180bn.
The UK leader in pension risk transfer and annuities

Brookfield Annuity (the Blumont brand) is Canada's only life insurer focused on group pension annuities and pension risk transfer for defined benefit schemes: ~$5.5bn of pension assets and payments to more than 33,000 beneficiaries a year. Brookfield owns 100%.
It extends the retirement business into the Canadian market.
~$5.5bn of pension assets, 33,000+ beneficiaries paid a year
A Canadian insurer specialising in group pension annuities

North End Re comprises Brookfield's reinsurance platforms in Bermuda and the Cayman Islands, which assume long-dated annuity obligations (reinsurance). Both are wholly owned by the BWS insurance business.
A capital-efficient structure for growing insurance liabilities.
two vehicles — Bermuda and the Cayman Islands

Argo is a specialty and commercial property & casualty (P&C) insurer. Since October 2025 American National's P&C units have been folded into it — making it the insurance business's single property platform. Brookfield owns 100% (a ~$1.1bn deal closed in November 2023).
It adds property insurance to a predominantly annuity portfolio.
A specialty and commercial property & casualty (P&C) insurer
port.brookfield.sectors.2.name: Real estate
port.brookfield.sectors.2.plain: Brookfield directly owns buildings worldwide — offices, shopping centres, warehouses, housing and hotels — which produce rental income and are sold on at a higher price over time.
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.0.b: Flagship business complexes and towers in key cities — London, New York, Toronto. The segment most sensitive to interest rates: with expensive money and remote working, offices fall in value, so Brookfield holds only quality assets in the best locations.
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.0.c: Canary Wharf is an entire London business district, with offices, shops and housing across 20m+ sq ft. Brookfield controls roughly 69% of it jointly with Qatar's investment fund (through the Songbird Estates vehicle), acquired in 2015 for around £2.6bn.
One of the largest office assets; an indicator of office property risk when rates rise.
a ~69% JV (with Qatar's fund, through Songbird)
London's largest business district: offices, shops, housing

Manhattan West is a roughly $8bn complex on 8 acres in New York: four office towers (including One Manhattan West at ~2.1m sq ft), a hotel, housing, shops and a public plaza. Brookfield owns about 56%, with Qatar's investment fund holding around 44%.
Brookfield's flagship New York development, and a marker for the quality of the office portfolio.
A complex of 4 office towers, a hotel, housing and shops in New York

Brookfield Place New York is a flagship ~8m sq ft office and retail complex on the Lower Manhattan waterfront (the former World Financial Center). Brookfield controls it and has invested around $300m in refurbishing the retail section.
A landmark office asset and the real estate platform's calling card.
A flagship office and retail complex on the Manhattan waterfront

Potsdamer Platz is a landmark mixed-use quarter in the heart of Berlin: 17 buildings, 10 streets and two squares totalling ~2.9m sq ft (offices, retail, housing, leisure and a hotel). Bought in January 2016 alongside Korea Investment Corporation for around $1.4bn.
An example of Brookfield's real estate strategy: a trophy asset in a supply-constrained location, bought at a discount from the previous owner for operational improvement.
A trophy quarter in central Berlin: offices, retail, housing, a hotel
offices plus a mall plus a hotel

The International Finance Center Seoul (IFC Seoul) is a complex of three office towers, a three-level shopping mall and the five-star Conrad hotel. Acquired at the end of 2016 as Brookfield entered the South Korean market.
The flagship Asian office asset; part of a global trophy office portfolio alongside Canary Wharf, Manhattan West and Potsdamer Platz.
3 office towers plus a mall plus a 5★ hotel
Seoul's international finance centre: 3 towers, a mall and the Conrad hotel

ARC is a science and innovation real estate platform: laboratory and research campuses across the UK and Europe (London, Uxbridge, Oxford) totalling ~1.6m sq ft, including the 700-acre flagship Harwell campus (a ~50% stake). Brookfield controls the platform.
A growing segment of specialised workspace for science and biotech — leased laboratory campuses.
~1.6m sq ft (a platform of 80+ properties, ~6m sq ft)
Campuses for laboratories and science (life sciences)
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.1.b: A network of top-tier US shopping centres, assembled around the GGP acquisition. These are places people go to shop, eat and be entertained; the income is rent from the shops and restaurants.
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.1.c: GGP is the largest top-tier shopping centre platform in the US, fully acquired by Brookfield in 2018 for $9.25bn in cash (more than $15bn including debt). Through it Brookfield owns more than 100m sq ft of retail space, including flagship malls.
The core of the retail segment, and a major candidate for gradual asset-by-asset monetisation.
The largest network of class A shopping centres in the US
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.2.b: Warehouses and distribution centres serving e-commerce and supply chains. A growing segment: online orders require more warehouse space close to cities.
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.2.c: IDI Logistics is a US warehouse and logistics property platform (formerly IDI Gazeley). It sits within Brookfield's overall logistics portfolio: more than 900 properties across 19 countries totalling 160m+ sq ft. The European arm was sold to GLP for €2.4bn in 2017.
Exposure to growing demand for warehousing and logistics (e-commerce).
part of a portfolio of 900+ properties totalling 160m+ sq ft
A US warehouse and logistics property platform
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.3.b: Hotels and resorts worldwide — from the luxury Leela chain in India to the Center Parcs holiday villages in the UK. Income depends on occupancy and room rates; the segment is more cyclical but delivers strong cash flow.
port.brookfield.sectors.2.subsectors.3.c: Center Parcs is an operator of short-break holiday villages: 6 operating across the UK and Ireland, with a seventh under construction. Brookfield controls the business, acquired in 2015 for £2.45bn.
Durable cash flow within the hotel part of the real estate segment.
An operator of short-break holiday villages

The Leela is India's largest luxury hotel chain: 13 operating hotels with roughly 3,550 rooms. Brookfield controls the business (the listed company Schloss Bangalore, following its May 2025 IPO), bought in 2019 for around Rs 3,950 crore.
An example of successfully monetising a real estate asset through a listing.
India's largest luxury hotel chain; now listed
port.brookfield.sectors.3.name: Power
port.brookfield.sectors.3.plain: Brookfield owns one of the world's largest clean power portfolios — hydro, wind, solar, storage — plus the nuclear business Westinghouse; all of it sells electricity, demand for which is being pulled up by data centres and AI.
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.0.b: Hydroelectric plants are the oldest and most predictable part of the portfolio: output is contracted years ahead, so revenue is stable. The cash flow base of the whole power segment.
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.0.c: A large Colombian hydro producer: 14 hydroelectric plants totalling more than 4,000 MW, with around 70% of output contracted for an average of 8 years ahead — meaning predictable revenue. In 2025 Brookfield invested a further ~$1bn, taking its stake to around 38% (with a further ~15% held by Qatar's QIA).
A stable, contracted hydro asset — the base of predictable cash flow in the power portfolio.
A Colombian hydro operator: 14 plants, with most of the output sold under long contracts
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.1.b: Onshore and offshore wind farms: operating plants plus an enormous development pipeline. The main source of future capacity growth against demand for electricity.
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.1.c: A developer and operator of onshore wind in the US: more than 1,200 MW of operating wind and a project pipeline (wind/solar/storage) of more than 22,000 MW across 24 states. Brookfield controls the company, bought in 2022 in a package with Standard Solar for around $1.5bn.
A large US development pipeline — fuel for future growth in clean generation.
>1,200 MW of wind operating, a pipeline of >22,000 MW across 24 states
A US developer of onshore wind, solar and storage

A Polish company that builds and operates onshore wind, solar and offshore wind farms. Brookfield owns around 51% (alongside Mansa Investments; the first 22.8% was bought in 2021). The ~€6.3bn financing of its offshore project is the largest in the history of Brookfield's power business.
An entry point into European offshore wind; a record-sized project financing.
Brookfield's largest offshore project ever (~€6.3bn of financing)
A Polish producer of wind (onshore and offshore) and solar
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.2.b: Utility-scale solar plants: several GW operating and under construction, with tens of GW in development. The fastest-growing form of generation by pipeline.
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.2.c: A developer of utility-scale solar plants and storage systems: around 3 GW operating and in construction plus a project pipeline of ~23 GW across 9-12 countries. Brookfield owns 100% (having bought out KKR's stake in 2023). In February 2026 the company was valued at more than €4bn, and Brookfield is exploring a sale.
A monetisation candidate: valued at more than €4bn, with Brookfield considering a sale.
Spain, US, Italy, Australia and others
~3 GW operating or in construction, a ~23 GW pipeline
A global developer of large solar plants and storage

A developer of solar and wind projects in the US (formerly called National Grid Renewables): more than 2 GW operating, around 1 GW in construction and a project pipeline of more than 20 GW. Controlled by Brookfield Asset Management and partners.
Another large US pipeline against rising demand for electricity.
>2 GW operating, ~1 GW in construction, a pipeline of >20 GW
A US solar and wind developer (formerly National Grid Renewables)
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.3.b: Battery storage and multi-technology platforms that smooth the uneven output of wind and solar, plus the world's largest corporate contract to supply clean power to Microsoft's data centres.
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.3.c: A French company that builds and operates solar, wind and storage plants, with particularly strong positions in Australia. Brookfield and co-investors (Temasek, CalPERS) bought control in December 2024 and took the stake to ~97.7% after a March 2025 offer, delisting it from Euronext Paris. The deal was worth around €6.1bn (the 53.12% stake cost ~€3.25bn).
One of the largest value drivers in power: a recent major acquisition extending the clean generation portfolio against demand for electricity.
a solar/wind/storage portfolio in France, Australia and Finland
A French producer of solar, wind and storage; a large portfolio in Australia and Europe

A framework agreement to supply more than 10.5 GW of new clean power capacity to Microsoft across 2026-2030 in the US and Europe — the world's largest corporate renewable energy contract. It is delivered through the BEP platform's plants. This is not an ownership stake but a long-term contract to sell electricity.
A direct link between Brookfield's clean power and the AI demand of a hyperscale cloud player.
A contract to supply more than 10.5 GW of clean power to Microsoft across 2026-2030
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.4.b: The Westinghouse nuclear business: fuel, plant servicing and new AP1000 reactors. The segment's main AI exposure and a candidate for a large re-rating in a possible IPO.
port.brookfield.sectors.3.subsectors.4.c: One of the world's largest suppliers of nuclear fuel, plant servicing and new AP1000 reactors. Brookfield (through the BEP power platform) and Cameco bought it in November 2023 for $7.9bn: 51% to Brookfield and partners, 49% to Cameco. In October 2025 it became the basis of a ≥$80bn reactor-building partnership with the US government; in June 2026 the US Department of Energy issued a conditional commitment for a loan of up to $17.5bn.
The main AI exposure and a candidate for a large re-rating: an IPO at a valuation of ≥$30bn would be several times the $7.9bn entry price (the trigger runs to January 2029).
global nuclear services plus the AP1000 reactor fleet
A nuclear business: fuel, servicing and AP1000 reactors for plants worldwide
port.brookfield.sectors.4.name: Infrastructure
port.brookfield.sectors.4.plain: Brookfield owns the economy's physical infrastructure: data centres and communications towers, railways and ports, gas pipelines and utility networks. Almost all the income is regulated or contracted.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.0.b: Data centres, telecom towers and fibre worldwide — Brookfield's main exposure to growth in computing and AI. The fastest-growing segment: FFO +46% over the year.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.0.c: Compass builds large data centre campuses to order for the cloud giants. Brookfield owns it jointly with the Ontario Teachers' pension fund through a consortium. It is one of the group's main bets on AI infrastructure.
Direct AI exposure: demand for compute pulls new campus construction along with it and raises the asset's value.
a JV with Ontario Teachers (the exact stake is not disclosed)
A developer of large data centres for cloud and hyperscale tenants

Centersquare is the combined Evoque and Cyxtera assets: around 80 data centres where companies rent racks and space for their own equipment. Brookfield controls the business and funds its expansion itself — in October 2025 it announced a $1bn programme from its own resources.
A large operating data centre platform in the US — the core of the digital segment and a candidate for further growth against AI demand.
~80 sites, >500 MW of operating capacity plus ~200 MW coming
A network of colocation data centres (Evoque and Cyxtera combined)

Data4 is a European platform of roughly 31 data centres across several countries. Brookfield controls it through a consortium. It gives the group an operating base to grow on in the European computing market.
European exposure to AI and cloud demand; a platform for further build-out.
DCI is a Brookfield-controlled data centre platform in Asia-Pacific, chiefly in Australia. It gives the group an entry point into the fast-growing Asian computing market.
Exposure to AI and cloud demand across Asia-Pacific.
A data centre operator in Asia-Pacific
the region's leading data centre operator
Ascenty is Latin America's largest data centre platform, owned by Brookfield jointly and equally with America's Digital Realty. It serves demand for computing in Brazil and neighbouring countries.
Exposure to digital growth in South America's emerging markets.
the region's leading data centre operator
A Latin American data centre platform (a JV with Digital Realty)

GD Towers is Deutsche Telekom's mobile tower estate: more than 40,000 sites across Germany and Austria. Brookfield and its partner DigitalBridge bought 51% at an enterprise value of €17.5bn for the whole business; Deutsche Telekom kept 49%. It is one of the largest telecom infrastructure deals in Europe.
The largest asset in the digital segment by disclosed price: steady rental payments from a telecom operator under long-term contracts.
a stake in the DigitalBridge/Brookfield consortium (51% jointly; DT retained 49%)
Deutsche Telekom's tower network in Germany and Austria
Summit Digitel is a large Indian telecom tower portfolio in which Brookfield holds around 17%. The towers are leased to mobile operators under long-term contracts.
Exposure to the fast-growing Indian telecom market, with steady rental payments.
A large telecom tower portfolio in India
Crest Digitel is an Indian portfolio of telecom towers and in-building connectivity solutions, with Brookfield holding around 17%. It complements the group's digital infrastructure in India.
Additional exposure to Indian telecom infrastructure.
a portfolio of towers and in-building solutions
Telecom towers and in-building solutions in India

A long-haul fibre network in the US, acquired in the third quarter of 2025. Brookfield does not disclose the brand name. Fibre is the carrier infrastructure that moves data between data centres and cities.
It completes the digital infrastructure chain: the data transmission links behind rising traffic.
A long-haul fibre network in the US
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.0.s: ~1.3 GW operating plus 1.1 GW in construction
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.1.b: Railways, ports, toll roads and containers — the infrastructure the economy's goods physically pass through. The largest infrastructure segment by revenue.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.1.c: Triton is the world's largest marine container fleet (around 7.6m TEU equivalent), leased to shipping lines. Brookfield took the company private in 2023 and controls it outright. The revenue is rental payments from the world's container fleet.
A key value driver in the transport segment: global exposure to trade, with long lease contracts.
The world's largest owner and lessor of marine containers

VLI is Brazil's largest integrated logistics business: around 8,000 km of railway plus nine inland and seven port terminals. Brookfield holds roughly 26.5%. The country's commodity and agricultural exports move through this network.
A key node in Brazil's export logistics — large-scale regulated and contracted infrastructure.
~8,000 km of rail, 9 inland and 7 port terminals

Arc Infrastructure runs the Western Australian rail network — around 5,500 km of track leased from the state on a long-term basis. Brookfield owns 100%. The network serves the state's resource exports.
Full control of a large freight rail network on a long lease — stable cash flow.
The Western Australian rail network, held on a long lease

Genesee & Wyoming operates many short-line and regional railways, mostly in the US. Brookfield holds around 9% of the economics but ~72% of the votes, so it runs the company. It is a network of lines connecting industrial customers to the trunk railways.
Management control of a large US freight rail network.
a ~9% economic stake, ~72% of the votes
An operator of regional and short-line railways
Arteris operates a network of toll motorways in Brazil, with Brookfield holding around 50%. The revenue is tolls, tied to traffic and tariff agreements.
Exposure to Brazilian traffic with tariffs linked to inflation.
A toll road network in Brazil
Two toll motorways in India, in each of which Brookfield holds around 29%. The revenue is tolls under long-term concessions.
Additional exposure to Indian road traffic.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.2.b: Gas pipelines, gas storage and gas processing — regulated infrastructure that transports and processes hydrocarbons under long-term tariffs and contracts.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.2.c: Inter Pipeline is a large Canadian midstream business: natural gas liquids pipelines, gas processing plants and the Heartland petrochemical complex in Alberta. Brookfield controls ~56%. The revenue comes from transporting and processing hydrocarbons.
A controlling stake in a major Canadian pipeline system — the segment's core asset.
NGL pipelines, gas processing, the Heartland Petrochemical Complex
A Canadian pipeline and gas processing business
NGPL is one of the largest interstate gas trunk pipeline systems in the US. Brookfield holds around 50%. It transports gas to key markets, including the Chicago hub, under regulated tariffs.
Half of one of the main US gas trunk lines — a steady regulated stream.
a major interstate gas trunk line
One of the largest interstate gas transmission systems in the US

NTS is the key trunk gas pipeline system across south-eastern Brazil (acquired by a consortium from Petrobras in 2017 for ~$5.2bn for 90%). Brookfield holds ~31% of the economics but ~92% of the votes and runs the asset. It carries gas to the country's largest industrial centres.
Management control of Brazil's main gas artery, on regulated tariffs.
trunk gas pipelines across south-eastern Brazil
a ~31% economic stake, ~92% of the votes
A trunk gas pipeline system across south-eastern Brazil
NorthRiver Midstream gathers and processes natural gas in Western Canada; Brookfield's stake is around 29%. It serves producer customers under long-term contracts.
Contracted cash flow from servicing Canadian gas production.
A gas gathering and processing system in Western Canada
PIPL (the former East-West Pipeline) is a trunk gas pipeline in India, with Brookfield holding around 21%. It transports gas across several states under contract.
Contracted exposure to Indian gas transit.
A trunk gas pipeline in India (the former East-West Pipeline)
Warwick is an underground natural gas storage facility in Canada, with Brookfield holding around 25%. Storage earns income from balancing seasonal gas supply and demand.
It completes the gas chain: income from storage and balancing the market.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.3.b: Regulated electricity and gas networks plus subscription-based home energy services — infrastructure with predictable income tied to tariffs and subscription fees.
port.brookfield.sectors.4.subsectors.3.c: Enercare rents water heaters, heating and air conditioning systems to households and services them. Brookfield holds around 26%. The revenue is recurring consumer subscription payments.
Stable consumer cash flow with predictably recurring payments.
rental of water heaters, HVAC and similar
Renting home energy equipment to consumers

HomeServe sells households subscriptions to repair and maintain their home systems. Brookfield holds around 26% in North America and 25% in Europe (a 2023 deal worth ~$1.2bn). The revenue is recurring subscription payments.
Subscription cash flow from home services across two continents.
subscriptions for home repair and maintenance
Subscription home repair and maintenance services

AusNet is a regulated electricity and gas transmission and distribution network in the Australian state of Victoria. Brookfield holds a minority stake of around 8% in a consortium. The revenue is set by the regulator.
Exposure to a regulated utility base with predictable tariff income.
electricity and gas transmission and distribution
A regulated electricity and gas network in the state of Victoria
port.brookfield.sectors.5.name: Operating businesses
port.brookfield.sectors.5.plain: Brookfield takes control of operating companies — manufacturing, services, car dealership software, lotteries — improves them and sells them on at a higher price over time.
port.brookfield.sectors.5.subsectors.0.b: Manufacturers that lead their niches: car batteries, trailer components, electric heat tracing systems, laboratory consumables. The largest and most mature group in the operating portfolio.
port.brookfield.sectors.5.subsectors.0.c: The world leader in advanced low-voltage automotive starter batteries: its batteries sit in roughly one car in three on the planet. Carved out of Johnson Controls in 2019. Brookfield holds a ~30% economic stake, with the rest held by co-investor partners (CDPQ and Brookfield's institutional funds).
The largest and most mature company in this group, and a clear candidate for monetisation (a sale or an IPO).
bbu.brookfield.com / the Q1 2026 letter / the 2019 press release
Car batteries — fitted in one car in three worldwide

A manufacturer of engineered components (axles, chassis, brakes) for trailers, recreational vehicles (RVs) and towable equipment. The leader in its core products across North America, Europe and Australia. Brookfield owns ~88% after selling a ~12% stake into an evergreen fund in July 2025.
A large industrial business with leading positions — a monetisation candidate as it grows.
the market leader in North America, Europe and Australia
Components and assemblies for trailers, RVs and towable equipment

The leader in electric heat tracing — cable-based heating for pipes and equipment. Carved out of nVent Electric and renamed Chemelex. The deal closed on 30.01.2025 at an enterprise value of $1.65bn. Brookfield controls it alongside institutional partners and CPP Investments.
A recent acquisition (a carve-out from nVent) — value is created through the separation and operational improvement.
Electric heat tracing systems for pipes and equipment

A manufacturer and distributor of specialty consumables and test equipment for diagnostics, environmental and life science laboratories. The deal closed on 28.05.2025 at an enterprise value of $1.34bn. Brookfield controls it with institutional partners and CDPQ.
A recent acquisition in the durable laboratory consumables segment.
Consumables and equipment for laboratories (diagnostics, environmental, biology)
port.brookfield.sectors.5.subsectors.1.b: Service businesses with durable recurring revenue: mission-critical subscription software for car dealerships, and Canada's largest private mortgage insurer.
port.brookfield.sectors.5.subsectors.1.c: Mission-critical software for car dealerships and manufacturers across the US and Canada — a dealership management system (accounting, sales, servicing). Brookfield owns ~93% after selling ~7% into its own evergreen fund in July 2025.
One of the key value drivers — durable subscription software with high customer switching costs.
Software for running car dealerships (accounting, sales, servicing)

Canada's largest private residential mortgage insurer (formerly Genworth MI Canada). In 2025 premiums on new insurance rose 26% year on year. Brookfield owns almost 100% after buying in the balance in 2020.
A cash-generative, profitable business, but sensitive to the Canadian housing market and interest rates.
~C$1.6bn — paid to buy in the balance in 2020
port.brookfield.sectors.5.subsectors.2.b: Services to industrial and infrastructure sites: lottery technology, modular building rental, work-access services on construction sites, and construction contracting (being exited).
port.brookfield.sectors.5.subsectors.2.c: The world leader in lottery technology: terminals, instant games and draw management systems. Carved out as Scientific Games' lottery division in 2022. Brookfield controls the business alongside institutional partners (its own share is not disclosed separately).
A regulated, protected business with stable cash flows — another monetisation candidate.
Lottery technology — terminals, instant tickets, systems

The leader in work-access services (scaffolding, hoists, insulation, coatings) for industrial and infrastructure sites. Brookfield owns ~95% at platform level after selling ~5% into an evergreen fund (July 2025); it originally entered with a ~45% stake in 2019.
A cyclical services business tied to industrial turnarounds and construction.
Work-access services at industrial sites — scaffolding, insulation, coatings

The leader in renting modular buildings and temporary space (to industry, construction and the public sector) across Europe and Asia-Pacific. Brookfield and institutional partners control 100% of the business (Brookfield's own share is not disclosed).
An asset-fleet rental business — stable cash flow.

port.brookfield.sectors.6.name: Credit
port.brookfield.sectors.6.plain: Brookfield is one of the world's largest lenders: through Oaktree and the credit firms it has acquired, it lends to businesses and earns on the interest and on fees for managing other people's money.
port.brookfield.sectors.6.subsectors.0.b: Credit firms bought into the platform: Oaktree at the core (distressed and opportunistic debt), surrounded by niche specialists (NAV lending, aircraft leasing, mortgages). The main source of Brookfield's share of fund profits.
port.brookfield.sectors.6.subsectors.0.c: The famous credit firm (founded by Howard Marks) specialising in lending to companies in difficult and complex situations, where others are afraid to put up money. It manages $223bn. Brookfield owns 100% after buying in the last 26% in 2025. It is the heart of the credit business: a whole set of acquired credit firms has grown out of it.
The main source of Brookfield's share of fund profits: $44.7bn of capital on which Brookfield earns its share of the profits (carry).
A lender to distressed and complex situations — the core of the whole credit platform

A firm that lends against the value of private equity fund portfolios — that is, it lends to managers against their assets without forcing them to sell stakes. The leader of this narrow segment; bought by Oaktree in March 2022. Its flagship fund closed at $7.5bn (Q1 2026 alone added $2.5bn) — the largest such strategy in the market.
A growing niche: the largest inflow of new capital into credit last quarter went precisely here.
The leader in lending against private equity fund portfolio values (NAV lending)

A credit firm specialising in lending against real assets — principally aircraft (aviation leasing) and other specialty finance. In September 2024 Brookfield bought 51% of its future management fees for $1.5bn.
It adds credit secured on physical assets to the platform, rather than only on corporate cash flows.
Lending against real assets — aircraft and specialty finance
A residential mortgage and consumer credit company: it originates the loans itself and manages them itself (vertical integration). Brookfield took control in October 2025.
It extends the credit platform into US retail mortgages and consumer lending.
Residential mortgage and consumer credit, with its own origination

A well-known US manager working in bonds and structured credit (securities backed by pools of loans). Oaktree has held a minority stake of around 20% since 2009 — a financial participation rather than control.
A long-standing minority link that broadens reach in the bond market.
A manager of bonds and structured credit
port.brookfield.sectors.6.subsectors.1.b: The platform's largest credit funds: Oaktree's opportunistic debt, direct lending into large deals, and NAV lending. The main generator of future fees and carry.
port.brookfield.sectors.6.subsectors.1.c: Oaktree's main fund, which buys debt and lends to companies in difficulty, expecting to earn on their recovery. It closed in February 2025 with $16bn of investor commitments — money investors have pledged to provide when the fund calls it; more than $7bn is already invested or reserved.
The newest and largest credit fund — the main generator of future fees and carry.
The flagship fund lending to distressed companies

A direct lending fund: it makes senior secured loans of $500m and above to large companies (with EBITDA of $100m and above) being bought by private equity funds. Launched in February 2023 with a $10bn capital target. "Senior secured" means that in a bankruptcy such a lender is repaid first.
Exposure to the fast-growing market for direct lending into large deals.
Direct lending to large companies behind private equity deals
port.brookfield.sectors.6.subsectors.2.b: Credit funds for a broad investor base, obliged to disclose their largest positions — the only public window into the platform's actual credit portfolio. Predominantly senior secured floating-rate debt.
port.brookfield.sectors.6.subsectors.2.c: A credit fund for a broad investor base (a non-traded BDC) that makes private loans to companies — more than 92.7% of it senior secured floating-rate debt, the least risky layer, with interest that rises with rates. Assets of $7.0bn (at 31.03.2026); it raised around $1.7bn in 2025.
One of the few funds on the platform obliged to publish its largest positions — a window into the actual credit portfolio.
$7.0bn of assets; more than 92.7% senior secured debt
A retail credit fund making senior secured private loans

A listed (NASDAQ-traded) credit fund lending to 163 companies: 85% senior secured debt (84% first lien, repaid first in a bankruptcy) and 91% floating rate. Net asset value per share is $15.69. Assets of $2.8bn at 31.03.2026.
A listed, liquid slice of the credit platform with disclosed positions.
A listed credit fund: loans to 163 companies, mostly senior debt
port.brookfield.summary: Brookfield earns in two ways: (1) it manages nearly $1T of other people's money for a fee — its largest and most valuable segment — plus a future share of its funds' profits; (2) it owns real assets itself — power plants, data centres, pipelines, roads, offices, hotels — and an insurance business that generates a continuous stream of cash. Today the money genuinely flows in two directions: into credit (through Oaktree, the largest segment by size) and into power and data centres against AI demand.
